# Governance: permissions, budgets, audit

URL: https://eucowork.ai/en/governance

Governance: permissions, budgets, audit | EU Cowork AI
-
-
-
-
-
-
-
-
-
-
-
-
-
-
Skip to content
- Home
- Governance
Governance
Governance: who may do what, and what it costs
In EU Cowork AI it is not the model that decides whether an access is allowed, but a chain of rules that is checked before every tool call. Permissions reach down to individual tools, every call is logged, and consumption is visible before it turns into an invoice.
In brief
- Access to connected systems is decided by the MCP gateway ahead of the model, not by the model itself.
- Permissions reach down to individual tools: allow reading invoices, deny reading payroll data, within the same connected system.
- The permission check follows the order individual user, role, group, server default. The first matching rule wins.
- Every tool call through the gateway, every admin action and every sign-in is logged and can be exported as CSV.
- Consumption is reported per person, group and model in tokens and euros and charged against a shared monthly budget.
On this page
- Why an AI platform needs its own permission management
- Where users, roles and groups come from
- Permissions down to tool level
- Audit: every access traceable
- Making costs visible and capping them
- Approving agents instead of banning them
- Frequently asked questions
Why an AI platform needs its own permission management
An AI platform needs its own permission management because a chat window without rules passes every question on to every connected system. Once the AI is connected to a company system, the question is no longer whether someone may chat, but which records the AI may read on that person’s behalf.
A ban only displaces usage, it does not end it
Anyone without an approved route takes the next best one. A ban shifts usage into private accounts with public providers, where neither contract nor log nor right to erasure applies. Company data then ends up in a service that nobody in your organisation administers and whose processing you cannot document.
The countermeasure that works is an approved route that is better than the private one. But it has to make four things controllable, otherwise you are merely shifting the risk inwards:
- Which people may use the platform at all, and through which sign-in.
- Which connected systems and which individual tools are open to a person.
- What actually happened, verifiable and exportable.
- What operation costs, itemised and cappable, before the invoice arrives.
These four control points are exactly the areas of the EU Cowork AI admin panel: user management, access rules, audit and consumption.
Where users, roles and groups come from
You maintain users, roles and groups in the admin panel or take them from Entra ID. A role bundles functional permissions, that is, what someone may do in the interface. A group bundles people for access and budget rules. The two can be combined independently.
Local accounts
Entra ID via OIDC, configurable per instance
SCIM planned
Local users and connection to Entra ID
Without an identity provider, EU Cowork AI works with local accounts: invitation by link, with the invited person setting their own password. Sign-in via Entra ID or another OIDC provider is supported by the platform and set up for your instance. Once it is in place, everyone signs in via OIDC, the account is created on first sign-in, and the group and role claims from the sign-in token are mapped onto your groups in EU Cowork AI.
Revocation therefore happens at the front door: anyone deactivated in Entra ID can no longer get in and thereby loses all access, including to the connected systems. Automatic provisioning and deprovisioning of accounts via SCIM is planned, but not available today.
What a role defines, and what a group defines
A role governs functional permissions in the platform, for example whether someone may build agents, use web search or open the admin panel. A group governs which data and tools someone reaches and which budget their consumption is charged to.
The three levels of user management and what you use them for.
Level
Governs
Typical example
User
Individual exception, stronger than any general rule
One person additionally gets access to a tool
Role
Functional permissions in the interface
Only a privileged role may create agents
Group
Access to systems, tools and budget
The Accounting group sees the invoice tools
Invitation, assignment, deactivation
An invitation goes out by email or link and can already carry the target group with it. Membership is applied as soon as the invited person has completed registration. That way nobody starts in a permission-less limbo, and you do not have to add anything after each registration.
There are two ways to end access. Blocking keeps the account but refuses sign-in. Deleting removes the account, conversations and search index entries; a data export for the person concerned is possible beforehand, so that both access requests and erasure requests are served.
Permissions down to tool level
Tool calls run through the MCP gateway, a component between the chat and the connected system. For the requesting person, the gateway checks whether the server and the specific tool are allowed, records the decision and forwards the call only if it is approved. Blocked tools do not appear in the user’s tool list; after a permission change this takes effect with a short delay. The actual barrier is the check on every single call.
Systems are connected via MCP, the open standard for tool access by AI models. The gateway sits in front of it so that approval is decided centrally per person, role and group instead of being scattered across the connected system. Which systems can be connected and which ones are prepared is described on the Integrations page; permissions without tools are moot.
The example: reading invoices yes, reading payroll no
A connected ERP does not offer the AI a single door, but many individual tools: search invoices, read customer data, read payroll data, write records. The Accounting group is granted the invoice tools, while the payroll tools remain reserved for HR. Same server, different tools, decided separately.
Beneath that lies a second boundary. If EU Cowork AI signs in to your ERP with the identity of the respective person, that system’s own access rules remain decisive: anyone who may only see certain records there sees no more through the AI either. If the connection runs through a shared service account, the gateway is the only enforcement point, and the tool selection then has to be cut correspondingly tight.
Permissions inside a tool, that is on individual fields or rows, are not enforced by EU Cowork AI itself. That is the job of the connected system’s permission management. A tool with a broad range of functions should therefore either not be released at all or only to a group that is allowed to see the data anyway.
The rule chain: user before role before group before default
Permissions are evaluated in a fixed order: individual user, then role, then group, then the server default. The first matching rule decides, and no further search follows. Every decision is therefore explainable, and a one-off approval needs no special role. The fact that permissions apply per individual tool is the distinguishing feature in the comparison with other platforms .
Order of the permission check in the gateway. The first match wins.
Order
Rule
What it is intended for
1. User
Exception for a single person
Time-limited approval without softening the group rule
2. Role
Applies to all accounts with this role
Baseline set-up according to function in the company
3. Group
Applies to all members of the group
Department or project scope, also from Entra ID
4. Server default
Default for all remaining requests
Basic stance per connected system, ideally deny
What happens when no rule applies
If no user, role or group rule applies, the default of the respective server decides. Set this default to deny immediately after connecting a system and then release individual groups deliberately. That way a freshly connected system cannot accidentally let anyone see more than intended.
If the permission check itself fails, for example because the rule database is unreachable, the gateway denies the call instead of letting it through. A malfunction therefore leads to an error message in the chat, not to open access. A read-only switch per server that blocks all writing tools at once is planned.
Audit: every access traceable
Every tool call through the gateway is recorded with time, person, target system, tool and decision, including denied ones. In addition, the platform keeps a continuously chained log of admin actions, sign-ins and permission changes. Both logs reside in your own instance and can be exported as CSV.
What is logged
- Tool calls to connected systems, with the decision taken, allowed or denied.
- Sign-ins to the platform and to the admin panel.
- Changes to roles, groups, permissions and access rules.
- Changes to the configuration of the instance.
- Creating, inviting, blocking and deleting accounts.
The audit log is a record of access, not a transcript of conversations. It answers who called which tool on which system and when. The conversations themselves are stored separately in your instance’s database and are subject to the configured retention period.
How long it is kept and where it can be exported
The logs stay in your instance, in your database. When you self-host, they never leave your infrastructure. The export is CSV, filtered by period and person, and can therefore be handed straight to an audit, to the legal department or to an audit tool.
The log of admin actions is chained: every entry carries a checksum over the preceding one, and a built-in check reports when the chain no longer adds up. Removing individual entries after the fact is thus noticed. For conversations the retention period is configurable; expired content is removed together with its search index.
Making costs visible and capping them
Consumption is recorded per person, group, model and day and reported both in tokens and in euros. A shared monthly budget caps the total for the whole organisation; an optional monthly limit per person caps individual accounts. Once a budget is used up, a soft block takes effect.
Consumption per person, group and model
The admin panel shows consumption in euros, broken down by person, by model and by day, along with the individual requests including model and timestamp. Amounts and breakdowns are visible to administrators; end users only get a note in the chat when the budget is exhausted. This takes cost pressure out of everyday work while keeping the figures visible where they belong.
Prices are stored per model so that the evaluation is not based on an approximation. This matters more than it sounds: for the same conversation, a frugal model and a very large one differ by a multiple in cost. A curated model selection is therefore part of cost control, not just a question of usability.
A shared monthly budget instead of individual limits
The monthly budget applies to the organisation as a whole, not per head. The reason is practical: consumption is never distributed evenly. Heavy users would get stuck on a rigid individual limit while other people’s allowances expire unused. A shared pot balances that out without anyone having to readjust limits.
For outliers there is also an optional monthly limit per person. It is switched off until you set it and is enforced strictly in the same reconciliation run as the overall budget. Typical use: a single account that sends automated requests should not drain the shared pot on its own.
A soft block instead of a silent overrun
Once the budget is used up, the soft block takes effect: the next request is refused, with a note in the chat instead of silently continuing to bill. A response already in progress is still completed. The admin can raise the budget at any time, after which operation resumes immediately. Without such an increase, no additional charge arises.
The reconciliation between recorded consumption and budget runs every minute, and the advance estimate of a request does not know its exact length. A single response can therefore still run slightly over the limit. This is a soft block that prevents runaway costs, not a second-by-second advance reservation.
Approving agents instead of banning them
Agents and skills are released in a curated way, neither allowed across the board nor banned across the board. Ordinary accounts use the agents assigned to them and never see the agent builder. A privileged role creates and shares agents, and the admin releases skills per person.
The reason lies in the permissions: an agent comes with a fixed set of instructions and a set of tools. If everyone could build and share their own agents, a second, uncontrolled distribution channel would appear alongside your rule chain. The gateway’s permission check would still apply to every call, but the overview of who works with what would be lost.
In practice this results in a few well-maintained agents per group instead of many half-finished ones: one for drafting quotes, one for evaluations from the ERP, one for internal knowledge search.
Frequently asked questions
How do we stop employees from entering company data into public AI tools?
By offering an approved route that is more convenient than the private detour. EU Cowork AI gives you your own instance with your accounts, your systems and your log. A mere ban only shifts usage into private accounts that you can neither inspect nor switch off.
Can the AI see payroll data if we connect our ERP?
Only if you release the corresponding tool. The connection consists of individual tools, and each of them is released or denied separately. Reading invoices can be allowed while reading payroll data remains blocked for the same person. In addition, your ERP’s access rules continue to apply.
How do we control which employee may see which data?
Through groups and per-tool rules. You create groups or take them from Entra ID and release to each group the tools it needs. The check runs in the order individual user, role, group, server default, with the first matching rule deciding.
How do we cap AI costs per employee?
Through a shared monthly budget for the organisation and an optional monthly limit per person. Consumption is reported per person, group and model in tokens and euros. Once a budget is exhausted, the next request is refused instead of quietly continuing. The admin can raise it at any time.
What evidence do we get for an audit?
A log of all tool calls with time, person, target system, tool and decision, plus a chained log of admin actions, sign-ins and permission changes. Both can be exported as CSV and stay in your instance. Whether that satisfies your specific documentation obligation is something to clarify with your legal advisers.
Do we need Entra ID for governance to work?
No. Roles, groups and rules work fully with local accounts that you create by invitation. Sign-in via Entra ID is supported and set up per instance; it saves you duplicate maintenance because accounts are created on first sign-in and group claims are taken from the sign-in token. Automatic provisioning via SCIM is planned.
Settle governance before the rollout
Request access now. Because demand is high, we allocate access to the managed Swiss instance in stages, and we set up permissions, logging and budget together with you before the first department starts.
Get started
Self-host

# Integrations: ERP and systems via MCP

URL: https://eucowork.ai/en/integrationen

Integrations: ERP and systems via MCP | EU Cowork AI
-
-
-
-
-
-
-
-
-
-
-
-
-
-
Skip to content
- Home
- Integrations
Connectors and MCP
Integrations: connecting EU Cowork AI to your systems
Five connections are prepared and ready to use without any development work: your ERP, SharePoint from Microsoft 365, web search with source references, the generation of Excel, Word and PDF files, and your own documents as a knowledge base. They are activated and released during setup in the admin panel. Every further system with a programming interface is connected via the Model Context Protocol.
In brief
- Five connections are prepared and are activated and configured per customer: your ERP, SharePoint and Microsoft 365, web search with source references, file generation for Excel, Word and PDF, and your company documents as a knowledge base.
- The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard. Any system with a programming interface can be connected without tying you to a single vendor.
- For widely used tools such as HubSpot, Slack, Jira, Confluence, Notion, Linear, GitHub, Sentry, PostgreSQL, Stripe and Google Drive, ready-made MCP servers exist in the open ecosystem.
- Connections with a shared service account run through the MCP gateway. There, permissions apply per server and per individual tool, evaluated in the order user, role, group, server default.
- If the person’s identity is passed through to the target system, for example with SharePoint via the Microsoft account, the target system enforces the permissions itself and its logging applies.
- Every tool call through the gateway lands in the audit log and can be exported. The Outlook add-in is in beta and in internal use today, the Excel add-in is in progress.
On this page
- Which connections are prepared
- What is MCP and why does it matter?
- Connecting any system with a programming interface
- Connected in three steps
- Access stays controlled
- Add-ins for Outlook and Excel
- Frequently asked questions
Which connections are prepared
These five connections need no development work. They are activated and configured during setup in the admin panel and released per person, role or group. What each of them can do is described in the following sections.
ERP connection
The ERP connection brings customers, invoices, projects and hours from your ERP into the chat. Typical everyday questions: “How many hours are booked on project X?” or “Which invoices have been open for more than 30 days?” The answer comes from your real data, not from the model’s training knowledge.
The benefit lies less in looking things up than in chaining steps: an analysis that would otherwise mean export, sorting and formulas comes about in a single sentence and returns as a finished Excel file. Which data is visible in the process is not decided by the model but by the permissions set beforehand.
SharePoint and Microsoft 365
The SharePoint connection searches your document libraries from Microsoft 365 and answers questions from them. Contracts, minutes, quotes and policies stay where they are today. Nothing is copied into a second repository.
Sign-in uses each person’s Microsoft identity. Through the chat, everyone therefore sees exactly the libraries and folders they are allowed to open directly in SharePoint. Existing permissions remain the boundary, without you having to maintain them a second time.
Web search with source references
Web search delivers up-to-date information with a link to the source, so that every statement remains verifiable. Searching runs through a self-operated search instance (SearXNG) that is part of the stack and builds no user profiles. To turn a hit into text that has actually been read, a page-fetching service is included, which we roll out during setup.
To be honest about it: the search queries are passed on to external search engines, without your user identity. The claim “everything stays in Europe” applies to storage and model processing, not to the search query itself. Anyone who does not want external queries switches web search off in the admin panel.
Generating files: Excel, Word and PDF
An instruction such as “Create the monthly report as Excel” produces a real file to download, not a table in the chat window. This applies to analyses in Excel, to reports and letters in Word, and to PDF documents.
The code runs in a sealed-off environment per session, not on your computer; the environment is discarded after the session. An egress proxy with an allow list for network access from this environment is in progress, as is an additionally hardened isolation layer.
Company knowledge as a knowledge base
Your own documents become a searchable knowledge base: manuals, process descriptions, quote templates, minutes. Uploading happens in the chat or centrally by the admin; the answer names the source so that you can check it.
The knowledge base resides on your instance and does not leave it. New employees ask the chat instead of interrupting someone, and recurring questions about internal procedures no longer cost anyone a search through the file share.
What is MCP and why does it matter
MCP stands for Model Context Protocol and is an open standard for how an AI talks to a business application. Instead of programming a separate interface for every combination of AI tool and application, there is one protocol: the application provides an MCP server, and that server tells the AI which tools it may call.
A tool here is a single, named capability: “search records”, “read invoice”, “store file”. Precisely this decomposition is why granting permissions works at a fine-grained level at all. Without named tools there would only be the choice between full system access and none.
The open nature of the standard matters. MCP has been published and is meanwhile supported by many AI applications and vendors. An MCP server that you build for your own system is therefore not an investment in EU Cowork AI, but in your own infrastructure: it keeps working even if you switch the platform on top of it.
For you that means: no lock-in when connecting, no point-to-point interfaces to maintain and ready-made servers from the ecosystem instead of in-house builds. The most common queries about MCP, permissions and costs are answered in the frequently asked questions .
Connecting any system with a programming interface
Any system that has a programming interface can be connected via MCP. For many widely used tools, ready-made MCP servers already exist; for everything else a REST API and a thin server in front of it are enough. Both are registered and released in the admin panel.
Ready-made MCP servers for widely used tools
The following MCP servers come from the open ecosystem around the standard, partly from the vendors themselves and partly from the community. These servers are not part of EU Cowork AI and are not maintained by us. You register them as servers, store the credentials and release the individual tools.
Widely used tools for which ready-made MCP servers exist in the open ecosystem, and what they are typically used for. As of August 2026. Scope of functions and maintenance rest with the respective server.
System
What is possible with it in the chat
HubSpot Look up and add contacts, deals and notes in the CRM.
Slack Search channels and messages and summarise discussions.
Jira Search and create issues and query the status of a sprint.
Confluence Search pages and summarise the content of a space.
Notion Read pages and databases and update entries.
Linear Search and create issues and check ownership.
GitHub Search and assess repositories, issues and pull requests.
Sentry Query error reports and assess clusters by version.
PostgreSQL Query databases read-only and generate analyses from them.
Stripe Look up payments, subscriptions and the status of invoices.
Google Drive Search files and draw on their content for an answer.
Your own systems via REST API
For your own industry solution, the time-tracking system or the warehouse program, a REST API is enough. In front of it comes an MCP server that translates between the protocol and your interface and thereby defines which tools exist at all. The server stays lean because the business logic remains in your system.
A practical note that determines later permission granting: cut the tools finely and unambiguously. A server with the separate tools “read invoices” and “read payroll” can be released cleanly. A single free-form tool that accepts arbitrary database queries cannot be limited sensibly and therefore belongs only in tightly restricted connections.
Connected in three steps
A new connection takes three steps in the admin panel. A newly registered server is reachable immediately, without the installation having to be rolled out again.
- Register the server. Store the address of the MCP server and the credentials in the admin panel. The tools the server offers are detected automatically.
- Define access. Decide per role, group and individual person which tools of this server can be used. Set the server default to “denied”, then only what you deliberately release applies.
- Use and verify. In the gateway’s audit log you see who called which tool on which server and when, and how it was decided.
For the prepared connections the configuration already exists. There it is straight to the question of who may use which tools.
Access stays controlled
Connections through the MCP gateway are checked on every single call. The gateway sits between the AI and the connected server and decides whether the requesting person may use this server and this tool; it writes the decision to the audit log. Where the person’s identity is instead passed through to the target system, for example with SharePoint via the Microsoft account, the target system enforces the permissions itself and its logging applies.
Permissions are evaluated in this order: individual user, then role, then group, and finally the server default. The more specific rule wins. If the check fails technically, access is denied instead of let through.
You maintain roles and groups either locally in the admin panel or take them from Entra ID. Anyone removed from a group there also loses the tool permissions attached to it.
Two ways to connect a system
There are two connection modes, and the choice determines where permissions are enforced. In the first mode the person’s identity is passed through to the target system; in the second a shared service account works behind the gateway.
The two connection modes and where permissions are enforced in each.
Mode
Sign-in to the target system
Who enforces the permissions
Identity passed through
Each person signs in to the target system once themselves.
The target system with its own user permissions. If the connection additionally runs through the gateway, its tool permissions are added.
Service account
One technical account for all users, stored in the gateway.
The gateway alone. Tool permissions are mandatory here, because the target system sees all requests as identical.
Where the target system has its own user accounts, the first mode is the better choice: the permissions of the target system continue to apply unchanged. The second mode suits systems without their own user management; there the gateway is the only checkpoint, and clean tool permissions are mandatory.
How roles, groups, audit log and cost budgets interact in detail is described on the Governance page.
Add-ins for Outlook and Excel
The Outlook add-in is in beta: it runs in internal use with us today and is not yet generally available. It opens as a pane next to the open email and summarises, drafts replies, translates and extracts tasks. The Excel add-in is in progress. The goal remains to make EU Cowork AI usable directly in the mail window and in the spreadsheet, instead of switching between application and browser.
Outlook add-in: beta, in internal use
Excel add-in: in progress
Until then, both run through the browser: paste in emails and spreadsheet excerpts, download generated Excel and Word files. The range of functions is the same, only the route is longer.
Frequently asked questions
What is an MCP server?
An MCP server is a small program that makes an application accessible to AI systems. It speaks the Model Context Protocol, an open standard, and reports to the AI a list of named tools such as “search records” or “store file”. The AI calls these tools instead of accessing the application directly.
Can we connect our ERP without everyone seeing everything?
Yes. Permissions apply per server and per individual tool, not only per system. A tool for reading invoices can be released to accounting while the tool for payroll data remains blocked for everyone except the management. If the user identity is additionally passed through to the ERP, the existing user permissions apply there as well.
What if there is no ready-made MCP server for our system?
Then you build one in front of it, provided your system has a REST API. The server translates between the protocol and the interface and defines which tools exist. The business logic stays in your system. Because MCP is an open standard, this server also keeps working with other AI applications.
Does all data stay in Europe with web search?
No, and we say so deliberately. Storage and model processing remain within Europe, but the search queries themselves are passed on to external search engines. Your user identity is not included. Anyone who does not want that switches web search off in the admin panel.
Is every access to our systems logged?
Yes, for every connection that runs through the MCP gateway. Every tool call is recorded there in the audit log, with time, person, server, tool and the gateway’s decision, including denied calls. The log can be exported and is therefore usable for audits and documentation obligations. Where the person’s identity is passed straight through to the target system, its own logging applies in addition.
Is your system on the list?
Request access now. Tell us which systems you want to connect; that feeds into the order in which we complete connections.

# Self-host an open-source AI platform

URL: https://eucowork.ai/en/self-hosting

Self-host an open-source AI platform | EU Cowork AI
-
-
-
-
-
-
-
-
-
-
-
-
-
-
Skip to content
- Home
- Self-hosting
Self-hosting
Self-host EU Cowork AI
Source code coming soon
EU Cowork AI runs as a Docker Compose stack on a single Ubuntu machine. Two scripts bring the stack up, the software will be released under the MIT licence shortly, and you need neither Kubernetes nor a GPU nor an account with us.
In short
- EU Cowork AI is operated as a Docker Compose stack on an Ubuntu machine, without Kubernetes and without a GPU in the app tier.
- The base stack uses around 0.7 GB of RAM when idle. Budget 1.5 to 2 GB per instance including a dedicated code sandbox.
- Two scripts are enough: setup-server.sh prepares the Ubuntu server, install.sh generates the secrets and starts the stack.
- For 1 to 15 users, three to five instances share one VM with 4 vCPU, 16 GB RAM and an 80 GB disk.
- In concrete terms, the MIT licence means: no seat limit, no mandatory branding, no feature gating, open source code. Self-hosting is free. The source code follows shortly.
On this page
- What you need
- Installation in three steps
- Which services make up the stack
- Three operating models, one architecture
- How updates work and what matters in operation
- One script for backup, restore and migration
- Licence: what MIT means in practice
- Frequently asked questions about self-hosting
What you need
For EU Cowork AI you need an Ubuntu machine with Docker Engine and Compose v2, a DNS record pointing to it and an API key for your model gateway. The stack runs entirely on this single host, because the computing load of the language models sits with the inference provider.
Server and system requirements
The minimum is 2 vCPU, 4 GB RAM, a 40 GB disk and Ubuntu 22.04 LTS. For production use we recommend 4 vCPU, 16 GB RAM and a 200 GB disk on Ubuntu 24.04 LTS; the breakdown by team size is in the table below. The hardened code sandbox additionally requires nested virtualisation.
Memory footprint when idle, measured on the running stack, as at August 2026.
Service
RAM when idle
Chat application (LibreChat) 374 MB
Database (MongoDB) 102 MB
Web search (SearXNG) 65 MB
MCP gateway 33 MB
Search index (Meilisearch) 29 MB
Base stack in total around 0.7 GB
Code sandbox in addition around 0.5 GB
Under load, practically only the memory of the chat application grows, while CPU utilisation stays close to zero. The images take up around 5 to 6 GB once and are shared between instances on the same machine. After that it is mainly the uploads that grow: the first limit in operation is disk space.
Rule of thumb for sizing, derived from the measurements above.
Team size
Recommendation
VM
1 to 15 users
three to five instances on one VM
4 vCPU, 16 GB RAM, 80 GB
15 to 50 users
dedicated VM
4 vCPU, 8 to 16 GB RAM, 100 GB
more than 50 users or a regulated industry
dedicated VM, dedicated host if required
8 vCPU, 32 GB RAM, from 200 GB
What you do not need
- No Kubernetes. Docker Compose is the supported architecture; a Helm chart is not included.
- No GPU for the app tier. GPU hardware is only needed by those who also want to run language models locally.
- No account with us. The installation runs without registration, without a licence key and without a licence server.
- No hyperscaler and no managed database. Any Ubuntu VM will do; database and search index run in the same stack.
Installation in three steps
Installing EU Cowork AI consists of two scripts and one entry in the .env . On a machine where Docker is already running, the first step is not needed.
Step 1: prepare the server
The GitHub repository is coming soon. Anyone who wants to start today can request access to the managed instance via the form . The commands show what the installation looks like afterwards: clone the repository, change into the distribution directory, run the preparation script.
cd distribution
./setup-server.sh
The script is idempotent and installs Docker Engine including Compose v2 from the official Docker source, because the Ubuntu package docker.io does not ship Compose v2. It also sets up log rotation, firewall rules for ports 22, 80 and 443, swap, time zone and automatic security updates. Then log in again once.
Step 2: install the stack
./install.sh --profiles production
The installer checks Docker and Compose v2, creates the .env from the template, generates all secrets, sets up data directories and the sandbox network, pulls the images and starts the stack. The production profile includes the reverse proxy, which obtains the TLS certificate automatically.
Step 3: enter model access
# .env
EUROUTER_API_KEY=<euer-api-key>
docker compose up -d
Without a key the stack still starts, but the chat reports a missing API key. Access is freely selectable, because EU Cowork AI talks to any OpenAI-compatible gateway. EuRouter provides more than 100 models with EU processing under a single access point; alternatively you enter your own endpoint.
Which services make up the stack
The stack consists of one docker-compose.yml ; several services sit behind optional profiles and only start when you switch them on. Every service is a well-known open source project and can be inspected, replaced or switched off individually.
The chat application is based on LibreChat under the MIT licence and provides the interface, accounts, conversations, file uploads and the model connection. EU Cowork AI keeps this part close to upstream so that the project’s security updates remain adoptable.
MongoDB stores conversations, accounts, roles and settings, as a container in the same stack and on your disk. There is no external database service to which content could flow away.
Meilisearch provides full-text search across your own conversations. The index is local and can be rebuilt; Meilisearch telemetry is disabled out of the box.
The RAG API with pgvector is optional and is added through the filesearch profile. The RAG API embeds files that users upload into the chat and returns the relevant passages to the model when it answers.
The MCP gateway sits between the chat application and every connected system and decides per tool call whether it is permitted. Evaluation follows this order: individual user, role, group, server default. Every call is logged, and if the check fails, access is denied.
The admin panel is the interface for users, roles, groups, access rules, audit log and budget. It is part of the stack, listens locally only and is reachable from outside exclusively through the reverse proxy.
The code sandbox executes the code generated by the model, turning a request into a real file you can download. It is placed alongside as its own Compose stack and connected via a dedicated Docker network. Two backends are available: a lightweight one as the default and a hardened one based on a microVM, which requires nested virtualisation on the host. An egress proxy with an allow list is in progress.
SearXNG provides web search from your own stack, without an account at a search service. To be honest about it: SearXNG passes the search terms on to external search engines, without disclosing the user’s identity. Conversations and files do not leave the machine.
Caddy terminates TLS, obtains the certificates automatically as soon as the DNS record points to the machine, and is the only service on ports 80 and 443. Variants are included for operation behind a WAF or with an internal certificate authority.
Three operating models, one architecture
There are three operating models and only one architecture: self-operated, in your cloud, optionally through your IT service provider, or managed by us. The stack is the same in all three cases. The only differences are who holds root, who manages the keys and who runs updates and backups.
Self-operated
You run the machine, hold root, manage your keys and handle updates and backups yourself. The software costs nothing; a support subscription is optional. This model is the benchmark: what an external administrator can bring up in two commands also carries the other models.
In your cloud
EU Cowork AI runs on any Ubuntu VM, in your own data centre just as well as at a Swiss or European cloud provider. There is no tie to a hyperscaler. IT service providers hosting for their customers use the same architecture: one stack per customer.
Managed by us
We take care of installation, updates, backups and monitoring and operate the instance in ISO 27001-certified data centres run by Green in Lupfig, Switzerland. The certificates are held by Green, not by EU Cowork AI; an ISO 27001 certification of EU Cowork AI itself is in progress.
Several instances on one machine
The tenant boundary is the Compose stack, not the VM: each instance has its own database, its own search index, its own uploads, its own secrets, its own Docker network and its own code sandbox. For small teams, three to five instances may therefore share the same VM.
What may be shared are the Docker images and a common reverse proxy. What is never shared are database, uploads, secrets, sandbox network and the model provider’s key: a shared key makes consumption per tenant impossible to attribute, and a shared sandbox network removes the separation exactly where third-party code runs.
How updates work and what matters in operation
Updates are reproducible because the application image is pinned to a digest rather than to a moving tag, and the remaining services run on fixed versions. A release of EU Cowork AI is therefore a tested combination of application image and services, and two instances on the same machine may run different versions.
git pull
./backup.sh backup
./install.sh --migrate
The --migrate option leaves the .env untouched and rebuilds the in-house services. A backup belongs before every update, followed by a short functional test. Rolling back is done via the previous version of the Compose file.
Two things matter in day-to-day operation: the log rotation that setup-server.sh sets up, and disk space with an alert from 70 per cent utilisation. Recurring questions about operation, updates and backups are answered in the frequently asked questions .
One script for backup, restore and migration
A single script covers backup, restore and server migration: backup.sh creates an archive from the database dump, the .env and uploaded files, and restores it as well. A migration is therefore a backup on the old server, copying the archive, and a restore on the new one.
./backup.sh backup # Archiv erzeugen
./backup.sh list # vorhandene Archive
./backup.sh restore <archiv> # ersetzt die Datenbank, fragt vorher nach
The archive contains secrets and conversations and is stored with restrictive file permissions. It never belongs in a repository and never unencrypted in someone else’s cloud. The search index is not backed up, because it can be rebuilt from the database.
The most expensive mistake during a migration is to have the encryption keys regenerated instead of carrying them over from the old .env . All credentials stored in the database then become unreadable. With carried-over values, the migration remains a maintenance window of 15 to 30 minutes.
Two rules from practice: mirror the backup target off the machine and test the restore once.
Licence: what MIT means in practice
Source code coming soon
EU Cowork AI will be released under the MIT licence shortly; the underlying chat application LibreChat is already under it today. Self-hosting is free, from a single user and without registering with us. What that means in detail, and why it is the decisive difference in the comparison with other platforms :
- No seat limit. Whether 3 or 300 people work on the instance makes no difference to the licence.
- No mandatory branding. Name, logo and colours are configuration, including for commercial use.
- No feature gating. Permission management, audit log, budgets and system connections all come from the same open source.
- Open source code. The LibreChat base is publicly viewable today; stack, scripts and services will be published under MIT shortly and will then be viewable, forkable and verifiable instead of resting on a promise.
Commercially, we sustain the model through operation and support, not through licences. That is why the path from managed operation back to self-hosting is open as well: the same architecture, the same archive.
Frequently asked questions about self-hosting
What does it cost to self-host EU Cowork AI?
The software costs nothing. EU Cowork AI will be released under the MIT licence shortly, without a seat limit and without a licence key, and self-hosting is free from a single user. Costs arise outside the software: for the machine, for access to the model provider and for operation.
Do I need a GPU for EU Cowork AI?
No. No GPU is needed for the app tier. The computing load of the language models sits with the inference provider, and CPU utilisation of the stack is close to zero in normal operation. GPU hardware is only needed by those who also want to run language models locally on their own machine.
How many users can one instance support?
For 1 to 15 users, three to five instances share one VM with 4 vCPU, 16 GB RAM and an 80 GB disk. From 15 to 50 users, an instance gets its own VM with 4 vCPU and 8 to 16 GB RAM. Above that, the VM grows accordingly.
Does EU Cowork AI run on Kubernetes?
The supported architecture is Docker Compose on an Ubuntu machine; a Helm chart is not included. At this scale, Kubernetes would be additional operational effort, since the base stack uses around 0.7 GB of RAM when idle. The Compose file still works well as a template.
May I fork EU Cowork AI and roll it out under my own name?
Yes. The MIT licence permits use, modification, distribution and commercial deployment, including under your own name and your own logo. There is no branding clause and no user count above which additional conditions apply. All you have to carry over is the licence text and the copyright notice.
Can I switch between self-hosting and managed operation later on?
Yes, in both directions. Both models use the same architecture, which is why the switch is a migration: create an archive, copy it to the new machine, restore it there. Conversations, accounts, settings and uploads are preserved, provided the encryption keys are carried over.
Prefer to start managed?
If you would rather not operate the stack yourself: we take care of installation, updates, backups and monitoring on Swiss infrastructure. Because demand is high, we allocate access to the managed offering in stages on request.
Get started

# Our vision: making Europe AI-ready

URL: https://eucowork.ai/en/vision

Our vision: making Europe AI-ready | EU Cowork AI
-
-
-
-
-
-
-
-
-
-
-
-
-
-
Skip to content
- Home
- Vision
Vision
Our vision: making Europe's companies AI-ready without loss of control
As a Swiss IT service provider we support companies in their day-to-day operations, and the same question comes up again and again: how do we use AI without giving up control over our data and our costs? The figures show how widespread this hesitation is: in 2025, 20.0 % of EU enterprises with 10 or more employees used AI technologies; among small enterprises the share was 17 % (Eurostat).
In brief
- In 2025, 20.0 % of EU enterprises with 10 or more employees used AI technologies, up from 13.5 % in 2024 (Eurostat, published in December 2025).
- The reasons most frequently cited against adopting AI are a lack of in-house expertise (70.9 %), unclear legal consequences (52.5 %) and data protection concerns (48.8 %); Eurostat survey 2025.
- EU Cowork AI is a thin fork of LibreChat and is published under the MIT licence: no seat minimum, no mandatory branding, free self-hosting from a single user upwards. The licence does not depend on the number of workplaces.
- The offering of Herr Informatik GmbH includes training courses and training materials, from the first prompt through to analyses in Excel and presentations in PowerPoint.
- EU Cowork AI is ready for production use; access to the hosted Swiss instance is allocated in stages on request because demand is high.
On this page
- Why Europe's companies hesitate
- Sovereignty comes from openness
- What we are building
- Training is part of it
- Who is behind EU Cowork AI
- Six principles
- What drives us
- Frequently asked questions
Europe's companies hesitate on AI, and their reasons are rational
In 2025, 20.0 % of EU enterprises with 10 or more employees used AI technologies, up from 13.5 % in 2024. Among small enterprises the share is 17 %. The range across member states runs from 42.0 % in Denmark to 5.2 % in Romania. Source: Eurostat, published on 11 December 2025 .
In Germany, 23 % of enterprises with 10 to 49 employees used AI technologies in 2025; the figure was 36 % for those with 50 to 249 employees and 57 % for those with 250 or more ( Federal Statistical Office of Germany ). The pattern repeats in every statistic: the smaller the company, the rarer the adoption.
The reasons companies give themselves are not hostility to technology but practical obstacles.
Reasons given by EU enterprises against adopting AI technologies. Source: Eurostat, 2025 survey; the basis is enterprises that considered using AI technologies but have not adopted them so far.
Reason
Share of responses
Lack of in-house expertise
70.9 %
Uncertainty about the legal consequences
52.5 %
Concerns about data protection and privacy
48.8 %
Technology assessed as not useful
20.7 %
We read four brakes into this. The first is cost: a price per workplace falls due before any benefit has been created. The second is missing knowledge, not a missing tool. The third is uncertainty about what is permitted and who is liable in case of doubt. The fourth is a lack of trust in services whose operation and data paths nobody inside the company can inspect.
The cost brake takes effect early and quietly. Anyone paying for every additional person grants access to those who are convinced anyway and leaves the rest of the workforce out. Budgets are tight, and a licence per workplace grows with every new hire. How the vendors cut their licences is set out in the comparison of AI platforms .
The trust brake deserves a clear name: the mistrust is directed at products from outside one's own legal jurisdiction, and it grows with distance. A contract with a vendor on another continent can be read, but not verified. Terms can change, in a dispute a foreign court has jurisdiction, and nobody gets insight into actual operations.
This reticence is a sober risk assessment, not resentment. The same companies work with technology from all over the world as a matter of course; they simply do not want to hand accounting, personnel files and customer data to a service they can neither inspect nor leave. Anyone able to run the system themselves does not need that leap of faith in the first place.
Sovereignty comes from openness, not from assurances
Trust in an AI platform cannot be asserted, trust has to be verifiable . That is why EU Cowork AI is published entirely under the MIT licence. The basis is LibreChat, an open-source project with more than 40,000 GitHub stars whose source code is publicly available today. Our own extensions will likewise be released under the MIT licence, in our GitHub repository, coming soon.
At EU Cowork AI, open source means that source code, configuration and data paths are open to inspection, including by your own IT department or an external auditor. No feature is locked behind a different licence, and no part of the system runs as a black box.
At EU Cowork AI, openness also means that you can leave at any time. The same software runs on your own hardware, from a single user upwards, with no seat minimum and no mandatory branding. Anyone who hands operations over to us does so out of convenience, not out of technical necessity.
Telemetry is switched off by default in EU Cowork AI, and customer data does not train any models. Anyone self-hosting keeps all content on their own infrastructure. The hosted variant runs in ISO 27001 certified data centres operated by Green in Lupfig, Switzerland; the certification is held by Green, and a dedicated certification for EU Cowork AI is in progress.
We name one limitation openly: web search forwards queries to external search engines, without user identity. The statement that everything stays in Europe applies to storage and inference, not to the search query itself.
What we are building: an AI coworker that stays in Europe
EU Cowork AI is a browser-based AI platform for companies: language models from many providers through a single point of access, processed in Europe, connected to the company's systems instead of being yet another isolated chat window. Files such as Excel, Word and PDF are created in the chat and can be downloaded.
At EU Cowork AI, permissions, costs and traceability are part of the product and not of an add-on package. The connection to the ERP system runs through the MCP gateway, which enforces permissions down to the individual tool: read invoices yes, salaries no. Consumption is visible per user, group and model and can be capped against a shared monthly budget that blocks softly once exhausted instead of quietly running on.
The full feature overview is on the home page , the technical details on running it yourself on the self-hosting page. Access to the hosted Swiss instance is allocated in stages on request because demand is high.
Technology alone does not make a company AI-ready
The most frequently cited reason against AI is a lack of expertise, not a lack of software: 70.9 % of EU enterprises that considered using AI technologies but have not adopted them so far give this reason (Eurostat, 2025 survey). The offering of Herr Informatik GmbH therefore includes training courses and training materials that take employees from the first prompt through to robust analyses.
First steps
Asking questions in a way that produces a usable answer. Drafting texts, summarising documents, checking translations. And recognising when an answer needs evidence.
In everyday work
Handing recurring tasks to curated role agents. Using company knowledge as a knowledge base. Web search with source references for answers that have to be current.
Advanced
Producing analyses from raw data in Excel, building presentations in PowerPoint, retrieving figures from the ERP system as far as the individual's permissions allow.
We train people to verify results rather than trust them. An analysis nobody can recalculate is not progress. Source references, traceable intermediate steps and the clearly stated limits of the tool therefore belong in every training session.
Enabling does not mean replacing. The tasks an AI usefully takes on in a company are routine: summarising, formatting, preparing, looking up. The decision about what happens with the result stays with the employees.
The training materials are created alongside the product and grow with every rollout. We agree scope and format with the company, from an introduction for all employees through to in-depth support for individual teams.
Behind EU Cowork AI stands Herr Informatik GmbH
EU Cowork AI is a product of Herr Informatik GmbH, Klosterzelgstrasse 1a, 5210 Windisch, Switzerland. The company is entered in the commercial register of the Canton of Aargau, UID CHE-112.168.836. Management: Naveein Theivendran and Josip Corković.
Herr Informatik is a Swiss IT service provider and supports companies in their day-to-day operations: infrastructure, operations, support. EU Cowork AI grew out of that work, and so did its requirements. What a business really needs shows up in the support ticket, not in a product presentation.
All details about the provider are set out in the imprint .
Six principles you can hold us to
Six principles apply to the product, documentation and communication of EU Cowork AI: open source, no lock-in, facts instead of adjectives, honest about status, data-minimal by default, traceable. They are deliberately worded so that a breach is noticeable and can be named.
The six principles of EU Cowork AI and what each one means in the product.
Principle
What this means in practice
Open source
MIT licence, thin fork of LibreChat. Source code and configuration can be audited.
No lock-in
Self-hosting from a single user upwards, with no seat minimum and no mandatory branding. Content and configuration are exportable.
Facts instead of adjectives
Every statement with a figure, a source or evidence. No testimonials, no benchmarks without a basis.
Honest about status
Whatever is not in place yet is marked as in progress or planned in the sentence itself.
Data-minimal by default
Telemetry off by default, no tracking without active consent, no model training on customer data.
Traceable
Every tool call, every admin action and every login is logged and can be exported.
What is in place today and what is not
EU Cowork AI is ready for production use, and we spell out what that means. Available today are operation on your own infrastructure, requesting access to the hosted Swiss instance, use as an installable PWA, and a configurable retention period including export and deletion of individual user accounts.
- In progress: the GitHub repository with our own extensions under the MIT licence, coming soon, the dedicated ISO 27001 certification of EU Cowork AI, and the general rollout of the Outlook add-in, which currently runs internally in beta, and of the Excel add-in.
- In progress: TOMs document, hosting fact sheet, no-training statement, and an audit and access concept.
- Planned: native apps for iOS and Android, SCIM provisioning, an egress proxy with an allow list for code execution, and hardened sandbox isolation.
What drives us: the potential of European companies
We are driven by what already exists inside European companies. The same knowledge sits there as anywhere else, and the same tasks could be completed faster with AI. What has been missing above all is a tool these companies are willing to entrust with their data. As long as that gap remains open, the productivity gain arises elsewhere.
Using AI on your own terms means the company decides: which data leaves the building, who may see which system, and when the provider is changed. Because the licence does not depend on the number of workplaces, a company can equip all its employees instead of just a selection. Whoever enables everyone gets ideas back from everyone.
Anyone who enables their people while keeping control over data and costs does not have to choose between progress and caution. That is exactly why we are building EU Cowork AI.
Hold us to it. The figures on this page are linked, the six principles above are written so that a breach is noticeable, and if any of it does not add up for you, write to us using the contact details in the imprint . We would rather correct a statement than defend it.
Frequently asked questions
Is EU Cowork AI really fully open source?
Yes. EU Cowork AI is published under the MIT licence and is a thin fork of LibreChat. You can audit the source code, run the software on your own infrastructure and modify it. There is no seat minimum, no mandatory branding and no feature lock that only opens with a different licence.
Are training courses part of the offering, or does every company have to teach itself?
Training courses and training materials are part of the offering of Herr Informatik GmbH. They range from an introduction for all employees through to in-depth support for individual teams, from the first prompt to analyses in Excel and presentations in PowerPoint. Scope and format are agreed with the company.
Can I already use EU Cowork AI today?
EU Cowork AI is ready for production use. Anyone self-hosting can run the open-source platform on their own infrastructure. Access to the hosted Swiss instance is allocated in stages on request because demand is high. A dedicated ISO 27001 certification of EU Cowork AI is in progress, and native apps for iOS and Android are planned.
Request access
Anyone requesting access now joins the next round on the hosted Swiss instance and helps shape the direction in which EU Cowork AI grows.

# What Switzerland keeps out of the cloud

URL: https://eucowork.ai/en/blog/ki-datenhaltung-schweiz

What Switzerland keeps out of the cloud | EU Cowork AI
