- Federal data stays on-premise
Public sector and data protection
The federal government has drawn a line through its own body of data: three workflows that respect it
The Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner, Switzerland’s national data protection authority, has successfully pressed for GEVER case files, the content of Outlook mailboxes and all sensitive personal data to remain in the data centres of the federal administration while the introduction of Microsoft 365 is under way. This article shows on three workflows what an AI workplace looks like under that condition, and it names the requirement our managed operation does not meet.
Public sector and data protection
3 September 2026
Reading time: 12 minutes
- Starting point
- Who this affects
- Opening up the files
- Answers with a source reference
- Several specialist systems
- Limits
- Frequently asked questions
- Sources
In brief
- In its 33rd activity report of 30 June 2026, the Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner, Switzerland’s national data protection authority, writes that the use of commercial language models entails storage in the provider’s cloud for at least some time and with it “inevitably a risk to data security”. That is why the report calls federally owned AI systems an essential precondition. 1
- The same report records that case files and data from GEVER, the electronic records management of the federal administration, the content of Outlook mailboxes and all sensitive personal data remain in data centres of the federal administration and are processed exclusively there, while the introduction of Microsoft 365 is under way. 2
- privatim, the conference of the cantonal and communal data protection commissioners in Switzerland, holds that public bodies moving such data into the services of large international providers is inadmissible in most cases, and allows it only where the responsible body encrypts the data itself and the provider has no access to the key. 3
- That is exactly the condition our managed operation in Lupfig does not meet. Anyone who has to meet it runs EU Cowork AI on their own server, and that is set out under Self-hosting .
On this page
- Starting point
- Who this affects
- Opening up the files
- Answers with a source reference
- Several specialist systems
- Limits
- Frequently asked questions
- Sources
Starting point: what the federal government has decided for itself
On 30 June 2026 the Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner, the FDPIC for short and Switzerland’s national data protection authority, published its 33rd activity report. In the chapter on artificial intelligence there is one sentence that went almost unnoticed in the coverage. Federally owned AI systems, it says, are an essential precondition for reaching the stated goals while complying with data protection and information security, because they make sure that prompts and the data they contain are processed locally and made accessible only to the authorised organisational units. The use of commercial language models, by contrast, brings with it “storage on the provider’s cloud for at least some time and thus inevitably a risk to data security”. 1
The second find sits a few pages earlier and is more concrete. In the reporting year the FDPIC successfully pressed for case files and data from the electronic records management of the federal administration, GEVER for short, along with the content of Outlook mailboxes and generally all sensitive personal data and personality profiles, to remain in data centres of the federal administration and to be processed exclusively there, that is with the federal government and not in the cloud. 2 The Cloud Enabling Büroautomation project carries on, the introduction of Microsoft 365 has been decided and begun. The body of data at issue here is taken out of it. So the federal government has not decided against the cloud, it has drawn a line through its own body of data.
The cantons are going the same way, only more sharply. privatim, the conference of the Swiss data protection commissioners, which brings together the data protection authorities of the cantons and communes, adopted a resolution in Bern on 18 November 2025. In it, it holds that public bodies moving sensitive personal data, or personal data subject to a statutory duty of confidentiality, into the software services of large international providers is inadmissible in most cases, Microsoft 365 in particular. As its conclusion the resolution names a single condition under which it works after all: the data has to be encrypted by the responsible body itself, and the cloud provider must have no access to the key. 3
Behind this lies no hostility to technology. Case numbers at the supervisory authority are rising: in the same reporting year 2,477 complaints reached the FDPIC, more than twice the 1,053 of the year before, along with 484 notified data security breaches against 363. 4 Those figures say something about the load on the authority and nothing about large projects. The experience with large undertakings rests on another finding: on 8 July 2026 the Swiss Federal Audit Office presented a synthesis report drawn from 24 audits of the federal government’s key IT projects, with an investment volume of three to five billion francs, and finds in it that the overall planning remains incomplete and that the focus on effect and benefit is missing, just as it was ten years earlier. 5 Anyone starting an AI project in this environment is asked first where the data sits, and only then what the model can do.
1
2
3
4
- The body of data sits in your data centres or on your own server
- For a single request, only the extract it needs goes out
- Answer with a source reference, entry in the log
- The body of data does not leave the controlled area; the single request goes to the model
The dividing line does not run between cloud and server, but between the body of data and the single request.
Who this affects, and what sets it off
The question of place does not arise for the federal government alone. According to the harmonised Eurostat survey, 19.95% of enterprises with ten or more employees in the EU used artificial intelligence in 2025, in Germany 25.97%, in Austria 29.95%. 6 For Switzerland this table holds nothing, and we come back to that in the section on limits. Anyone working around the public sector notices the movement in questionnaires anyway, not in statistics.
That is because the position of the FDPIC and the privatim resolution reach well beyond the administration. They appear in tender documents, in data processing agreements and in the security questionnaires suppliers have to fill in. A fiduciary office working for a commune is handed them. A software house running a specialist application for a hospital likewise. The requirement travels down the supply chain long before it stands in a statute.
Five groups ask about it today, and they ask for different reasons. The table sets out what sets off the need in each case and what an AI workplace can contribute there. It does not set out what is legally permissible; that is decided case by case and under the data protection law that applies.
Who is asking
What sets off the need
What EU Cowork AI contributes there
Federal administration and federal offices
After the FDPIC intervened, GEVER case files, Outlook content and sensitive personal data stay in data centres of the federal administration
Operation on your own infrastructure under the MIT licence, with no channel back to the provider, telemetry off by default
Cantons and communes
The privatim resolution requires sensitive data to be encrypted by the body itself, with no provider access to the key
Self-hosting on your own server, so that the body of data and the key stay in the same hands
Hospitals, schools and social insurance bodies
Patient, pupil and insured person data is sensitive, and official and professional secrecy come on top
Knowledge bases from your own documents with a source reference, permissions in the order user, role, group, server default
Suppliers and contractors of the public sector
Security questionnaires and tenders take over the requirements of the contracting body, often word for word
Data processing agreement and subprocessor list to hand over, audit log to export, details on governance
Law firms, fiduciary offices and practices with public sector mandates
Professional secrecy under article 321 of the Swiss Criminal Code, for fiduciary mandates the contractual duty of confidentiality, plus the requirements of the commissioning body
Connection to specialist applications over MCP, with permissions per tool and one log entry per call
What connects these five groups is not their legal form but the burden of proof. They have to make sure data stays in the right place, and they also have to be able to show it later, to someone else and without going through the whole case again. A tool that assures you it is safe does not help with that. A tool that logs what it has done and states where a statement comes from does help. This article is no substitute for legal advice.
Use case 1: opening up files and minutes without the body of documents leaving Switzerland
A department has twenty years of minutes, directives and parliamentary motions on file, neatly ordered by the records classification scheme and still not findable. The question is rarely what a single document says. It is when a rule was last changed and on what grounds. You put the body of documents into a knowledge base, that is a place for your own documents from which the AI colleague fetches only the matching extracts for each question. Back comes an answer stating which document and which passage it comes from.
What matters is where that place sits. It is on the instance, the installation that is run for your organisation. With self-hosting it stands with you; in managed operation it stands with us in Lupfig, in the ISO 27001 certified data centres of Green, where the certification covers the data centres and not us, and the body of documents then sits outside your own administration. To answer a single question, only the extract that question needs goes out, and it goes to the model; which model that is in managed operation is set out further down under Limits. The body of documents does not travel with it, and no model is trained on your content. What that means technically is set out under Security .
1
2
3
- Minutes, directives and motions in the knowledge base
- Only the matching extract goes to the question
- Answer with document and source reference, entry in the log
An archive turns into a reference work. The assessment stays with the case handler.
The limit belongs in the same place as the benefit. A source reference does not prove that the answer is correct. It makes it possible to check what the answer rests on, and that is something else. A language model can attribute a passage wrongly or take a repealed version for the one in force, and it does so all the more readily as the body of documents grows. Anyone passing an answer on opens the passage it names.
Use case 2: the answer from your own body of documents, with a source reference
At the counter and on the phone the same questions come back again and again. Which enclosures does an application need, which deadline applies, what does a permit cost, who is responsible. The answers sit in regulations, information sheets and fee ordinances, spread over several filing places and not everywhere at the same version. The AI colleague answers the question from that body of documents and names, for every statement, the document, the section and the version.
The benefit lies less in speed than in traceability. Anyone giving out an answer has to be able to back it up if it comes to that, later and to someone else. That is why the source reference is not an extra here, but the actual point. Personal data of the person asking is not needed for it. The question can be put in the abstract, and what is not put in cannot go out either.
1
2
3
- Regulations, information sheets and fee ordinances in the body of documents
- The question put in the abstract, without personal data of the person asking
- Answer with document, section and version
The answer stays an answer given by people. What becomes checkable is what it rests on.
And the limit we draw here explicitly: this is not a chatbot for your website, and we do not recommend it as one either. A system that answers the outside world directly moves the risk to where nobody reads it over any more. The sensible way is the other way round. The answer is drafted inside, a person checks it, a person gives it out. Legally binding rulings do not come about this way in any case.
Use case 3: the case that runs across several specialist systems
An application comes in, and the answer sits in three systems. The person in the residents’ register, the plot in the geoinformation system, the correspondence so far in the records management system. Today someone clicks through all three and writes up the result by hand. The AI colleague can take these steps over, provided the systems are connected. It plans the order, calls the released tools one after another, checks every intermediate result and finally puts up a draft for approval.
The connection runs over MCP, the Model Context Protocol, an open standard through which an AI system can address other systems. Such a connection to a single system is called a connector and is released individually. Permissions apply per tool and in the order user, role, group, server default. Write access has to be released separately. Every call stands in the audit log, the record of who used which tool and when, and you can export it. Which software can be connected today is listed on the Integrations page.
1
2
3
- The application as it comes in
- Calls to the register, geoinformation and records management, each one released separately
- Draft for approval, every call in the log
Permissions apply per tool. What is not released is not called.
Here too the limit, and it is a fundamental one. The system does not create human oversight, it makes it provable. Whoever approves the draft decides, and no log changes that. A log is also not an AI inventory. It shows what has gone through this route, and not what else is in use as AI in your organisation.
Limits: where we do not meet the requirement
Now the part a provider is better off saying itself, and we start with the limitation that weighs more. In managed operation, what goes out for a single request goes to a commercial language model, for Anthropic’s models through Amazon Bedrock under its European inference profile; how that path runs in detail is set out in the article on the Anthropic models on Amazon Bedrock . Amazon is one of the providers privatim names in its resolution, and AWS is a US company, so the CLOUD Act applies. The FDPIC’s sentence on commercial language models therefore applies to us as well. Anyone who has to rule that out runs the model and the instance themselves. The second limitation concerns the key. The privatim resolution names exactly one condition, and it is narrow. The data has to be encrypted by the responsible body itself, and the provider must have no access to the key. 3 Our managed operation in Lupfig does not meet that. We run the instance, and we can access it under instruction if something goes wrong. A data centre in Switzerland changes nothing about it, because the condition does not ask about the place but about who holds the key. Anyone who has to meet it gets there with us only through self-hosting on your own server. The GitHub repository under the MIT licence is coming soon; until then the installation guide is available. And a point about ourselves that matters for federal offices and cantons: EU Cowork AI is ready for production use, and access to the managed instance is allocated in stages because demand is high.
Just as honest is the other direction, even though it serves us here. The resolution addresses public bodies, not private companies. It is a joint position of the data protection supervisory authorities and not a legal norm; a court is not bound by it, and anyone quoting it as a ban overstates it. Not even all of them back it: the canton of Glarus made use of the opt-out under article 18.2 of the statutes. 3 Conversely, anyone who ignores it underestimates how strongly such positions carry over into tenders and questionnaires. What applies in your case follows from the cantonal or federal law that applies. This article is no substitute for legal advice.
1
2
3
4
- Managed operation in Lupfig: we run the instance and manage the keys
- Self-hosting: the body of data and the keys stay with you
- For sensitive data in the services of large international providers, privatim requires the second route
- The server location alone does not answer this question
The condition does not ask where the data sits, but who holds the key.
With the FDPIC too, the small print is part of it. It writes about federally owned AI systems, that is systems of the federal government for the federal government, and it accompanies the preparations of the Federal Chancellery and the Federal Office of Information Technology, Systems and Telecommunication. It does not write about providers like us, and we do not read its statement as a recommendation for us either. What is usable is something narrower: the yardstick it applies. Requests are processed locally, and only the authorised organisational units have access. 1 Anyone who wants to can be measured against that yardstick, and with self-hosting and a model of your own it is within reach.
The fourth point weakens our own market argument, and it belongs here all the same. On the use of AI in Swiss companies there is no official figure. In the harmonised Eurostat survey, which for 2025 reports values for the EU as a whole, for every member state and for Norway, Turkey and several candidate countries, Switzerland is missing entirely. 6 What circulates for Switzerland, a usage rate of 57% for instance, comes from surveys commissioned by providers, in the case named by Amazon Web Services, and the sample size is not stated consistently across the reporting. 7 Such provider studies are not worthless, but they are no substitute for official statistics, and we carry them here only to name the gap. Solid alongside them is the Austrian survey: 30% of enterprises with ten or more employees use AI, and of the enterprises without AI, 77% have never even considered using it. 8 The obstacle there is therefore not rejection, but never having looked at it.
Lastly Austria, because two things are running there at once. The Network and Information System Security Act 2026 enters into force on 1 October 2026. Affected entities have to register from that day and by 31 December 2026 at the latest, and it concerns some 4,000 companies from 18 sectors instead of the roughly one hundred operators of critical infrastructure as before. 9 At the same time a formal designation under article 70 of the European AI Act was still outstanding in June 2026, even though the deadline for it was 2 August 2025; by way of preparation, the AI service point at the RTR has been in place since 2024. A parliamentary question puts fifteen questions on the subject, 10 and the answer of 2 June 2026 merely points to the lack of competence of the ministry asked. 11 For companies that means: the cybersecurity duties come with a date, AI supervision comes without one. If you have to plan, you plan by the calendar you have. This section is no substitute for legal advice.
Frequently asked questions on the cloud, federal data and AI in public administration
May public authorities use Microsoft 365 for sensitive personal data?
privatim holds this to be inadmissible in most cases and allows it only where the responsible body encrypts the data itself and the provider has no access to the key. That resolution is a joint position of the data protection supervisory authorities and not a legal norm, and the canton of Glarus has not signed up to it. What counts in the end is the applicable data protection law and the assessment in the individual case. This section is no substitute for legal advice.
What exactly stays on-premise with the federal government?
According to the FDPIC’s 33rd activity report, case files and data from the GEVER electronic records management, the content of Outlook mailboxes and generally all sensitive personal data and personality profiles remain in data centres of the federal administration and are processed exclusively there. On-premise here means on your own infrastructure, not with a cloud provider. The introduction of Microsoft 365 in the federal administration carries on independently of that. So the federal government has not rejected the cloud, it has taken part of its body of data out of it.
Does EU Cowork AI meet the requirement of the privatim resolution?
With self-hosting on your own server yes, because the body of data and the keys stay there and we have no access. In managed operation in Lupfig no, because we run the instance and manage the keys. We would rather say that plainly than leave it open. Which route fits depends on whether you process sensitive personal data in the exercise of official duties or not.
Is a Swiss data centre not enough?
For many applications yes, for the case privatim describes no. The condition in the resolution does not attach to the location but to the power of disposal over the key. A location in Switzerland makes the risk smaller and still does not answer the question that was asked. Anyone who has to answer it will not get past self-hosting.
What does self-hosting cost?
The GitHub repository under the MIT licence is coming soon, and self-hosting is free. You carry your own infrastructure and the operating effort, and you enter yourself which models should be reachable, or run one of your own. Managed operation costs CHF 14 per person per month, outside Switzerland €15, of which CHF 7.50 or €8 is model credit in the shared pool of your organisation. All the details are on the Pricing page.
Does our data train the models?
No. Customer data does not train models, and telemetry is off by default. What goes to the model is the text of the single request along with the extracts that belong to the answer, while the body of data stays on the instance. What we commit to contractually is in the data processing agreement , and everyone involved in the chain is named in the list of subprocessors .
How many Swiss companies use AI?
There is no official answer to that. Switzerland is not included in the harmonised Eurostat survey on the use of AI in enterprises, which for 2025 reports 19.95% across the EU. 6 The figures circulating for Switzerland come from surveys commissioned by providers, and we use them only with that label attached. If someone sells you a Swiss AI rate as official, ask which body collected it.
What changes in 2026 for Austrian companies?
The Network and Information System Security Act 2026 enters into force on 1 October 2026, and affected entities have to register by 31 December 2026 at the latest; some 4,000 companies from 18 sectors are expected. 9 With the European AI Act it looks different: a formal designation under article 70 was still outstanding in June 2026, even though the deadline expired on 2 August 2025; by way of preparation, the AI service point at the RTR has been in place since 2024. So plan by the cybersecurity calendar, which is settled, and keep the AI side open. This section is no substitute for legal advice.
Work through it on a body of documents of your own
Bring an anonymised extract from a file, a set of regulations or a typical case, and we work through the process together, once in managed operation and once with self-hosting, so that the difference becomes visible. Or sign up and try it out yourself.

# Two deadlines almost nobody has in the diary

URL: https://eucowork.ai/en/blog/ai-act-fristen-dezember-2026

Two deadlines almost nobody has in the diary | EU Cowork AI

- Two deadlines hardly anyone has in the calendar
Law and deadlines
2 December 2026 and 12 January 2027: three workflows that stand up to both deadlines
The regulation that postponed the AI Act’s high-risk deadlines in July 2026 places two obligations on 2 December 2026 at the same time. A good six weeks later, every charge for switching provider comes to an end. This article puts both dates in context, shows three workflows that go with them and says precisely who the obligations reach and who they do not.
Law and deadlines
3 September 2026
Reading time: 12 minutes
- What has changed
- Who it reaches
- Showing what was generated
- Assess once
- Preparing the exit
- Limits and counterarguments
- Frequently asked questions
- Sources
In brief
- Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 of 8 July 2026 moved the AI Act’s high-risk deadlines to 2 December 2027 and 2 August 2028. 1 Almost everywhere that was read as the all-clear.
- The same regulation places two obligations on 2 December 2026. Providers of systems that generate synthetic content and were placed on the market before 2 August 2026 have until then to meet the machine-readable marking required by Article 50(2). 2 And two newly inserted prohibitions apply from exactly that day. 3
- A good six weeks later, on 12 January 2027, providers of data processing services may no longer charge anything for a switch, data egress charges included. 4
- According to Eurostat, 19.95% of EU enterprises with ten or more employees used artificial intelligence in 2025. 5 For most of them, 2 December 2026 reaches their supplier and not them, and that distinction is exactly what the later part of this article works out.
On this page
- What has changed
- Who it reaches
- Showing what was generated
- Assess once
- Preparing the exit
- Limits and counterarguments
- Frequently asked questions
- Sources
What changed in July, and what got lost in the noise
On 8 July 2026 Parliament and Council adopted Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, the Digital Omnibus Regulation on artificial intelligence. It was published on 24 July 2026 and has been in force since 27 July 2026. 1 The headline was the same everywhere: the obligations for high-risk systems are coming later. That is true, and it is half the news. The other half sits in the same two articles that carry the postponement, and it points in the opposite direction.
The new Article 111(4) reads, in substance: providers of AI systems, including general-purpose AI systems, that generate synthetic audio, image, video or text content and that were placed on the market before 2 August 2026 shall take the necessary steps to comply with Article 50(2) by 2 December 2026. 2 Article 50(2) requires the outputs of such a system to be marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated, as far as technically feasible and taking into account the state of the art. The obligation falls away where the system performs an assistive function for standard editing and does not substantially alter the input data or their meaning. 6 Article 111(4) is a transitional rule for existing systems, and it runs out in three months.
The new Article 113(3), point (a), sets two newly inserted prohibitions to 2 December 2026, while the rest of Chapter II has applied since 2 February 2025. 3 Point (ba) prohibits AI systems that generate or manipulate realistic content depicting the intimate body parts of an identifiable person, or an identifiable person engaged in sexually explicit conduct, without that person’s express consent. Point (bb) covers the generation or manipulation of material within the meaning of Directive 2011/93/EU on combating the sexual abuse of children. 7 Fines for infringing Article 5 reach up to €35 million or 7% of worldwide annual turnover, and for infringing the transparency obligations in Article 50 up to €15 million or 3%. 8
The second date sits in a different law and is named even less often. Under Article 29(1) of the Data Act, providers of data processing services may no longer impose switching charges from 12 January 2027. 4 Switching charges mean more than the words suggest: every charge for the actions involved in switching, expressly including data egress charges, but not the standard service fees and not the early termination penalties. 9 On 25 June 2026 the European Commission reached the preliminary view that two large cloud services should be designated as gatekeepers, and expressly based that on lock-in and high switching costs. 10 How deep the dependency runs shows in the official statistics: in 2025, 52.74% of EU enterprises with ten or more employees bought paid cloud services, and 77.53% of them count as highly dependent under the Eurostat classification, because they buy sophisticated cloud services. 11
1
2
3
4
- 8 July 2026: the high-risk deadlines are postponed
- 2 December 2026: marking for existing systems, two new prohibitions
- 12 January 2027: no more switching charges
- 2 December 2027 and 2 August 2028: high risk under Annex III and Annex I
Four dates on one line. The postponement concerns the two at the back; the ones usually missing from the calendar are the two at the front.
Who it reaches, and how you can tell
The first question is not what to do, but which role your company is in. The AI Act knows providers and deployers, and it means two different sets of obligations by that. A provider is anyone who develops an AI system, or has one developed, and places it on the market or puts it into service under their own name or trade mark. A deployer is anyone who uses an AI system under their own authority. 12 The 2 December 2026 deadline in Article 111(4) is addressed to providers. Buy a model and use it inside your own company, and you are a deployer to begin with.
The line does not run along the purchase receipt, though. Anyone who makes a bought-in system available under their own name, say as an enquiry service on their own website or as a tool for customers, puts it into service under their own name and thereby becomes a provider within the meaning of the regulation. 12 That is the route by which a deployer slips into a provider’s obligation, and it happens more often than project plans say. So check first whose name a system carries towards the outside world, and only then which deadline applies.
The second question is who carries the assessment work. A survey by Bitkom Research on data protection under the GDPR, among 603 companies in Germany with 20 or more employees interviewed by telephone, records that for 77% the roll-out of new tools sets the assessment going all over again, that 82% see uncertainty about the exact requirements and that 54% complain of inconsistent interpretation within the EU. 13 That survey comes from an industry association, and we present it as what it is. The counter-figure from the same survey belongs next to it: 53% consider European data protection an advantage for developing AI in international comparison, 36% a disadvantage. 14
Who
What triggers the deadline
What EU Cowork AI contributes there
Companies that make an AI system available under their own name
Article 50(2) applies directly; only for systems placed on the market before 2 August 2026 does Article 111(4) give time until 2 December 2026
A log entry for every call with model, time and person, exportable; the machine-readable marking itself is delivered by the provider of the model
Communications, marketing and editorial work
Article 50(4): disclosure for deepfakes and for published text on matters of public interest
History and source references for each draft, so that human review and editorial responsibility stay demonstrable
Procurement and IT management
Data Act: no switching charges from 12 January 2027, plus exit clauses that already have to be in the contract today
MIT licence, source code coming soon, self-hosting without licence costs, export of knowledge bases, conversation histories and audit log
Legal, data protection and compliance

Permissions per tool and per model in the order user, role, group, server default, every call in the audit log
Public administration and its suppliers

Operation in Green’s ISO 27001 certified data centres in Lupfig or on your own server, where the certification covers the data centres and not us, plus subprocessor list and data processing agreement
The dependency is not a feeling either. In the DIHK digitalisation survey 2026, an association survey with 4,686 responses, 68% of companies rate themselves as largely or completely dependent when it comes to artificial intelligence, and 55% for cloud services. 15 Among the companies without AI in use, only a small share have ever considered it, namely 14.21%, and only within that group do missing expertise at 70.89%, unclear legal consequences at 52.52% and data protection concerns at 48.83% come out on top. 16 Those shares hold for that group and for nobody else. The table below assigns the two dates to five groups.
Use case 1: showing what was generated when and by which model
A customer notice goes out; three weeks later somebody asks whether the text came from a model and from which one. Today the answer is a reconstruction from memory and mailbox. In the AI workspace it sits in the audit log, the running record of every call: which model, which access, which time, which person, which knowledge base. You export the section that belongs to the case and put it on file.
That is not just tidiness, it is the evidence one of the exceptions in Article 50(4) hangs on. Anyone publishing text in order to inform the public on matters of public interest has to disclose that it was artificially generated, unless the content underwent human review or editorial control and a natural or legal person holds editorial responsibility for it. 17 That exception is not a claim, it is a question of fact. Anyone relying on it should be able to show who reviewed it and when.
1
2
3
- Query, chosen model and chosen knowledge base
- A log entry on every call, on your server
- Export of the section that belongs to the case
The evidence comes about while the work happens, not once somebody goes looking for it.
The limit here, plainly stated: a log entry is not a machine-readable marking within the meaning of Article 50(2). That marking has to sit on the output content itself, and producing it is the business of the provider of the respective model and not ours. The audit log also only sees what runs through EU Cowork AI. It does not build an inventory of the AI systems in your company and it finds nothing that is used alongside.
Use case 2: assess once instead of afresh with every tool
The sequence almost every company knows: a department wants a new tool, and the assessment starts from the beginning. Data processing agreement, technical and organisational measures, subprocessors, processing location, deletion periods, roles and permissions. With the next tool, the same again. In the association survey on data protection named above, for 77% of companies the roll-out of new tools sets the assessment going all over again. 13
The workflow instead: you assess the instance once, meaning the one installation operated for your company, and after that only the additions. Over 100 models are available through one access, processed on the EU side via EuRouter, plus the Anthropic models through Amazon Bedrock in the European profile. External systems join through MCP, the Model Context Protocol, an open standard for connecting external systems. Every connector, meaning each single link to such an external system, brings permissions per tool with it, and every call lands in the log. Which software can be connected today is listed on the Integrations page.
1
2
3
- One instance, assessed once
- Models and connectors as additions, each with its own permissions
- One set of contracts, one subprocessor list, one log
Many full assessments turn into one assessment and a series of small additions.
The limit: the assessment does not fall away, it gets smaller and it moves. Every new model in the catalogue and every new connector still has to be assessed, and responsibility for the use stays with the deployer. We supply the documents in one place, in the data processing agreement and in the subprocessor list . Anyone who reads that as meaning the requirements are settled is reading it wrong.
Use case 3: preparing the exit before it is needed
Take the contract for your current cloud or AI service and read it against Articles 23 and 25 of the Data Act. Does it state a maximum notice period for the initiation of the switching process of no more than two months? A transitional period of no more than 30 calendar days? An exhaustive list of the data that can be exported? A retrieval period of at least 30 calendar days after the transition? 18 Wherever one of those points is missing, you have already found your question for 12 January 2027.
The second part is an exercise and not a clause. You export knowledge bases, conversation histories, accounts and the audit log, set up a second instance and read everything back in there. EU Cowork AI is under the MIT licence, self-hosting costs nothing beyond your own infrastructure, and that is exactly why this route can be rehearsed without negotiating with us, as soon as the release repository is published. Until then, the full installation guide is available under Self-hosting . Anyone who has rehearsed the exit once negotiates differently.
1
2
3
- Read the contract against Articles 23 and 25
- Export of knowledge bases, histories, accounts and log
- Reading it back in on a second instance, under the MIT licence
The exit gets rehearsed while nobody needs it.
The limit: a successful export is a technical statement and not a legal one. The Data Act prohibits charges, it does not prohibit effort, and it does not turn two systems into the same functionality. What a switch really costs is counted in working days and not in a line on an invoice.
Limits, counterarguments and what does not stand here
First the distinction this article would fail on if it did not draw it cleanly. Article 50(2) is a provider obligation, and so is paragraph 1. The deployer obligations sit in paragraphs 3 and 4. 17 The 2 December 2026 deadline in Article 111(4) therefore reaches providers of existing systems and not the companies that use those systems. The two new prohibitions also reach deployers only in one narrow case: under Article 5(1a), point (b), the use is prohibited only where the deployer uses the system for the purpose of generating or manipulating such material. 7 Anyone blurring that difference is selling fear instead of information.
Second, against the grain of most pieces on this subject: the AI literacy obligation in Article 4 was weakened and not tightened. Providers and deployers take measures to support the development of AI literacy among their staff, and since July 2026 the legal text says expressly that this obligation does not oblige anyone to guarantee a particular level of AI literacy for any person. 19 Anyone selling you a hard training obligation with compulsory proof is quoting a version that no longer applies. Measures stay sensible; the legal position is simply a different one from the one advertised.
1
2
3
4
- Provider: marking under Article 50(2)
- Deployer: disclosure under Article 50(4)
- Put a system into service under your own name and you become a provider yourself
- The new prohibitions reach deployers only where the use serves that purpose
Two roles, two sets of obligations. 2 December 2026 reaches one of them, not both.
Third the Data Act, and here the same holds in the other direction. What is prohibited from 12 January 2027 is charges, not effort. The transitional period of 30 calendar days is not absolute: where it is technically unfeasible, the provider reports that within 14 working days, gives reasons and states an alternative period of no more than seven months. 20 Article 31 exempts from the charging ban those services whose main features have been largely built for a single customer and that are not offered at broad scale in the provider’s catalogue. 21 And whether a pure language model service is a data processing service within the meaning of Article 2, point (8), at all is judged differently in the specialist literature and has not been settled. 22 We do not claim the opposite.
Fourth, what nobody knows and what we do not deliver. A further Digital Omnibus proposal, running under procedure 2025/0360(COD), would release providers of data processing services that are small or medium-sized enterprises from the switching obligations for contracts up to 12 September 2025. The ban on switching charges under Article 29 of the Data Act is expressly excluded from that exemption and continues to apply. It has not been adopted, and we predict neither that it will come nor that it will fail. 23 On our side: EU Cowork AI does not build an AI inventory by itself, it only sees what runs through its own instance. It does not create human oversight, it makes it demonstrable. Source references do not prevent hallucinations, they make them checkable. And managed operation does not meet a requirement that calls for customer-held keys without access by the provider; only self-hosting leads there.
Fifth the most uncomfortable point, and it belongs in every article that deals with sovereignty. The Ontario Court of Justice ordered a French cloud company to hand data over to the Canadian federal police. 24 The company challenged the order before the Ontario Superior Court of Justice; in January 2026 the proceedings were still open. A European base is therefore no immunity against access by foreign authorities. That holds for us too: the Anthropic models run on Amazon Bedrock, and AWS is a US company, so the CLOUD Act applies. Where the servers stand does not protect against that, and encryption does not help at the moment of processing. Article 32 of the Data Act requires providers to take adequate measures against unlawful access from third countries and makes decisions of third-country courts enforceable only on the basis of an international agreement, but it does not resolve the conflict. 25 What stays effective is what we say everywhere: give away less and know where things are held. This article is no substitute for legal advice.
Frequently asked questions about 2 December 2026 and 12 January 2027
What exactly applies from 2 December 2026?
Two things. First, providers of AI systems that generate synthetic audio, image, video or text content and that were placed on the market before 2 August 2026 have to meet Article 50(2) by that day, meaning they mark their outputs in machine-readable form as artificially generated. Second, from that day two newly inserted prohibitions from Article 5(1) apply, points (ba) and (bb), together with the accompanying paragraphs 1a and 1b. Both sit in the same regulation that postponed the high-risk deadlines in July 2026. This section is no substitute for legal advice.
Does Article 50(2) concern us if we only use AI?
As a rule, no. Paragraph 2 is addressed to providers, that is, to whoever develops a system or has one developed and places it on the market or puts it into service under their own name. Anyone using a bought-in system inside their own company is a deployer and has the obligations from paragraphs 3 and 4. The role can change, though: anyone who makes a system available under their own name, say as an enquiry service for customers, becomes a provider themselves. Check that system by system and not in one sweep for the whole company.
Have the high-risk obligations really been postponed?
Yes. For systems under Annex III, Chapter III applies from 2 December 2027, for systems under Annex I from 2 August 2028. The postponement concerns neither the prohibitions in Article 5 nor the transparency obligations in Article 50, which have had to be applied since 2 August 2026. That is exactly why the reading that everything has been postponed is wrong.
Do we now have to train all our staff?
There is no training obligation with a guaranteed outcome, and since July 2026 that stands expressly in the legal text. Article 4 requires measures to support AI literacy and at the same time records that nobody has to guarantee a particular level for any person. Anyone selling you something else is quoting the old version. Measures are sensible all the same, just as an effort and not as an owed result.
What changes in practice on 12 January 2027?
From that day a provider of data processing services may no longer charge anything for the switching process, and data egress charges are expressly included. Standard service fees and early termination penalties are untouched by this. Anyone renewing contracts today should check whether the exit clauses under Article 25 are in them at all, because that obligation already applies. This section is no substitute for legal advice.
Does a language model service fall under the Data Act at all?
That is open. The Data Act defines a data processing service through on-demand network access to a shared pool of configurable, scalable computing resources. Whether pure model access falls under it is judged differently in the specialist literature and has not been settled. We therefore do not build our statements on the answer turning out in one particular direction, and we recommend the same for your contract planning.
What does the provisional gatekeeper designation of the large cloud providers mean?
Provisional means first of all: there is no designation decision. On 25 June 2026 the Commission reached the preliminary view that two large cloud services should be designated as gatekeepers, and in doing so made lock-in and high switching costs the reason itself. Which concrete obligations follow from that depends on the further procedure, and we do not predict its outcome. What counts in practice is the finding behind it: switching is expensive today, and from 12 January 2027 it may no longer be so where charges are concerned.
What does EU Cowork AI do here, and what does it not do?
It makes three things demonstrable: which model was called when and by whom, which permissions per tool applied and what can be exported. It does not build an inventory of your AI systems, it does not produce machine-readable marking on other providers’ model outputs, and it does not meet any requirement in your place. Managed operation costs CHF 14 per person per month, outside Switzerland €15, of which CHF 7.50 or €8 is model credit; all the details are on the pricing page. Anyone who needs customer-held keys without access by the provider gets there only through self-hosting.
Put the two dates next to your own contracts
Bring a cloud or AI contract along and a list of the tools in use at your place. We go through together which role you are in for each system and what actually sits with you by 2 December 2026 and by 12 January 2027. Or you sign up and try the workspace out yourself.
Book a live demo
Get started

- Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Article 50(1) to (4): paragraphs 1 and 2 are addressed to providers, paragraphs 3 and 4 to deployers; paragraph 4 contains the exception for content that has undergone human review or editorial control and for which a natural or legal person holds editorial responsibility: eur-lex.europa.eu
- Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 (Data Act), Articles 23 and 25(2): maximum notice period for the initiation of the switching process of no more than two months under point (d), binding transitional period of no more than 30 calendar days, exhaustive specification of the data and digital assets that can be exported, retrieval period of at least 30 calendar days after the end of the transitional period: eur-lex.europa.eu
- Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Article 4 in the version of 27 July 2026: providers and deployers take measures to support the development of AI literacy among their staff; the text goes on to say, word for word, that this obligation does not oblige providers or deployers to guarantee a particular level of AI literacy for any person: eur-lex.europa.eu
- Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 (Data Act), Article 25(4): where the binding transitional period is technically unfeasible, the provider informs the customer within 14 working days of the switching request, gives reasons for the technical unfeasibility and states an alternative transitional period of no more than seven months: eur-lex.europa.eu
- Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 (Data Act), Article 31(1): Article 23, point (d), Article 29 and Article 30(1) and (3) do not apply to data processing services whose main features have largely been tailored to the needs of a single customer and that are not offered at broad scale through the provider’s service catalogue: eur-lex.europa.eu
- Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 (Data Act), Article 2, point (8), the notion of a data processing service: a digital service enabling ubiquitous and on-demand network access to a shared pool of configurable, scalable and elastic computing resources: eur-lex.europa.eu
- European Commission, proposal COM(2025) 837 final of 19 November 2025, Digital Omnibus, Article 1 point 15, new Article 31(1b) of Regulation (EU) 2023/2854: providers of data processing services that are small or medium-sized enterprises or small mid-cap enterprises are exempted, for contracts up to 12 September 2025, from the obligations of Chapter VI, expressly with the exception of Article 29, and contractual clauses to the contrary are deemed null and void: europarl.europa.eu ; state of play under file reference 2025/0360(COD), the procedure has not been concluded: oeil.europarl.europa.eu
- heise online of 26 November 2025 on the proceedings of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police against the OVH Group: production order of the Ontario Court of Justice of 19 April 2024 under section 487.014(1) of the Canadian Criminal Code, dismissal of the application to set it aside by Justice Heather Perkins-McVey on 25 September, deadline for handing over the data on 27 October, challenge at the end of October before the Ontario Superior Court of Justice: heise.de ; on the state of play, The Register of 27 November 2025 with an update of 26 January 2026 stating that the proceedings are ongoing: theregister.com . The decision has not been officially published and is not available on CanLII.
- Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 (Data Act), Article 32: providers take adequate technical, organisational and legal measures to prevent access and transfer to third-country authorities where this conflicts with Union law; decisions of third-country courts are enforceable only on the basis of an international agreement: eur-lex.europa.eu

# Agentic AI: who releases the tools

URL: https://eucowork.ai/en/blog/ki-agenten-governance

Agentic AI: who releases the tools | EU Cowork AI

- Agentic AI and control of the tools
Agents and oversight
Agentic AI in France: three workflows, and who releases the tools
In July the French data protection authority wrote down what worries it about agentic AI: that personal data circulates between many services and that control over it is lost. Eight days later a new version appeared of the protocol through which such systems drive their tools. This article follows three workflows to show how tool permissions, sign-off and the audit log fit together, and it names the limit at which our managed operation is out for French public administrations.
Agents and oversight
3 September 2026
Reading time: 12 minutes
- Starting point
- Who is affected
- Several business applications
- Write access
- Proof after the fact
- The limits
- Frequently asked questions
- Sources
In brief
- On 20 July 2026 the CNIL, France’s data protection authority, and the Conseil de l’IA et du Numérique, the country’s advisory council on AI and digital affairs, published an exploratory note on agentic AI. Presenting the note, the CNIL sums up the finding in two phrases: personal data circulating between numerous services, and a real risk of losing control over one’s own data. 1
- Eight days later, on 28 July 2026, the new specification of the Model Context Protocol appeared. It makes the transport stateless and puts the extension regime in order; managed authorisation for enterprises is kept there as an extension of its own. 2
- Only 6% of organisations are rated very well prepared for the AI Act by their own data protection officers, out of 2,390 officers surveyed. 3
- The limit, named openly: the French requirements framework for particularly sensitive state data comes from ANSSI, the national cybersecurity agency, and accepts as proof only a qualification from ANSSI or a certification issued in the EU or the EEA and recognised as equivalent by the agency. Switzerland is neither one nor the other. 4
On this page
- Starting point
- Who is affected
- Several business applications
- Write access
- Proof after the fact
- The limits
- Frequently asked questions
- Sources
Starting point: two documents from the same July
On 20 July 2026 the Commission Nationale de l’Informatique et des Libertés, France’s data protection authority and known as the CNIL, and the Conseil de l’IA et du Numérique published a joint note on agentic AI. It describes the architecture first: an orchestrating agent, specialised agents beside it, and behind them connected services, applications, databases, search tools. The finding, as the CNIL sums it up when presenting the note, comes in two phrases. Agentic AI puts personal data into circulation between numerous services, and for the people using it a real risk arises of losing control over their own data. 1 A second point comes on top of that, and it weighs more in daily operation than it sounds: because several parties take part in one automated sequence, it becomes harder to see who answers for which step.
Eight days later, on 28 July 2026, the new version of the Model Context Protocol, MCP for short, appeared. MCP is an open standard for how an AI system addresses external tools, in other words an interface: an agreed way for two programs to talk to each other. The version of 28 July 2026 makes the transport stateless. The opening handshake and the session identifier fall away, and every request carries its own protocol version, its origin and its capabilities with it. On top of that come a hardened authorisation, closer to the procedures common in enterprises, and an orderly extension regime; managed authorisation for enterprises is kept there as an extension of its own. 2
The two documents are not answers to one another, and we do not present them that way. They describe the same problem from two sides. One asks who keeps control over the data in an acting system and who answers for which step. The other sets out how a single tool call is declared, authorised and passed on. Anyone who wants to answer the first question in practice ends up at the second, because control over an acting system is in the end control over its tools.
How widespread agentic AI already is in France cannot be pinned down cleanly, and the reason sits in the official statistics themselves. According to Insee Première number 2120 of 21 July 2026, 18% of French companies with ten or more employees used at least one artificial intelligence technique in 2025, surveyed among around 11,000 companies from a population of some 194,000. The methodology section carries the sentence that matters: the answers do not as a rule include use that employees run occasionally and for themselves. 5 Surveys that ask employees directly therefore land on quite different figures. The Baromètre Phygital Workplace, run by Ifop on behalf of a consultancy among 1,003 employees from companies with 1,000 staff or more, gives 62% usage against 34% with formalised rules. 6 Those are two questions put to two different populations, and neither figure disproves the other. Turning them into a single percentage sells a precision that does not exist. What remains is the pattern: more is used than is governed. The same Insee survey names, among the companies already using AI, 43% with concerns about data protection and privacy and 42% citing a lack of legal clarity. 5
1
2
3
4
- A request, put by a person with a role and permissions
- A plan of individual steps, each step a tool call
- Every call checks the permissions, write access needs a separate sign-off
- The result, the source reference and the log entry stay with you
The path of a request. What is not released is not called, and what is called is in the audit log.
Who is affected, and what triggers the need in each case
The narrowest group is the one most often drawn too wide. The implementing decree to Article 31 of the loi SREN, the French law on regulating and securing the digital space, was issued on 14 April 2026 and names the administrations of the State, their operators and six groupements d’intérêt public listed by name, public interest groupings under French law. Local and regional authorities are not named in the decree; they therefore do not fall under this duty. Nor does every public body fall under it automatically. 7 In substance the duty also bites only for data whose breach could harm public order, public security, the health or life of people, or the protection of intellectual property. Anyone reading today that the whole of France has to host sovereignly is reading in something that is not there.
On the data protection side the pressure is of a different kind, but it can be measured. For 2025 the CNIL published a record of 83 sanctions with a total of 486,839,500 euros, 78 of them fines. 8 Those proceedings did not concern agentic AI, but they describe the supervision that controllers work under. Allowing a system to act in several business applications shifts no responsibility, it widens it.
The people expected to carry this in daily work say themselves that they are not there yet. In the survey by the Observatoire des DPO, run from 5 to 21 November 2025 among 2,390 data protection officers, 6% of organisations count as very well prepared for the AI Act. 27% of respondents say they know the text of the regulation well, 85% have not yet attended any training of their own on artificial intelligence. 3 That the obligations for high-risk systems apply only from 2 December 2027 under Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, and from 2 August 2028 for embedded systems, buys time but does not take the work away. The survey is carried by the French employment administration DGEFP and the CNIL, together with the professional association of data protection officers and Afpa, which ran it, so it is not a vendor study but a self-report from the profession.
Who is asking
What triggers the need
What EU Cowork AI contributes there
Administrations of the French State and their operators
Article 31 of the loi SREN requires, for particularly sensitive data, proof through a qualification from ANSSI or a certification issued in the EU or the EEA and recognised as equivalent by the agency
Only self-hosting remains here: the duty attaches to obtaining a cloud service from a private provider. The software is under an MIT licence, managed operation in Switzerland is out
Local and regional authorities, hospitals and public bodies outside the decree
Not covered by the duty, yet sovereignty turns up in tenders as an award criterion, often next to requirements on logging and permission management
Managed operation in Lupfig or self-hosting, in both cases with permissions per tool and an exportable audit log
Data protection officers and compliance teams in companies
The AI Act, the CNIL note on agentic AI, and a usage that the official statistics expressly do not capture
What runs through the platform becomes visible: which user, which tool, which sign-off, what time, executed or refused
Banks, insurers and healthcare organisations
Supervision of outsourcing, requirements on how health data is held, plus Article 22 GDPR for automated decisions
Write access has to be released separately, so that the human step is not merely claimed but evidenced
Law firms, fiduciaries and HR departments
Professional secrecy and personnel data, plus the question of which document an acting system may touch at all
Permissions in the order user, role, group, server default, plus knowledge bases from your own documents with a source reference
Five groups, five different triggers, and one shared question behind them: who decides which tool an agent may call, and how can that be shown after the fact? The answer differs by group, and for one of these groups it goes against us. That stands further down in the section on the limits, and it stands there at length.
Use case 1: the case that runs across several business applications
A request comes in, and the answer is spread across three programs: the contract in the file store, the delivery status in the ERP system, the last correspondence in the mailbox. Today a person clicks through all three. The AI colleague can take over that path if the systems are connected. It plans the steps, calls the released tools one after another, checks every intermediate result and finally puts up a draft for sign-off. The point is not that it can do this. The point is that every single call can fail on a permission beforehand and stands in the audit log afterwards.
The connection runs over MCP. A connector is the single link to one particular program, an instance is the standalone installation running for your organisation. What the AI colleague is not allowed to see, it does not see: the order is user, role, group, server default. A tool that is not released for a role does not even appear in the plan, so it is not refused, it does not occur. Which software can be connected today is on the integrations page.
1
2
3
- The request as it comes in
- A plan of steps, each step a released tool
- A draft for sign-off, plus one entry per call in the audit log
Three programs, one case. What is not released does not appear in the plan.
The limit of this workflow: a permission per tool is not a permission per record. If a connector allows search across the entire file store, then it allows it across the entire file store, even when the case needs a single contract. How finely that can be narrowed depends on the connected system and not on us. Check it connector by connector before you release one broadly, and start with the smallest scope that carries the task.
Use case 2: the write access that has to be permitted separately
Reading is one half. The other begins when a system is to change a record, send a message or delete an entry. This is exactly where the platform separates: reading and writing tools are not the same permission. Write access has to be released separately, and where that has not happened, the process ends with a draft instead of a posting. That is unspectacular, and it is the difference between a proposal and an accomplished fact.
The CNIL note goes in the same direction without meaning any product. It suggests ranking the possible actions per service by risk, from reading through changing and deleting to sending data out of the system, and requiring human sign-off before execution above a certain level. Alongside that it names compartmentalising the memories per agent, a separated execution environment, and a way to stop a running process at any time. 1 Translated into operation that means: the question is not whether an agent may act, but which action it may complete on its own. That setting is made by the administrators, not by the model.
1
2
3
- Reading tools, released per user, role or group
- Writing tools, to be released separately, otherwise it stays a draft
- Every execution and every refusal lands in the audit log
Two classes of tools, two decisions. The second one is made by a person.
The limit: a sign-off is only worth the attention behind it. Anyone confirming twenty times a day will end up confirming everything. Human oversight does not come about because a window opens, but because few and important steps need that intermediate step while the rest are not released at all. Making that selection is work, it belongs to your organisation and cannot be bought in. The platform does not produce human oversight, it makes it demonstrable.
Use case 3: tracing what an agent actually did
Four weeks later someone comes back with a question: internal audit, a customer, a supervisory authority, or the data subject in person. The question is similar every time. Which data was drawn on, which tool was called, released by whom, and in what order? Without a log the answer is a reconstruction from memory and screenshots. With a log it is a query.
In EU Cowork AI every tool call is in the audit log, the running record of operations, and that log can be exported. Refused calls stand there just as executed ones do, which in an audit is often the more interesting part. This is exactly the building block the CNIL note also suggests: making visible for each executed task which personal data was drawn on, which agents were involved, which third party services were called and in what chronological order. 1 How that translates into policies and responsibilities is set out under Governance .
1
2
3
- One entry per call: user, tool, time, result
- Refused calls are in the log just like executed ones
- Export for internal audit, for supervisors or for a response to a data subject
The log answers what happened. Whether it was right is answered by a person.
The limit, and it is bigger than it sounds: the log shows what ran through EU Cowork AI. What someone does alongside it in a private account with some other provider is not in there. A tool does not create a register of all AI use in the company, it only sees its own path. This is exactly where the gap left open by the official statistics sits as well. Anyone who needs a complete picture will not get around organisational work.
The limits: where this route does not fit for France
The most uncomfortable sentence first, and it concerns us. For particularly sensitive data of the French State, Article 31 of the loi SREN requires proof, and the arrêté of 12 August 2026 approving the requirements framework allows exactly two routes: a qualification from ANSSI or a certification from a member state of the European Union or a party to the European Economic Area agreement that the agency recognises as equivalent. 4 That framework, known as SecNumCloud, itself requires under number 19.6, for protection against non-European law, that the provider’s registered office, central administration and principal place of business be located in a member state of the Union. 9 Switzerland is neither a member of the European Union nor a party to the EEA. A Swiss data centre cannot meet this requirement as things stand, however well it is run. And the requirement reaches further than location. Number 19.6 letter a concerns our registered office, letter c concerns any third company outside the Union that could technically reach the data processed in the service or the technical data. 9 Anyone who has to furnish this proof therefore has to examine the model path as well: our access to Anthropic’s models runs through Amazon Bedrock, and AWS is a US company. That holds in self-hosting just the same if you keep this path. For French public administrations that fall under this duty, our managed operation in Lupfig is therefore not the right route. What remains is self-hosting: the duty attaches to obtaining a cloud service from a private provider. If you run the software yourself, that question no longer arises for us, only for the inputs you buy yourself. The software is under an MIT licence and self-hosting costs nothing with us, as set out under Self-hosting . We would rather say this ourselves than let you find it out in a tender procedure.
So that the limit does not grow larger than it is: this duty does not apply to the public sector as a whole. The implementing decree of 14 April 2026 names the administrations of the State, their operators and six groupements d’intérêt public listed by name. Local and regional authorities are not named in the decree; they therefore do not fall under this duty, and between private companies it does not apply in any case. 7 Anyone supplying the French State should nonetheless read the circulars as well: circular number 6519/SG of 5 February 2026 makes digital sovereignty the second priority objective of the State’s digital procurement, after functional performance, and takes it to include independence from non-European law with extraterritorial reach. 10 Whether and how that bears on your particular case is decided by the contracting authority and not by a blog article. This article is no substitute for legal advice.
1
2
3
4
- What we limit: which tool is called, by whom, reading or writing
- What we make demonstrable: every call, every sign-off, every refusal in the log
- What we do not prevent: a malicious tool server and instructions hidden in content
- Where we are out: with a duty that requires a qualification from the EU or the EEA
Four statements, two of them uncomfortable. We would rather list them ourselves than hear them come back at us.
A second sentence is literally true and still leads astray. It is correct that no large American provider holds this qualification under its own name. Concluding from that that American technology is therefore ruled out would be wrong. Since 17 December 2025 the PREMI3NS offering from S3NS has been qualified, a joint venture of Thales and Google Cloud that builds on Google technology. 11 The route through a French company that licenses the technology and takes responsibility for running it is open, and it is being taken. Anyone claiming in a tender or a sales conversation that US technology is off the table will be proved wrong. That applies to us as much as to everyone else, and it is a reason not to play that card.
One caveat belongs with the CNIL note, and we expressly let it stand. The note is exploratory. It is not a recommendation, not a guideline and not a binding framework, and it does not announce one either. It names the Model Context Protocol exactly once, in a footnote, as an example of a widespread exchange protocol, and draws no conclusion from it, neither for nor against any particular approach. 1 Anyone quoting it as confirmation for a product decision is stretching it. We read it as what it is: a description of the risks the competent authority is currently working with, and a collection of building blocks that nobody has decided on yet.
Finally the technical limit, and it is the hardest. Our platform does not detect a malicious tool server. Nor does it prevent prompt injection, an instruction hidden in a document, a message or a web page that a model misreads as a task while reading it. What it does is narrower and more honest. It limits the blast radius, because a tool that is not released is not called and write access needs a second decision, and it makes the process auditable, because every call is in the log. Source references in a knowledge base likewise do not stop a model from claiming something false, they only make it checkable. An offer that promises you security at this point instead of limitation and evidence deserves a closer look; what we do and what we do not do is set out under Security and Trust . And once more, because this section has been much about law: this article is no substitute for legal advice.
Frequently asked questions about agentic AI, tool permissions and France
What does the CNIL note of 20 July 2026 say about agentic AI?
In it the CNIL and the Conseil de l’IA et du Numérique describe how agentic AI is built and which risks for personal data follow from that. Presenting the note, the CNIL sums up the finding in two phrases: that personal data circulates between numerous services, and that a real risk of losing control over one’s own data arises from it. As possible building blocks the note names, among others, traceability per task, a risk ranking of the possible actions and human sign-off before critical steps. The note is expressly exploratory and therefore neither a recommendation nor a binding framework. This article is no substitute for legal advice.
Does EU Cowork AI meet Article 31 of the loi SREN?
In managed operation it does not, and we would rather say so ourselves. The proof can only be furnished through a qualification from ANSSI or a certification issued in the EU or the EEA and recognised as equivalent by the agency, and Switzerland belongs neither to the Union nor to the European Economic Area. For bodies that fall under this duty, what remains is self-hosting: the duty attaches to obtaining a cloud service from a private provider. The software is under an MIT licence, and what that means in operation is set out under Self-hosting .
Does this duty also apply to local authorities and to private companies?
No. The implementing decree names the administrations of the State, their operators and six groupements d’intérêt public listed by name. Local and regional authorities are not named in the decree; they therefore do not fall under this duty, and between private companies it does not apply in any case. Sovereignty still turns up in tenders there, but usually as an award criterion and not as a ground for exclusion. What applies in your procedure is in your tender documents and not in this article.
What does the MCP version of 28 July 2026 change in practice?
It makes the transport stateless: the opening handshake and the session identifier fall away, and every request carries its own details with it. For operation that mainly means tool servers are easier to run behind a load balancer, because no session is tied to a particular instance. On top of that come a hardened authorisation and an orderly extension regime; managed authorisation for enterprises is kept there as an extension of its own. Which version is used in your environment is something we settle case by case. Permissions per tool and an entry in the log do not depend on any particular protocol version.
How is an agent stopped from changing or sending something?
Reading and writing tools are separate permissions. Write access has to be permitted separately, otherwise the process ends with a draft. Permissions apply in the order user, role, group, server default, and a tool that is not released does not appear in the plan. Executed and refused calls both stand in the audit log, which you can export.
Does this show us all the AI use in our company?
No, and that expectation could not be met either. What runs through EU Cowork AI becomes visible, not what happens alongside it in private accounts. How large that gap is cannot be pinned down cleanly: the official statistics expressly do not count individual use by employees, which is why surveys among employees land on considerably higher figures than surveys among companies. A register of all the AI systems in use does not come out of this by itself, that remains organisational work.
Does this protect against prompt injection?
No. Prompt injection means that an instruction is hidden in a document, a message or a web page and a model misreads it as a task while reading. No permission management helps against that, and we do not claim otherwise. What the platform does is limit the blast radius and make the process auditable: a tool that is not released is not called, write access needs a second decision, and every call is in the log. The same goes for a malicious tool server: the platform cannot detect it, what it can do is limit the damage it causes.
What does it cost, and what is different when self-hosting?
Managed operation costs CHF 14 per person per month, outside Switzerland €15, of which CHF 7.50 or €8 is model credit in the shared pool of your organisation. Operation runs in the ISO 27001 certified data centres of Green in Lupfig; that certification is the one held by the data centres and not ours. When self-hosting you determine the whole chain yourself, the software is under an MIT licence and costs nothing. All details are on the pricing page.
Walk through one of your own workflows
Bring a process that today runs across several programs, and we will go through it step by step: which tool, which sign-off, which entry in the log, and at which point a person decides. Or sign up and try it out yourself.

# Italy’s AI decrees: not yet in force

Italy’s AI decrees: not yet in force | EU Cowork AI

- Oversight as a criminal offence in Italy: not yet in force
Law and operations
When human oversight becomes a criminal offence: three workflows, and what did not yet apply at the time of writing
The Italian Council of Ministers has given final approval to two implementing decrees under the country’s AI law. They provide for making the failure to supervise high-risk systems a criminal offence, for adding AI offences to the liability of the company itself, and for rendering void a dismissal based solely on automated processing. This article works through three workflows to show what can be prepared today, and it says first what was not yet in force.
Law and operations
3 September 2026
Reading time: 12 minutes
- Where things stand
- Who is affected
- Demonstrating oversight

In brief
- On 4 August 2026 the Italian Council of Ministers gave final approval to two implementing decrees under its AI law. One of them adds Article 437-bis to the codice penale, Italy’s criminal code: one to five years in prison where the prescribed technical safety measures or the human oversight of a high-risk system are omitted and a concrete danger to life or physical integrity follows from that. 1
- When this text went to press on 2 September 2026, the two decrees had not been published in the Gazzetta Ufficiale, Italy’s official journal. 2 Numbering and wording become binding only with publication, and until then Italy had no AI criminal offence.
- A second new article, 25-vicies, adds AI offences to the liability of the company under decree 231, the Italian law that makes the organisation itself answer for offences committed in its interest, with 600 to 1,000 quotas and disqualification sanctions on the draft wording. 1 At a quota value of 258 to 1,549 euros that works out at 154,800 to 1,549,000 euros. 3 A provision of the same package renders void a dismissal based solely on automated processing. 1
- What a platform can contribute to this is narrowly bounded: logs, permissions and a record of who intervened and when. The risk analysis, the procedures and the oversight itself remain the job of your company, and for the strategic data of a public administration our Swiss operation is not enough on the wording of the ACN rulebook. This article is no substitute for legal advice.
