Where things stand: a criminal offence that is not yet in the official journal
Italy passed its AI law almost a year ago. Legge 132/2025 entered into force on 10 October 2025 and instructed the government to align national law with the EU AI Act within twelve months and to regulate the cases of unlawful production and use of AI systems. 4 On 10 June 2026 the Council of Ministers approved two drafts on a preliminary reading, and on 4 August 2026 it adopted them on the final reading. 1
At the core of it sits a new Article 437-bis of the criminal code. It punishes anyone who omits the prescribed technical safety measures or the human oversight of a high-risk AI system and thereby triggers a concrete danger: one to five years in prison where the life or physical integrity of individuals is at stake, two to eight years where the danger is directed at public safety or the security of the state. Alongside it come the new Article 25-vicies, which adds AI offences to the list of predicate offences for the liability of the company under decree 231 of 2001, and a provision of the same decree, which renders void a dismissal based solely on automated processing. 1 Liability under decree 231 falls not on the person who acted but on the organisation, and besides the fine it also carries a ban on entering into contracts with the public administration. 3
And now the part that an article about new criminal law has to say first. When this text went to press on 2 September 2026, the two decrees had not been published in the Gazzetta Ufficiale. 2 What the Council of Ministers adopts is a text on its way to the official journal: the order of the articles, their numbering and their wording become binding only with publication, and until then no AI criminal offence applies in Italy. Anyone selling you a finished checklist on Article 437-bis today is selling you the reading of a text whose final version they do not know. Check the published wording before you build anything on it. This article is no substitute for legal advice.
Against that background it is worth looking at where the country stands. According to the survey by the Italian statistics office Istat, which rests on a sample of 26,246 companies and is representative of 218,446 companies with ten or more employees, 16.4% of companies used at least one AI technology in 2025; among large companies the figure is 53.1%, among small and medium-sized ones 15.7%, and the gap between the two has widened from 20 percentage points in 2023 to 37 percentage points. 5 More telling for our subject is another figure from the same survey: 33.4% of the companies that use AI name none of the proposed fields of application, and 83.3% of those are businesses with 10 to 49 employees. 6 Anyone who cannot say what they use AI for cannot say either whether one of those systems falls into the high-risk category.
1
2
3
4
- Legge 132/2025, in force since 10 October 2025, with a mandate to the government
- Council of Ministers of 10 June 2026, two drafts on a preliminary reading
- Council of Ministers of 4 August 2026, adopted on the final reading
- Publication in the Gazzetta Ufficiale, still open at the time of writing
The path of the two decrees. The wording becomes binding only with the last step.
Who this affects, and who it does not
The criminal offence hangs on a single word, and that word is high-risk. The EU AI Act, Regulation 2024/1689, lists in Annex I the systems built into a product as a safety component, and in Annex III the fields of use that count as high-risk in their own right, among them employment and recruitment, creditworthiness assessment, critical infrastructure, education and parts of law enforcement. Article 14 requires such systems to be built so that people can effectively oversee them, and Article 26 requires the deployer to assign that oversight to natural persons who are trained for it and hold the authority to carry it out. 7
These obligations do not apply yet, however. The Digital Omnibus, adopted as Regulation 2026/1744 and published in the Official Journal of the Union on 24 July 2026, has narrowed the high-risk article further and postponed its application: to 2 December 2027 for standalone high-risk systems and to 2 August 2028 for systems built into a product. 8 How a national criminal offence relates to that postponed calendar is one of the questions only the published wording will answer. We put that on record here rather than making the urgency look greater than it is.
The second question is how many companies would even know whether they are affected. Sound figures on this are scarce: the best known survey of AI governance in large Italian companies, the Osservatorio Artificial Intelligence of the Politecnico di Milano, is sponsor-funded and does not disclose its sample, which is why we do not repeat its shares here. 9 From the same direction comes a figure from the statistics office that Italian reporting regularly gets wrong: of the companies that do not use AI, 11.5% have considered using it at all, and the obstacles reported refer to that subgroup alone, namely a lack of skills at 58.6% and a lack of legal clarity at 47.3%. 10 That is not a statement about the Italian economy as a whole, and anyone using it that way is talking a problem up.

AI as a safety component of a product falls into the high-risk category under Annex I of the AI Act, and that is exactly what the planned criminal offence attaches to

Selection, assignment and termination of employment appear in Annex III; the nullity provided for hits the dismissal decided solely by automated means
Drafts with the source reference in the documents, without a decision, plus a note naming the person who decided

Creditworthiness assessment of natural persons, together with risk classification and pricing in life and health insurance, is named in Annex III
Permissions per tool, so that a model reaches only the records belonging to the task

A register of what actually runs through the platform, with accounts, connectors and permissions
The overview below sorts by who has to carry out the assessment, not by who is doing something wrong. The right-hand column contains only what a platform can contribute, which is evidence. The assessment itself belongs in your company, and in regulated fields with your legal counsel as well.
Use case 1: setting up human oversight so that it can be demonstrated
In most companies the oversight has long been happening. A specialist looks at what a system proposes and decides. It is just that nothing is left of it afterwards: no timestamp, no source reference, no note, nothing that could be shown to an authority two years later. In the AI workspace this step runs inside one case file. The proposal from the specialist system is opened together with the documents it rests on, the responsible person records the review and the decision in the same case file, and the call appears with timestamp, account and tool in the audit log, the running record of every access, which you can export as a file.
Two settings decide whether this becomes usable evidence. First the permissions: they apply in the order user, role, group, server default, and write access to connected systems has to be approved separately. Second the source references: answers from a knowledge base, that is from your company’s own documents, are shown with the place where they appear. That way you can later show not only that someone reviewed the case but what they reviewed it against. Which settings your administration sets for this is described under Governance .
1
2
3
- Proposal from the specialist system, opened with the documents it rests on
- Review, note and decision by the responsible person in the same case file
- Entry in the audit log with timestamp, account, tool and outcome
The oversight happens anyway. What is new is that it leaves a trace.
The limit to this, and it is the most important one in this article: the product does not create human oversight, it makes it demonstrable. Anyone who confirms a proposal without reading it produces a log entry and not oversight. Whether oversight is sufficient in substance is judged in the end by a supervisory authority and a court, not by a log.
Use case 2: a register of what actually runs
The first question in an audit is never whether your company uses AI, but which AI. It can only be answered if the points of access come together in one place. Through EU Cowork AI your staff reach over 100 models through a single access, processed on the EU side via EuRouter, together with the Anthropic models via Amazon Bedrock in the European profile. Third-party systems are connected via MCP, the Model Context Protocol, an open standard for connecting to external programs; a single connection of that kind is called a connector, and permissions apply per tool.
What comes out of this is not a piece of paper but an analysis: which models are available at all in your instance, that is in your own installation of the software, which model is the server default, which knowledge bases exist and who may read them, which connectors are set up, which tools those release and who actually makes use of them. Consumption is broken down per model. Which software can be connected today is listed on the Integrations page.
1
2
3
- All model access runs through one point of access instead of scattered accounts
- Connectors to third-party systems via MCP, with permissions per tool
- Analysis: model, knowledge base, tool, account and consumption
What runs through the platform becomes visible. Everything else stays invisible, and that is part of the statement.
The limit: no automatic AI inventory comes out of it. The platform sees what runs through it, and nothing else. A browser extension, a private account on a phone, a model inside a specialist application, all of that stays invisible. That is exactly why the 33.4% of users who name no field of application are an indication of how much runs alongside the official routes. 6 A register that holds up in an audit under decree 231 or under the AI Act is broader, and it is kept by people.
Use case 3: preparing personnel decisions without taking them by automated means
A job advertisement brings in more applications than can be read in an afternoon. The usual route is automatic ranking, and that is precisely the route Italy is narrowing. The workflow that remains looks like this: the specialist unit sets the criteria from the advertisement and approves them. The AI colleague then compiles, for each application, what the documents say on those criteria, each time with the place where it appears, and what is missing. Nothing is ranked, nothing is weighted, nothing is discarded.
The decision stays with a person and is recorded as that person’s decision, with reasons, date and name. What the General Data Protection Regulation prohibits is the decision based solely on automated processing with a significant effect, not support in reaching it. 13 The adopted provision of the same decree draws that line more sharply for dismissal by placing the legal consequence not in a fine but in nullity. 1 On top of this comes an obligation that already applies in Italy: Legge 132/2025 requires employees to be informed in writing about the use of AI systems in the employment relationship. 4
1
2
3
- Criteria from the advertisement, set and approved by the specialist unit
- A compilation per application, with the source reference in the documents
- Decision, reasons and the name of the deciding person in the case file
The draft comes from the system. The decision comes from a person and is recorded as such.
The limit, and an Italian case helps here. On 14 May 2026 the Garante, Italy’s data protection authority, issued a formal warning to the provider of a browser add-on that was meant to infer employee stress from messages in chat programs; what mattered was not the intention but that the aggregated analyses could put the employer in a position to learn something about the emotional state of individuals, even indirectly. The warning also relies expressly on Article 5(1)(f) of the AI Act, which prohibits systems that infer emotions in the workplace. 14 Carried over, that means: a signature under a ranking that has effectively already decided is not a human decision. Anyone who draws the shortlist so tightly that only one person is left has decided by automated means and had a human sign it.
Limits: what is not being claimed here
First the restriction that takes the scale out of the whole article. The criminal offence applies to high-risk systems. An ordinary chat assistant that someone uses to draft a text, produce a summary or put a question to their own documents is normally not one. Anyone suggesting that every company is affected from now on is not being serious, and the Digital Omnibus has narrowed the high-risk article further and pushed back its application. 8 Checking whether one of your systems falls into that category still makes sense, and it is a legal check and not a technical one.
Second: no product makes a Modello 231 compliant, that is the organisational and control model decree 231 requires. What a platform delivers is logging and permission control, in other words evidence. The organisational model itself consists of a risk analysis for your company, of procedures, of a supervisory body and of a system of sanctions, and if it comes to it a court decides whether it was adequate. Compliance is not met by introducing a piece of software, and a provider who hints otherwise is selling you a problem for later.
1
2
3
4
- No high-risk system, no strategic data: managed operation in Lupfig
- A high-risk system in use: oversight, procedures and assessment with you
- Strategic data of an administration: all metadata within the territory of the Union
- This case: self-hosting on your infrastructure, with no us in between
Four rows. At the third one our operation in Lupfig does not fit on the wording, and the fourth is the answer to that.
Third: what is prohibited is the solely automated personnel decision, not the assistance. Anyone concluding from this that AI has become unusable in HR is reading the rule too broadly; anyone concluding that a signature is enough is reading it too narrowly. What counts is whether a person actually assessed the case and was in a position to assess it, and for that they need time, access to the documents and the authority to decide differently from the proposal.
Fourth, the point where our own offering does not fit. The ACN cloud rulebook for the public administration classifies data and services as ordinary, critical or strategic, where strategic means that an impairment can touch national security. For strategic data and services it requires all types of metadata to be processed on infrastructure located within the territory of the European Union; the requirement carries the number 8_S in Annex 2 and the number 17_S in Annex 3, and the only exception is the metadata needed to provide the services expressly named there. 11 Switzerland is not part of the territory of the Union. On the wording, our managed operation in the ISO 27001 certified data centres of Green in Lupfig is precisely not enough for this case, and the certification of those data centres changes nothing about that, because it concerns the security of the operation and not the location. The honest answer here is self-hosting : you run the software under the MIT licence on your own infrastructure within the territory of the Union, the model path stays within the Union as well, and we have no part in it.
Fifth, the other direction, so that no false fear grows out of this. That cloud rulebook applies to the public administration and to those who supply it, not to private companies. For a private company it is a benchmark and not an obligation. And where a tender calls for a data centre in Italy, that is as a rule a criterion set by the contracting authority and not a statutory requirement. What applies to you depends on your classification, your sector and your contracts. This article is no substitute for legal advice.
Frequently asked questions on Article 437-bis, the Modello 231 and human oversight
Does a prison sentence for missing AI oversight apply in Italy from now on?
No, at least not as at the editorial deadline of this article. The Council of Ministers adopted the two decrees on the final reading on 4 August 2026; on 2 September 2026 they had not been published. Article numbering and wording become binding only with publication in the Gazzetta Ufficiale. Check the published text before you base measures on it. This section is no substitute for legal advice.
Is our chat assistant a high-risk system?
As a rule, no. Under the AI Act, high-risk covers systems built into a product as a safety component and systems in the fields of use in Annex III, such as recruitment, creditworthiness assessment, critical infrastructure or education. An assistant that drafts texts and answers questions put to your own documents normally does not fall under it. What is decisive is not the tool but the purpose you use it for, and that classification is made by your company.
Does a platform make our Modello 231 compliant?
No, and no product can. An organisational model under decree 231 consists of a risk analysis, of procedures, of a supervisory body and of a system of sanctions. A platform supplies evidence for it: logs of who called which tool and when, and permissions showing who was allowed to reach what. Whether the model is effective is decided if it comes to it by a court, not by a provider.
Are we still allowed to use AI in recruitment?
Under the adopted text, what is prohibited is the solely automated decision, not the support. You can open up documents, set criteria against each other and have drafts produced. The decision has to be taken by a person who actually assessed the case and could have decided otherwise. In Italy there is the additional duty to inform employees in writing about the use of such systems in the employment relationship.
What does the Digital Omnibus change about the deadlines?
Regulation 2026/1744 was published in the Official Journal of the Union on 24 July 2026. It postpones the application of the obligations for high-risk systems to 2 December 2027 for standalone systems and to 2 August 2028 for systems built into a product. It changes little about the obligations themselves and a great deal about when they start. How a national criminal offence relates to this can only be judged from the published wording.
Is a server location in Switzerland enough for Italian administrations?
For strategic data and services it is not, on the wording of the cloud rulebook. There, all types of metadata have to be processed on infrastructure within the territory of the European Union, and Switzerland is not part of it. For that case, self-hosting on your own infrastructure is the form that fits, not our managed operation in Lupfig. For private companies this rulebook does not apply; there it is a benchmark and not an obligation.
What is in the audit log, and what is not?
The log holds the calls that run through the platform: timestamp, account, model used, tool called and outcome, exportable as a file. What it does not hold is what happens outside it, so a browser extension, a private account or a model inside a specialist application. An AI inventory does not come out of it on its own. Telemetry is switched off by default with us and customer data does not train any models; both are set out in the data processing agreement .
What does it cost, and what is free?
The software is under the MIT licence, and self-hosting is free of charge. Managed operation costs CHF 14 per person per month, €15 outside Switzerland, of which CHF 7.50 or €8 is model credit in your organisation’s shared pool. If your case calls for all metadata to be processed within the territory of the Union, self-hosting is not the cheaper of the two forms but the only one that fits. All the figures are on the Pricing page.

48 invented judgments: three workflows in which every statement brings its source reference
A Spanish court has fined a lawyer for citing 48 judgments that do not exist. The case is less about regulation than about craft: an answer without a checkable source is worthless, however well it reads. This article walks through three workflows in which the source reference travels with the answer, and names what it does not do.
Knowledge bases and proof
3 September 2026
Reading time: 12 minutes
- Starting point
- Who is affected
- Your own knowledge base
- Checking against your documents
- Draft with sources
- Limits of the source reference
- Frequently asked questions
- Sources
In brief
- On 10 February 2026 the High Court of Justice of the Canary Islands, the top court of that Spanish region, fined a lawyer 420 euros because his written submission cited 48 authorities that do not exist. 1
- The court sets that sum expressly at half an annual subscription to an AI tool built for legal work, and calls the episode a breach of the fundamental duty of human oversight. 1
- The largest obstacle to artificial intelligence in Spanish companies is nevertheless not regulation but a shortage of skilled staff, named by 45.8% of the companies in the Banco de España business survey. 2
- That is why this article is about craft and not about compliance: EU Cowork AI puts the place a statement stands in right next to the statement. That does not prevent invented answers, it makes them checkable.

- Starting point

Starting point: 48 citations that do not exist
On 10 February 2026 the criminal chamber of the High Court of Justice of the Canary Islands fined a lawyer 420 euros. In an appeal submission he had cited 48 authorities, judgments of Spain’s Supreme Court and a report by the country’s judicial governing council, which do not exist. The court records that a general AI tool was used rather than one built for the law, and that the cross-check against the official case law database never happened. It sets the size of the fine at half the approximate annual cost of a subscription to an AI tool built for legal work. The ruling also went to the bar association at which the lawyer is registered. 1
It did not stay a single case. On 7 July 2026 the labour chamber of the High Court of Justice of Galicia imposed 1,800 euros on a lawyer whose submission carried 24 citations that were invented, distorted or unrelated to the case; there too the court took its bearings from the annual cost of a tested legal tool. 3 Cases of this kind are known from several European countries, and the duty behind them is older than the tools. As early as 9 September 2024 the First Chamber of Spain’s Constitutional Court formally reprimanded a lawyer for quoting verbatim from 19 decisions of that court, not one of which existed. 4 For the judiciary itself, the Consejo General del Poder Judicial, the self-governing body of the Spanish courts, issued an instruction in January 2026 that requires real, conscious and effective human control over every use of such systems. 5
From the other direction comes a recommendation that leaves many businesses at a loss. On 27 January 2026 the Spanish data protection authority published ten recommendations on handling AI tools. For work it advises sticking to your own organisation’s information and security rules and entering nothing that would give away confidential data about the company, its staff or its customers. 6 It names no alternative. Anyone who follows that advice and still wants to work with their own documents needs a place where those documents are allowed to sit.
Now to the official surveys, because they refute a convenient thesis. According to the Banco de España business survey of around 6,300 companies, 19.9% use an AI system, 60% of them only on a trial basis and a mere 6% intensively. The obstacle in first place is a shortage of skilled staff at 45.8%, then excessive cost at 40.8% and the availability of a company’s own data at 37.8%. Regulatory hurdles including data protection were on the list of options as well, and landed behind those three. 2 For the first quarter of 2025 the national statistics institute counts 21.1% AI use among companies with ten or more employees and 13.4% among the smaller ones. 7 Anyone telling the story that regulation is holding Spain back is writing past these figures. The bottleneck is knowledge, and knowledge grows where an answer can be checked.
1
2
3
4
- The question, put to your own documents
- The passage the answer comes from
- The answer with the place it stands in
- Open, read, release: this step stays with a person
The chain does not end at the answer. It ends at the person who opened the source.
Who is affected: five groups that need a source reference
The question of where a sentence comes from is rarely a matter of taste. Behind it there is usually someone who has to answer for that sentence: before a court, before a regulator, before customers or before their own management. That is why the source reference is not an extra but the part of the answer that makes it usable at all.
Spain’s business structure makes the subject broader than it first sounds. As at 1 January 2025 the national statistics institute counted 3,310,824 active companies. 54.4% of them had not a single employee, and 95.1% stayed below ten. 8 At that size there is no IT department to assess a tool, approve it and monitor it. There is one person finishing something off in the evening.
That data protection is no side note here shows in the authority’s annual figures: 30,931 complaints in 2025, up 64% on the year before, and fines totalling 48,108,765 euros. 9 These figures cover data protection as a whole and not artificial intelligence in particular; we do not present them as AI statistics. They describe the setting into which a tool is introduced.
Who is asking
What creates the need
What EU Cowork AI contributes there
Law firms and legal departments
Every citation in a submission has to hold, and the courts now punish the opposite with fines and reports to the bar
Answers from your own documents with the place they stand in, plus model choice and permissions through the administration
Tax advice, fiduciary services and bookkeeping
Client files are covered by professional secrecy, and the data protection authority advises against copying them into outside tools
An access route where the files stay on your own server or in Lupfig and customer data trains no models
Public administration and its suppliers
Decisions have to be reasoned and traceable, and tenders ask for the proof
An audit log over every call, that is a record that can be exported, plus permissions down to the individual tool
HR departments and internal rulebooks
Instructions, collective agreements and handbooks keep changing, and answers given to staff have to be backed up
A knowledge base built from whichever version is in force, with a source reference on both sides of the comparison
Micro-businesses without their own IT
Staff use AI anyway, only without a rule, without a record and without proof
A managed access route instead of use in the shadows, telemetry off by default, permissions in the order user, role, group, server default
What connects the five groups below is not the sector but the kind of responsibility. At the end stands a statement that someone puts their name to. For statements like that, an answer without a source reference is not half as good, it is unusable.
Use case 1: the knowledge base in which every statement shows where it stands
Your company puts its documents into a knowledge base: contracts, instructions, minutes, handbooks, the correspondence on a matter. Someone asks which notice period applies to a particular type of contract. What comes back is not a smooth paragraph but an answer with the place it comes from behind it: document, section, passage of text. One click opens that passage in its context.
The difference lies not in the wording but in the checkability. An answer without an origin has to be believed. An answer with an origin can be checked, and checked at the place itself. That is exactly the step missing in the court cases described above, and exactly the step that turns a tool for drafting text into a tool for work.
1
2
3
- Your documents, in the state they are in today
- The question reaches only the passages that belong to the answer
- Answer with document, section and passage of text
The collection stays where it is. Only the passage a single question needs travels.
The limit here: a knowledge base is only as good as its contents. If an outdated version sits in it, that version gets quoted with a source reference and looks more credible for it than before. Whoever puts documents in has to settle which version applies and who maintains it. That is work, and it cannot be handed over to a model.
Use case 2: an outside document against your own documents
A draft contract, an audit report or the new version of a rulebook comes in. The question is the same every time: what in it departs from what applies here? You set the outside document beside your own knowledge base. What comes back is a list of divergences: covered, open, contradictory, and for every line the place on both sides, in the outside text and in your own.
This task shows why the source reference has to sit on both sides. A divergence only becomes a divergence once someone has read the two formulations side by side. If one side is missing, what remains is an assertion nobody can retrace, and the check starts again from the beginning.
1
2
3
- The outside document, as it arrives
- Your instructions, templates and contracts in force
- List of divergences with a source reference on both sides
Two collections, one list. What follows from it is still decided by the professionals.
The limit here: the result is a pointer and not a decision. A language model can miss a divergence or invent one that is not there, and the longer the texts get, the more readily that happens. In regulated areas the list replaces neither the qualified professional nor the internal sign-off. This article is no substitute for legal advice.
Use case 3: the draft that stays recognisable as a draft
At some point the check turns into a text: a statement of position, an answer to a customer, an internal note. The AI colleague puts up a draft, and visibly as a draft. Every statement taken from your documents carries its source with it, and the source can be unfolded. Anything formulated without a basis in your documents is marked as such.
The gain lies in the order of reading. Someone handed a finished text reads it for style. Someone handed a draft with sources to unfold reads it for sources. That second posture is the one missing in the court cases. The design of a tool can encourage it, it cannot compel it.
1
2
3
- Instruction and passages from your own documents
- Draft with a source at every supported statement
- Sign-off by a person, and only then dispatch
Nothing goes out that nobody has released. The release stands in the log.
The limit here: a draft does not become correct by showing sources. What counts is that someone opens them. Where deadlines press, that is exactly what gets skipped, and no tool can prevent it. Anyone introducing this workflow should plan the check in as a step of the work and not as a good intention.
Limits: what a source reference does not do
The most important sentence in this article is the most uncomfortable one. Source references do not prevent invented answers. They make them checkable. A language model produces text that sounds plausible, and it does so even when the basis is missing. Human control remains mandatory, and that is exactly what the courts say: the High Court of Justice of the Canary Islands speaks of a breach of the fundamental duty of human oversight, which it calls indispensable whenever AI tools are used, and requires such systems to be treated as an aid and never as the deciding authority. 1 Anyone who promises you something else at this point is selling you a certainty that does not exist.
On top of that comes an error harder to spot than a freely invented source. A language model can also attach a source reference to the wrong place: the document exists, the section exists, only it does not carry the statement. In the Galician proceedings part of the criticised citations were of exactly that kind, formally present and unrelated to the case in substance. 3 From that follows a plain rule: the source has to be opened, not merely present. A source reference that nobody clicks on is decoration.
1
2
3
4
- The model names a place
- The place is opened and read
- If it does not carry the statement, the sentence goes
- Only after that does the text go out
The source reference is an opportunity to check and not an assurance. The checking is done by hand.
On the state of the law, without turning it into advice. In Spain a bill on the governance of artificial intelligence has been tabled, published in the official gazette of the Congress of Deputies on 12 June 2026; it is in parliamentary deliberation and is not law in force. 10 The European directive on network and information security, NIS2 for short, is not transposed into Spanish national law; on 8 July 2026 the European Commission therefore took Spain, together with three other member states, to the Court of Justice of the European Union. 11 We therefore claim neither that your company meets one of these requirements with our tool, nor that it would already have to meet them today. Check that for your own case, and if in doubt with your trade association. This article is no substitute for legal advice.
And now the awkward point, the one about money. The state programmes with which small Spanish businesses financed their digitalisation are taking no new applications. The large digitalisation programme closed its final two calls on 31 October 2025, by its own account with around 850,000 supported businesses and more than 3.4 billion euros. 12 The programme for subsidised digital consulting took its last applications back in March 2025 and has been in settlement since. 13 Whoever starts now pays for it themselves. That argues for a low entry price and for free self-hosting under the MIT licence. Only self-hosting presupposes IT competence, and by the official figures that is precisely what these businesses lack most. 2 We do not resolve this contradiction. For a business without its own IT, managed operation is the more honest route, even though it costs money.
Finally, what we do not claim. EU Cowork AI does not compile an inventory of all the AI systems in your company, it sees only what runs through itself. It does not create human oversight, it makes it demonstrable. Managed operation meets no requirement that calls for customer-held keys without provider access; only self-hosting can do that. And the Green data centres in Lupfig are certified to ISO 27001, which is that operator’s certification and not ours.
Frequently asked questions about source references, knowledge bases and proof
Does a knowledge base with source references prevent invented judgments?
No. It makes it possible to spot an invented item in seconds, because next to every statement stands the place it is supposed to come from. Whether anyone opens that place is decided by the person at the screen. That is precisely the step the Spanish courts called for in the cases that became known, and precisely where the failure lay. A tool can make the check easy, it cannot take it off your hands.
Are we allowed to put client files into an AI tool at all?
The Spanish data protection authority expressly advises against entering confidential information about the company, its staff or its customers into AI tools. It draws no distinction by form of operation. It names no alternative. With a managed or self-hosted workplace the difference lies in where the files sit and who is allowed to reach them; whether that is enough for your case depends on your contracts and your professional duties. This article is no substitute for legal advice.
Is there already a dedicated AI law in force in Spain?
No. There is a bill, published in the official gazette of the Congress of Deputies on 12 June 2026 and currently in parliamentary deliberation. Until it is passed it is not law in force, and its wording can still change. Offers that already derive duties or fines from it today are worth examining on exactly this point.
What does NIS2 mean for us in Spain?
The directive is not transposed into Spanish national law. The European Commission therefore took Spain to the Court of Justice of the European Union on 8 July 2026, together with three other member states. What follows from that for your company depends on the sector and can only be answered conclusively once the national law exists. We claim neither compliance nor non-compliance on this point.
Is there still state funding for digitalisation?
Not under the known programmes. The large digitalisation programme for small businesses closed its final two calls on 31 October 2025, and the programme for subsidised digital consulting took its last applications in March 2025. Whoever starts today funds it themselves. That is why the entry price is the decisive figure for small businesses, and why the software is available under an MIT licence for self-hosting .
We have no IT department. Can we still run this?
Self-hosting costs nothing, but it presupposes that someone sets up a server, updates it and backs it up. Where that competence is missing, managed operation is the more honest route, even though it costs money. We say so openly, because a shortage of skilled staff is the largest obstacle in the official surveys and a free offer does not solve that problem, it shifts it. What self-hosting means day to day is set out under Self-hosting .
Does our data train the models?
No. Customer data is not used to train models, and telemetry is switched off by default. Your documents, knowledge bases, conversation histories and accounts sit in the Green data centres in Lupfig or on your own server. Only the passage a single request needs goes to the model. The commitment stands in the data processing agreement , the parties involved in the subprocessor list .
What does managed operation cost?
It costs 15 € per person and month, in Switzerland 14 CHF, of which 8 € or 7.50 CHF respectively is model credit in your organisation’s shared pool. One access route opens more than 100 models, processed on the EU side, plus the Anthropic models through Amazon Bedrock in the European profile. The administration settles which models are on offer and which one is the server default. All the details are on the pricing page.
Try it on a document of your own
Bring an anonymised file, a rulebook or a set of internal instructions, and we will walk through the workflow together, expressly including the points where the answer is wrong. Or sign up and open the sources yourself.

Models and operation
Claude Opus and Sonnet on Amazon Bedrock: three workflows, and where the data is really processed
Anthropic’s top models can be reached through EU Cowork AI, run on Amazon Bedrock under its European profile. DORA, the proposed Cloud and AI Development Act and Chapter V of the GDPR all put the same question to you: where the processing happens. This article walks through three workflows, explains the architecture behind them and names the drawback that stays.

In brief
- In a Swiss survey, 51% of the companies asked call it business critical that AI systems meet Swiss or European data protection requirements. 1
- EU Cowork AI gives you access to Anthropic’s models, Claude Opus and Claude Sonnet. They run on Amazon Bedrock, the model service from AWS, and specifically under its European inference profile.
- Your documents, knowledge bases, conversation histories and accounts stay on the Swiss server or on your own. Only what a single request needs goes to the model, and it is not stored there.
- The drawback, stated plainly: AWS is a US company, so the CLOUD Act applies. Where the servers stand does not protect against that, and encryption does not help at the moment of processing.

Starting point: the best model or the right place
In European companies artificial intelligence has arrived in everyday work. Scaling it has not. A Swiss survey by EY among 604 people in Swiss companies records that for half of the respondents, exactly 51%, it is business critical that AI systems meet Swiss or European data protection requirements. 1 Not desirable, not important: business critical. That makes the location of the data something other than an argument for the second meeting. It is a condition a project fails on.
The European statistics show the same thing from the other side, and for this audience they are the figures to start from. According to Eurostat, 20.0% of enterprises in the EU with ten or more employees used artificial intelligence in 2025. Among those that looked at it and then let it go, 48.8% named concerns about data protection and privacy. 2 That number covers the whole Union rather than one country, which is why it carries more weight here than any single national survey. In Germany, 54% of the companies surveyed say data protection is holding back the use of AI in their own business. 3 Three surveys, three sets of countries, one finding.
The obvious answer is to use a European model instead. The same body of research shows that this answer does not sell. In the Bitkom Cloud Report, a German survey, 78% of the companies asked consider Germany too dependent on US cloud providers, but 65% would accept none of the drawbacks put to them in exchange for digital sovereignty: not longer waits for new features, not missing features, not higher costs. 4 Sovereignty is wanted and not paid for as soon as it costs performance. That is uncomfortable, and it is the most honest number in this article.
That sets the task. Not to replace the good model with a European one. Instead, to bring in the model people will choose anyway, in a way that keeps the body of documents where it belongs and lets someone say afterwards what happened where. The next sections show what that looks like, first in three workflows, then in the architecture, and last in the limit that stays.
1
2
3
4
- Your documents and knowledge bases stay on your server
- Only the extract a request needs goes with it
- The model runs inside a European set of regions
- Answer with its source, log entry on your side
The path of a single question. Anything not on that path stays where it is.
Who asks for this: a sober look at the demand
The question about location is rarely a matter of taste. In most cases someone stands behind it who has a regulation, a contract or a supervisor at their back. Chapter V of the GDPR sets the frame for everyone: a transfer to a third country needs a legal basis and it has to be documented, whatever the service is called. For banks and insurers in Europe, DORA, the regulation on digital operational resilience in the financial sector, goes further and requires the contract for an IT service to state in which regions and countries the service is performed and where data is stored, with advance notice when that changes. 5 National supervisors ask for the same evidence in their own audits. Because we operate from Switzerland, the FINMA outsourcing circular applies here as well: the institution, its audit firm and the supervisor must be able to exercise their inspection and audit rights even when a service is outsourced abroad, and the information needed for a resolution has to be accessible in Switzerland at all times. 6
For the public sector, a preference is turning into a procurement condition right now. The European Commission has proposed a Cloud and AI Development Act which sets out four sovereignty levels for cloud and AI services. The first requires that data is processed and stored in infrastructure inside the Union. 7 That is a proposal and not law yet, but anyone supplying public administrations today already knows the direction from the questionnaires.
So why Anthropic’s models in particular? Because companies pick them anyway. A survey by Menlo Ventures among 495 decision makers puts Anthropic’s share of the enterprise market for language model interfaces at 40%, and at 54% in the coding segment. 8 That sample is American, and we do not pass it off as a European figure. The European figure alongside it says something else. According to Synergy Research, the three large American providers hold around 70% of the European cloud market, and the European providers together hold 15%. 9 Anyone serious about sovereignty has to work with that picture instead of arguing against it.
Who asks
What triggers the need
Where the top model makes the difference
Banks and insurers
DORA requires the regions and countries of processing to be named in the contract, and national supervisors ask for the same evidence; in Switzerland the FINMA circular adds inspection rights and access in the country
Holding new circulars and regulations against your own internal rules, with a source on both sides
Public administration and its suppliers
The proposed Cloud and AI Development Act provides for processing and storage inside the Union at its first level
Opening up long consultation and tender documents, in several languages
Law firms, accountants, medical practices
Professional secrecy under national criminal law, plus client, payroll and patient data
Opening up files, contracts and correspondence without losing the source
Manufacturing and construction
Design and costing data are trade secrets; customer audits ask about the chain
Reading tenders, specifications and revised standards in full and finding the contradictions
Engineering and digital teams
Source code and system knowledge should not leave the organisation
Reading large code bases, preparing changes, finding faults along the chain
What links these five groups is not the sector but the kind of work: a lot of text at once, a rule that has to be followed exactly, and a chain of steps that has to hold together. That is precisely where the difference between a small model and a large one shows. For classification, extraction and short summaries a small model is still enough, and it costs a fraction as much. The administration makes that choice, not chance.
Use case 1: the long document nobody reads in full
A tender arrives with the main document, seven annexes and references to three standards. By the time anyone knows whether a bid is worth making, two days are gone and the deadline for questions is running. You put the whole set into the workspace for that case. Back comes a list: every requirement on its own, with the passage it comes from, next to it what your organisation can already evidence, and what is missing.
The difference from a smaller model is not in the single sentence, it is in the span. A requirement in Annex C contradicts an assurance in the main document. A date in a footnote on the price sheet does not match the deadline in the schedule of works. Contradictions like that only show up for a reader who holds the whole text in view at once. That is exactly what the large models are built for.
1
2
3
- Main document, annexes and references to standards, as they arrive
- Opened up against your organisation’s own documents
- Requirements with evidence, open gap and question to ask
The stack becomes a working list. Whether you bid is still your own decision afterwards.
What does not happen: nothing is submitted and nothing is promised. A language model can miss a requirement or attach the wrong source to a line, and it does so more readily the longer the text gets. A large context window is a possibility, not a promise: what fits into it is not therefore found again reliably. That is why every line carries the passage it comes from, and why the list is a draft to be checked, not a statement of eligibility.
Use case 2: the new rulebook against your own practice
A regulation is revised, a circular comes out, a standard appears in a new version. The question is the same every time and tedious every time: which parts of this concern us, and where does our current practice differ? The AI colleague puts the new rulebook and your own instructions, templates and process descriptions side by side and delivers a list of deviations: covered, open, contradictory, each with a source on both sides.
This task is the reason why the choice of model is not a detail. A small model finds the literal matches. The difference lies in the place where two formulations mean the same thing without using the same words, and in the place where two similar formulations do not mean the same thing at all. Anyone who has ever built a list of deviations by hand knows that this is where the work sits.
1
2
3
- The new rulebook in the version in force
- Your instructions, templates and process descriptions
- List of deviations with a source on both sides
Two bodies of text, one list. Judging what follows from it stays with the specialists.
The same limit applies here as everywhere: the result is a pointer, not a decision. In regulated areas it replaces neither the qualified professional nor the internal sign-off, and it is not legal advice in any case.
Use case 3: the case that runs across several systems
An enquiry comes in, and the answer sits in three programs: the contract in the document store, the delivery status in the ERP system, the last exchange of letters in the mailbox. Today a person clicks through all three. The AI colleague can take that over once the systems are connected. It plans the steps, calls the released tools one after another, checks every intermediate result and puts a draft up for approval at the end.
This chain is the real test. Hardly any model fails on a single step. What fails is holding out across seven of them: keeping the task in view, recognising an empty result as empty instead of inventing one, and stopping once the answer is there. Models in the Opus and Sonnet class are built for that, and that is what we use them for.
1
2
3
- The enquiry as it arrives
- The AI colleague plans the steps
- Calls into the connected systems, draft for approval
Every system is connected through MCP. Permissions apply per tool, and every call is recorded in the log.
MCP stands for Model Context Protocol, an open standard for connecting external systems. What the AI colleague is not allowed to see there, it does not see: the order is individual user, role, group, server default. Write access has to be released separately. Which software can be connected today is listed on the Integrations page.
The architecture: what runs where
The split is simpler than it sounds. Your documents, your knowledge bases, your accounts, the conversation histories and the audit log stay where they are today: in the ISO 27001 certified data centres run by Green in Lupfig, or on your own server. In the model access, the only thing that changes is the moment a question reaches a model.
That moment runs through Amazon Bedrock, the model service from AWS. Bedrock is not a program sitting in a cabinet at our office, it is a service AWS operates. For a request, your instance assembles what the model needs: the question, the course of the conversation and the extracts from your documents that belong to the answer. That package goes out encrypted, the model runs, the answer comes back and is filed with you. The body of documents does not travel with it. What never becomes part of a request, Bedrock never sees.
1
2
3
4
- Documents, knowledge bases and accounts on your server
- Only the extract the question needs leaves the instance
- Execution under the European profile of Amazon Bedrock
- Answer and log entry come back to you
The body of documents stays where it is. Only what the single question needs is in transit.
Now the question of regions, and here we would rather say it ourselves than leave it to someone else. The starting point is the AWS region Zurich. Anyone concluding from that the model runs in Zurich is wrong. AWS offers three modes for models: In-Region, where a request never leaves the chosen region, a geographic profile that distributes within one area, and a worldwide profile. For Claude Opus and Claude Sonnet, In-Region is not on offer in Zurich. 10 That is why we use the European profile. For it AWS undertakes that the data stays in European regions, and AWS itself decides which region processes the individual call. 11
For the processing itself, AWS states three undertakings you can look up. By default, inputs and outputs are not stored. Nobody operating the service sees them. And the model provider gets no access to them: the models run in separate accounts held by the Bedrock team, which the provider cannot enter. No model is trained on your inputs and outputs. 12 The small print belongs here too. For a few individual models AWS names an exception, under which data is kept for up to 30 days for abuse detection, in the region that processes the call. Opus and Sonnet are not on that list. 21 On our side the same undertaking is written into the data processing agreement , and everyone involved in the chain is named in the subprocessor list .
On our side everything stays as it was, and that is the point. The administration decides which models are available at all and which one is the default. Permissions apply down to individual tools. Every call is in the audit log, which you can export, and usage is broken down per model. If you self-host, you set up the route to the model yourself in any case, and you can leave this one out.
The drawback: AWS is a US company
Up to here a lot of this has sounded like an advantage. Now the part a provider had better say itself. Amazon Web Services is a US company, so the CLOUD Act of 2018 applies. The law obliges providers to hand over data in their possession, custody or control, and it says so expressly whether the data sits in the United States or anywhere else. 13 AWS writes itself that the law applies to all providers that operate in the US or have a legal presence there. 14 Where the servers stand does not protect against that. Anyone claiming otherwise is selling you a map instead of an answer.
The opposite is just as untrue. The European Data Protection Board and the European Data Protection Supervisor state in their joint assessment that the CLOUD Act does not permit systematic, large scale or indiscriminate collection, but governs targeted requests with procedural safeguards. 15 For content data, a judicial order is required as a rule.
What a provider can say about this was shown at a hearing in the French Senate on 10 June 2025. Before the committee of inquiry, where witnesses are sworn in, a representative of Microsoft France was asked whether he could guarantee that data belonging to French citizens would never be handed over on an order from the US government. His answer: no, he could not guarantee that, although it had never yet happened. 16 Both halves belong together. We could not give you that guarantee either, and nobody in Europe using an American model can give it.
How often it happens is published by Amazon twice a year. In the first half of 2026, AWS handled 2,310 government requests worldwide. In one single case content data was handed over, in all the others only subscriber and usage data. Asked in how many cases content data belonging to enterprise or government customers outside the United States went to the US government, AWS answers in its own report with one word: none. 17 Three qualifications belong to an honest reading of that. It is self reported, it covers only this narrowly drawn group, and requests in the field of national security are not included; by law those may only be reported as a range from 0 to 249.
Encryption is often brought up at this point, and this is exactly where care is needed. Encryption with your own key works for stored data and on the transport path. It does not work at the moment of processing, because a language model has to be able to read the text in order to answer it. The European Data Protection Board set this out in its Recommendations 01/2020: where a service provider needs the plain text, it sees no effective technical protective measure given the current state of the art. 18 An offer that promises you encryption at precisely this point is worth a closer look.
What is left is unspectacular and effective: give away less. Your documents, knowledge bases, histories and accounts sit on the Swiss server or on your own. What goes to the model is the text of the single request, and it is not stored there. A provider can only hand over what it has. That is not legal immunity, but it reduces the scope and the time window of a possible access. If even that is too much, there are two routes: keep using the existing access through EuRouter, or self-host and determine the chain yourself from the first link to the last. The EU Data Act, which has applied since 12 September 2025, works in the same direction. It caps notice periods for cloud services, and from 12 January 2027 it bans switching charges. That turns leaving a provider into a date instead of a feeling.
For completeness the legal framework, without turning it into advice. Transfers to the United States fall under Chapter V of the GDPR, and on both sides of the border an adequacy decision is in place. The Swiss Federal Council added the United States to its list of countries in September 2024, but only for companies certified under the Swiss-U.S. Data Privacy Framework. 19 On the European side the adequacy decision of 2023 applies. The General Court of the European Union dismissed an action against it on 3 September 2025, and an appeal is pending, so the matter is not settled. 20 For those bound by professional secrecy, national criminal law comes on top, in Switzerland Article 321 of the Swiss Criminal Code. Whether an AI service with an American subprocessor is permissible there is judged differently in the literature and has not been decided. Check this for your own case, and if in doubt with your professional association. This article does not replace legal advice.
Frequently asked questions about Claude Opus, Claude Sonnet and Amazon Bedrock
Does this mean Claude Opus and Claude Sonnet run in Switzerland?
No, and we would rather say that plainly. The starting point is the AWS region Zurich, and execution runs under the European inference profile. AWS undertakes that the data stays in European regions, but decides itself which region processes the individual call. A mode that ties Claude Opus or Claude Sonnet to a single region is not offered by AWS in Zurich. Your documents are untouched by this and stay on the Swiss server or on your own.
Does Anthropic train on our data?
No. For Amazon Bedrock, AWS states that neither AWS nor the model providers use inputs or outputs for training, and that the model providers get no access to requests and responses at all: the models run in separate accounts held by the Bedrock team. On our side the same undertaking is in the data processing agreement .
What does the CLOUD Act mean for us in practice?
That a US authority can demand data from AWS which AWS holds, regardless of where it is stored. What AWS holds in the course of a model request is the text of that request, and it is not stored. Your documents, knowledge bases, histories and accounts sit outside that area. This is not a guarantee, it is a smaller attack surface. Anyone who does not want even that uses the existing access through EuRouter or self-hosts. This section does not replace legal advice.
Does encryption not solve the problem?
Not at this point. Encryption protects what is stored and the transport path. But a language model has to read the text in order to answer it, and for exactly that case the European Data Protection Board states that it sees no effective technical protective measure given the current state of the art. So the only thing that works is data minimisation: what does not go out cannot be handed over.
Does access through Amazon Bedrock replace the existing access through EuRouter?
No, it sits alongside it. More than 100 models remain available through EuRouter, processed on the EU side. The administration decides which routes and which models are available in your organisation and which model is the default. There is no obligation to use one route or the other.
Which model should we use?
For classification, extraction and short summaries a small model is enough, and it is considerably cheaper. A top model pays off when a lot of text has to stay in view at once, when a task runs across several steps and tools, or when a rule has to be followed exactly. Usage is broken down per model so that this choice stays traceable.
What does this cost on top?
The price does not change. Managed operation costs €15 per person per month, in Switzerland CHF 14. Of that, €8 or CHF 7.50 is model credit in the shared pool of your organisation. Top models use up that credit faster than small ones, which is exactly why the choice of model is a setting and not a side issue. All the details are on the pricing page.
Does this work with self-hosting too?
Yes, and there you determine the whole chain yourself: you enter the access details for whichever model service you want, or you leave it out and run a model of your own. The software is under the MIT licence. What that means in operation is described under Self-hosting .
Walk through it on a document of your own
Bring an anonymised tender, a rulebook or a case, and we will walk through the workflow together. Or sign up and try it yourself.
Book a live demo
Get started

# AI for trades in Europe: Lexware, Fortnox

AI in everyday work
AI in trades and SMEs across Europe: three workflows that give office time back
Quotes, site reports, invoice formats: in trades and SMEs the office eats the evening, for different reasons in every country. This article walks through three workflows. You see how an AI colleague works with your company’s knowledge, what can be connected, and where the limits are.
Trades and SMEs
18 August 2026
Reading time: 10 minutes
- Starting point
- Quotes and correspondence
- From the job site to the report
- The company knowledge base
- Connectors to industry software
- Data protection
- Frequently asked questions
In brief
- In a German association survey of 10,630 trade businesses, 74% report rising bureaucratic effort, and electronic invoicing sets hard deadlines in several countries. 1
- EU Cowork AI works with your company’s knowledge: quote templates, price lists, regulations and past reports become a knowledge base you can query.
- Your data stays in the EU or on your own server and does not train any models.
- Software with an open interface can be connected, for example Lexware Office, Pennylane, Fatture in Cloud, Holded or Fortnox. An interface is the point where two programs exchange data. The route for this is called the Model Context Protocol (MCP).
On this page
- Starting point
- Quotes and correspondence
- From the job site to the report
- The company knowledge base
- Connectors to industry software
- Data protection
- Frequently asked questions
Starting point: the paperwork grows faster than the business
Trades and SMEs are the same kind of company all across Europe: few people, a full calendar, an office that happens in the evening. The pressure comes from a different direction in every country.
In Germany, 74% of the businesses in an association survey with 10,630 participants report rising bureaucratic effort. 1 On top of that come hard dates. Since 1 January 2025 every domestic company must be able to receive electronic invoices. From 2027 businesses with more than €800,000 in prior-year revenue must issue them too, and from 2028 everyone must. 2 In France the deadline is closer: all companies must be able to receive from 1 September 2026, and even the small ones must send from 1 September 2027. 3 There, 69% of small businesses have invoicing software, but only 20% issue in a structured format. 4 In Austria the obligation carries a different name. Under section 131b of the Federal Fiscal Code (BAO) a business needs a cash register from €15,000 in annual revenue as soon as cash takings exceed €7,500 a year. Debit and credit card payments count as cash too. 10
In Italy, deadlines and obligations cost micro and small enterprises 238 hours a year according to the trades association Confartigianato, 56 more than the OECD average. 5 In Spain the subject is late payment: the average payment period in 2025 was 80.5 days, 34% above the legal maximum, and 96.5 days in construction. 6
In the north it sits elsewhere. The Swedish association Företagarna calculates eight to ten hours of administration per week and owner. 7 In Norway it is the next generation: two out of three construction businesses report an unmet skills need. 8 And everywhere the same gap: in 2025, 17.0% of EU companies with 10 to 49 employees used at least one AI technology, against 55.0% of those with 250 or more. 9 What small businesses lack is not the technology but an entry point that fits twelve people and three vans.
Use case 1: quote, cover letter and payment reminder from your own company knowledge
An enquiry arrives by email: bathroom renovation, three keywords, two photos. The AI colleague knows the company’s quote templates, price lists and past offers. It suggests line items, writes the cover text in the company’s tone and files the draft for review.
The same mechanism carries the correspondence around it: rescheduling, variations, replying to a complaint, a payment reminder. The payment reminder in particular is more than a courtesy in Spain and France, because every late payment ties up liquidity. 6
1
2
3
- Enquiry, open invoice or complaint, as brief as it arrives
- The company’s templates, price lists, contracts and earlier letters
- A draft for the offer, the cover letter and the payment reminder, in the customer’s language
Three drafts from the same company knowledge. Line items and prices are decided by the business.
Working across languages is not an extra, it is everyday life: the client writes in French, the supplier in Italian, the foreman would rather read his mother tongue. The draft is produced from the same documents, in the language it is needed in. For binding texts the contract language remains authoritative.
The difference to a chat in the browser: the draft is based on your documents, and your costing stays in your own instance. An instance is your own copy of the system, kept separate from other customers.
Use case 2: from the job site to a clean report
On the way home the technician dictates three sentences into the phone: what was done, what was used, what stood out, plus two photos. Out of that come the time-and-materials report in the company format, the materials list and a defect description for the site management: worded, numbered, ready to file. A quantities summary is drafted too. The checking stays with the business.
EU Cowork AI runs as a PWA on iPhone, Android devices and the desktop. A PWA is a web application that can be installed on the device like an app. Notes are taken where the work happens. The report waits in the office for approval.
1
2
3
- Keywords or a dictation from the job site, with two photos
- One input, the company’s own document standard
- Report with photo, materials list and defect points, ready to file
Notes from the job site become a document in the company format. Approval happens in the office.
The benefit is not the nicer wording, it is the chain that follows: a report sitting cleanly in the system the same evening becomes an invoice at the end of the month instead of waiting in a drawer.
What deliberately does not happen: no document is sent automatically, none goes into a government reporting system. Notices of obstruction, defect notifications and handover records are legally effective declarations. They wait for approval.
Use case 3: the company’s knowledge becomes queryable
What does this bill of quantities require for insulation? How did we service this installation two years ago? Today, questions like these interrupt the management. A knowledge base is a collection of your own documents that the AI colleague is allowed to search: instructions, manuals, regulations and past reports. From those it answers such questions and names the source. That way the answer can be checked in seconds.
That meets the businesses who cannot spare a training day. A tool that answers in the middle of the work does not ask for a training day. New employees ask in their own language and get answers from the same documents. For safety briefings the official version remains authoritative.
1
2
3
- The company’s regulations, installation manuals, contracts and past reports
- Permissions per tool, every access logged
- An answer with its source, in the employee’s language
The knowledge base answers from the company’s documents and shows where each answer comes from.
One limit belongs here: standard texts are protected by copyright. Whether a DIN, an ÖNORM, an NF or a UNI may go into your knowledge base depends on your licence from the publisher. Your own documents and reports make up the larger part anyway.
Permissions apply down to individual tools: whoever may not see the payroll folder does not see it through the AI either. Every access is recorded in the audit log, the running record of who retrieved what and when.
Connectors: what can be linked to your software
An AI colleague is only as useful as what it is allowed to reach. A connector is the ready-made link between EU Cowork AI and another program. It becomes possible when that program has a documented API, that is, an interface through which programs exchange data. The framework for this is MCP, an open standard for connecting external systems. Permissions apply per tool, and every call is logged. The state of play in August 2026, from the AI connection to Lexware Office and Pennylane through to Fortnox:
Software (country)
Interface
Connection to EU Cowork AI
Lexware Office (DE)
Open REST API documented, with rate limits and event subscriptions
Connection via MCP possible: contacts, vouchers, invoices
weclapp and Xentral (DE)
Open REST API documented, with an OpenAPI reference at Xentral
Connection via MCP possible: orders, articles, stock
Pennylane and Qonto (FR)
Open REST API documented, OAuth 2.0 and webhooks
Connection via MCP possible: vouchers, open items, incoming payments
Fatture in Cloud and Aruba (IT)
Open REST API documented, OAuth 2.0
Connection via MCP possible; sending through the SdI remains a step with approval
Holded (ES)
Open REST API documented, webhooks
Connection via MCP possible: quotes, invoices, projects
Fortnox (SE)
Open REST API documented, OAuth2, documented rate limit
Connection via MCP possible: customers, projects, invoices

Open documentation, with a test environment at Tripletex
Connection via MCP possible; for your own company a self-issued token is enough, a key you create in the program yourself
BMD NTCS and RZL (AT)
No publicly documented REST API, RZL with a partner programme
Access only through the vendor’s partner channel
Bygglet and Cordel (SE, NO)
No public API, only ready-made integrations
The route runs via the connected accounting software or via exports
One sentence of honesty: in the trades, data exchange traditionally runs not through REST interfaces but through industry standards. These are agreed file formats that a whole sector has settled on. Wholesaler article and price data arrive as DATANORM, the shopping basket via IDS-Connect, bills of quantities as GAEB, costing data in Spain as FIEBDC-3. Invoices follow the EN 16931 standard, from XRechnung and Factur-X to FatturaPA and the Norwegian EHF.
These standards move the master data, and AI changes nothing about that. The AI colleague works one level above, on the documents: bill of quantities, offer, report, contract. Is your software missing from the list? Much of the daily work runs without any system connection. How MCP works is described on the integrations page.
Data protection: your costing and customer data stay in the business
Quotes, costings and customer files are trade secrets. Under the GDPR the business remains responsible for personal data even when an AI tool processes it. If a provider processes that data for you, a data processing agreement under Article 28 is required. That is the contract setting out what the provider may do with the data.
When personal data goes to a recipient outside the European Economic Area, Chapter V of the GDPR applies on top. It then takes a legal basis for the transfer and an assessment of the legal situation in the destination country. If storage and processing stay inside the Area, that step falls away. This does not make the processing automatically lawful, it makes it easier to justify.
A large share of the AI running in European businesses is off-the-shelf commercial software: in Norway that applies to 71.0% of the companies using AI, in Sweden to 62.1%. 9 Such tools can do a lot, but they do not know your business: neither your price list nor your framework contracts.
EU Cowork AI runs managed in data centres certified to ISO 27001, or on your own server. Customer data does not train any models. Requests to the language model are processed in the EU. The data processing agreement and the subprocessor list are published openly on the website. This article is not legal advice.
Frequently asked questions from trades and SMEs
My trades software has no interface, for example Bygglet, Cordel or BMD NTCS. Is EU Cowork AI still useful for me?
Yes. Quotes, reports, correspondence and the knowledge base work with documents and need no system connection. Where a connection is missing, the route runs via exports, via DATANORM, IDS-Connect and GAEB, or via the accounting software.
Does this make us ready for the electronic invoicing obligation?
No, not on its own. You meet the obligation with an invoicing system that produces the required format. In France an approved platform comes on top, the plateforme agréée. The AI colleague replaces neither. It can explain the formats and draft the questions for your adviser.
Does the AI write my quote on its own, and does it send payment reminders?
No. It writes drafts from your templates and price lists. Line items, quantities and prices stay with you. Tools that only read are free. Tools that write or send something need a confirmation: payment reminders, terminations and every report to an authority go out only after approval.
Does this replace the tax adviser or the bookkeeping?
No. In Germany, commercial assistance in tax matters is reserved to authorised professionals under section 5 of the Tax Advisory Act, and comparable professional reservations apply in the other target markets. The AI colleague sorts documents and prepares questions. The adviser decides.
Does our business fall under the AI Act?
As a user, generally not as the operator of a high-risk system. Two points still apply: since February 2025 the AI literacy obligation is in force, meaning training and documented rules of use. And an AI that screens applications would be high-risk under Annex III. Those obligations apply under Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 from 2 December 2027, and from 2 August 2028 for embedded systems.
What does it cost for a ten-person business?
Managed operation costs €15 per person per month, in Switzerland CHF 14. Of that, €8 or CHF 7.50 is model credit that everyone in your organisation shares. If you self-host, the software costs nothing: it is MIT licensed.
Where is our data held, and do we need an IT department?
In the managed variant in data centres certified to ISO 27001, with self-hosting on your own server. Requests to the language model are processed in the EU. You do not need an IT department. In the managed variant the operator takes care of operation, updates and backups. Otherwise someone who can maintain a Linux server with Docker is enough, which can also be an IT service provider.
See it on a case of your own
Bring a quote, a site report or a bill of quantities, and we will walk through the workflow together.
Book a live demo
Get started

- ZDH, special survey on bureaucratic burden in the trades (2023, DE, 10,630 businesses): zdh.de
- German Federal Ministry of Finance, FAQ on mandatory electronic invoicing (DE): bundesfinanzministerium.de
- impots.gouv.fr, facturation électronique, calendar of obligations (FR): impots.gouv.fr
- France Num, Baromètre France Num 2025 (FR): francenum.gouv.fr
- Confartigianato Imprese, Ufficio Studi, 238 hours of tax bureaucracy per year (IT): confartigianato.it
- CEPYME, Observatorio de Morosidad, second half of 2025 (ES): cepyme.es

# AI in manufacturing: connect your ERP
