Is your software missing from the list? The three workflows above work with documents and need no system connection at all. To begin with, an export from your MES, that is from your production control system, or from your test equipment system is enough. How a connection via MCP works in principle, and which systems are prepared, is described on the integrations page.
Trade secrets: your design data stays in your hands
The decisive point in this industry is not primarily data protection law but manufacturing and business secrecy. Article 162 of the Swiss Criminal Code makes the betrayal of such secrets a criminal offence. Exactly those secrets sit in your design data, your costings and your customer specifications, often protected by a non-disclosure agreement on top. Anyone supplying medtech, pharmaceuticals or aviation also carries their customers’ contractual requirements against any flow of data into third-party clouds. This article is not legal advice.
Hence the core statement: your design data stays in your own instance. An instance is the installation that runs for your business alone, with permissions per tool and a log for every access. It runs in ISO 27001 certified data centres operated by Green in Lupfig (Switzerland) or on your own server. Model requests are processed in the EU, and customer data does not train any models. Telemetry, that is the reporting back of usage data, is switched off by default. If customer requirements mean that nothing at all may go outside, you run the instance in your own data centre; the software is MIT licensed.
For personnel data the revised Swiss Data Protection Act applies on top. The business remains responsible even when an AI tool processes the data. If a provider is involved, that requires a data processing agreement, a contract setting out what this provider may do with the data. The data processing agreement and the subprocessor list are published openly on the website, the technical measures in the Trust Center .
Frequently asked questions from manufacturing and food production
Our documentation grew over decades and is anything but consistent. Is this still useful for us?
Yes, with one honest caveat. The knowledge base takes PDFs, scanned reports and entire folder structures, but the quality of the answers grows with the quality of the archive. Start with one machine type or one series, check the answers against cases you know, and expand afterwards. A clean-up project up front is not necessary, and it would never be finished anyway.
Does the AI understand our technical drawings?
Text and tables yes, geometry only to a limited extent. Bills of materials, title blocks, stamps, revision notes and handwritten remarks on the drawing are read; a language model does not assess a drawing in the sense of a design review. That is enough for finding documents and notes again, and not enough for approving a design.
Does our design knowledge stay protected?
Permissions apply down to individual tools, in the order user, role, group and server default, and every access is recorded in the exportable audit log. Managed operation runs in Switzerland, self-hosting runs on your own server; in neither case does customer data train any models. If you have to meet contractual requirements from your customers, you run the instance inside your own company.
What does it cost?
Managed operation costs €15 per person per month, in Switzerland CHF 14. Of that, €8 or CHF 7.50 is model credit: a shared pot for your organisation that pays for the requests to the language model. If you self-host, the software costs nothing: it is MIT licensed, a free licence with no licence fee. All details are on the pricing page.
Can we start with a single department?
Yes, and that is the usual route: service or quality assurance with a clearly defined knowledge base. You manage users, permissions and the shared monthly budget in the admin panel, and the budget has a soft limit so that costs stay predictable. Further departments follow once the first one is visibly working.
Does this replace our ERP or PLM, and does it work with Abacus, SAP Business One or Odoo?
No, nothing is replaced. Your ERP remains the leading system for master data, orders and bills of materials, your PLM for revisions and releases. The AI colleague works on top of them: it reads, summarises and drafts. The AI connection to Abacus, SAP Business One, Dynamics 365 Business Central or Odoo runs via MCP and their documented interfaces; the table above shows what is possible for each system. Permissions per tool and a log for every call apply throughout.
We write multilingual operating instructions and labels. How far can we rely on this?
The draft is produced with your company glossary and uses the same terms across every language. Professional approval remains mandatory: product liability hangs on instructions and labels, and a language model can produce errors. For machinery the operating instructions are part of conformity, and the language version for the destination country is a legal requirement; approval remains with the manufacturer. No draft is a legally sound declaration. This answer is not legal advice.
See it on a case of your own
Bring a customer specification, a stack of service reports or your audit question catalogue, and we will walk through the workflow together. Or sign up and be among the first to start.

AI in the mandate
AI in law firms and fiduciary offices: three workflows that respect professional secrecy
Reading the file, checking contracts, writing to clients: the work nobody can bill eats the day. This article walks through three workflows to show how an AI colleague works with your firm’s own documents. You see what professional secrecy demands along the way and where the limits are.
Fiduciary and legal
28 April 2026
Reading time: 12 minutes
- Starting point
- Opening a new case file
- Contracts and year-end files
- Client communication
- Connectors to practice software
- Professional secrecy and data protection
- Frequently asked questions
In brief
- Only 47% of the Swiss law firms surveyed use document management software; more than half therefore search for documents without any structure. 1
- EU Cowork AI works with your firm’s own material. Case files, model contracts, your clause library, fact sheets and circulars become a knowledge base: a collection you can question in plain language. Every answer names its source.
- Your data stays in Switzerland or on your own server and does not train any models; the data processing agreement and the subprocessor list are public.
- Vertec, justitia.swiss and Microsoft 365 have a documented interface: a publicly described way for two programs to exchange data. EU Cowork AI can be connected through it, via the Model Context Protocol (MCP), with permissions per tool and a log for every access.
On this page
- Starting point
- Opening a new case file
- Contracts and year-end files
- Client communication
- Connectors to practice software
- Professional secrecy and data protection
- Frequently asked questions
Starting point: the billable hour is getting scarce
A survey by the Swiss Bar Association and the Swiss LegalTech Association shows how far apart firms are when it comes to their filing: 63% of the firms surveyed work with practice management software, but only 47% with document management software. 1 More than half therefore look for documents in the folder tree, in the mailbox or in a paper file. What that costs is visible in an international comparison, a so-called benchmark. Average utilisation there sits at 38% of working time. That is roughly three billable hours per eight-hour day. Almost half of the non-billable time goes into administration. 2 That figure comes from international data, not from a Swiss survey; the direction is familiar to every firm nonetheless.
In fiduciary practice the picture is the same, with different labels. That fiduciaries spend more than 60% of their working time on administration has been documented for years. 3 On top of that comes pressure from the client side: financial reporting and audit at 53% and value added tax at 51% are among the five regulatory areas that weigh most heavily on Swiss companies. 4 What burdens the client lands on the fiduciary’s desk. There it meets a capacity limit, and that limit does not stretch during the year-end season.
The profession knows this and is looking for the way forward: on 14 June 2024 the Swiss Bar Association published guidance on dealing with artificial intelligence. 5 So the question is no longer whether a firm uses AI, but under which conditions it may. This article is not legal advice.
1
2
3
4
- Prior files, correspondence and enclosures of the mandate
- Indexed with a reference to the exact page
- Assessment and approval in the firm
- Filed in the case file, every access logged
How a mandate moves through the firm: from the prior files to the filed result. The legal assessment stays with a person.
Use case 1: opening the case file at the start of a mandate
A new mandate arrives with several hundred pages: the prior representative’s files, two years of correspondence, enclosures in no particular order, part of it scanned. You load the whole set into the mandate’s workspace. What comes back is a chronology of events, an overview of the parties involved and a list of the disputed points, each with a reference to the place in the file the statement comes from.
The reference is the actual point. You are not reading a summary you have to trust; you jump in seconds to the page where the statement stands. What follows from it is your decision: the legal assessment, the argument and the strategy stay entirely with the lawyer. The AI colleague provides the overview you would otherwise put together over the weekend.
1
2
3
- Prior files, correspondence and enclosures, exactly as they arrive
- Indexed against the files of this mandate
- Chronology, parties and disputed points, each with its source
The overview is built from the files of the mandate, not from the model’s memory. Every statement shows the place where it stands.
What does not happen: no deadline is calculated and nothing is filed. A language model can miss a consideration or attribute a reference to the wrong place. That is why every output is a draft with evidence for you to check, and not a statement to rely on.
Use case 2: checking contracts and year-end documents against your own practice
In the law firm an NDA, an employment contract or the other side’s standard terms land on the desk. The AI colleague compares the document with your own clause and template library and returns a list of deviations: which clause is missing compared with your template, which one differs, which wording you have already negotiated differently in comparable cases. The result is a pointer, not an approval decision.
In fiduciary practice it is the preparation of the year-end file. Contracts, minutes of the general meeting, loan and leasing agreements are reviewed and condensed into a structured summary; alongside it comes one bundled list of open questions for the client instead of six separate emails over three weeks. A knowledge base of circulars from the Federal Tax Administration, VAT information and your own fact sheets supplies the source reference. That way the question to the client comes with its reasoning.
1
2
3
- The contract or year-end document, as it comes in
- The firm’s clause library, templates and fact sheets
- List of deviations and open questions, each with its source
The check runs against your own practice, not against general model knowledge. Negotiating and approving happens in the firm.
The limit is clear: the AI colleague gives no legal advice and makes no approval decision. It shows where a document deviates from your practice and names the place in your own library where you can read it up.
Use case 3: client communication in German, French, Italian and English
A firm writes all day long: a request for an extension of a deadline, a follow-up for missing documents, notice of the fee note, a plain-language summary of a judgment or a contract for a client without legal training. Each of these letters is routine and still costs half an hour, because it has to be clean.
From one sentence of context and the firm’s model letters, the draft appears in minutes. It comes in German, French, Italian or English, in the tone your firm uses. That is more than translation: the salutation, the structure and the phrasing come from your own templates and from the earlier correspondence in the mandate. You read, cut, add and approve.
1
2
3
- The occasion from the mandate, in one sentence
- Model letters and earlier correspondence, permissions per group
- A draft in the client’s language, ready for approval
The draft is built from the firm’s model letters. What gets signed is what a lawyer or a fiduciary has approved.
No letter leaves the firm without approval. Who produced which draft and who changed it is recorded in the audit log, the record of every access. Permissions per tool decide who can reach which template library at all.
Connectors: what can be linked to your industry software
An AI colleague is only as useful as what it is allowed to reach. The link to another program is called a connector. It runs over MCP, an open standard for connecting external systems. The prerequisite is a documented interface, an API in technical language: the vendor publicly describes how other programs may retrieve data. Some vendors already ship a ready-made connecting piece for this, an MCP server. Permissions apply to each individual tool, and every call is logged. This is the state of play for common law firm and fiduciary software, checked in August 2026:

Is your software missing from the list? Much of the daily work runs with documents and needs no system connection at all, from opening a case file to correspondence. How the AI connection to a law firm or fiduciary software works in principle via MCP, and which systems are prepared, is described on the integrations page.
Professional secrecy and data protection: the precondition, not the extra
For a law firm the starting point is not a data protection argument but the criminal code. Article 321 of the Swiss Criminal Code names lawyers explicitly. Whoever discloses a secret entrusted to them in their profession faces up to three years of imprisonment or a monetary penalty. On top of that comes Article 13 of the Lawyers Act (BGFA): the duty of confidentiality applies without any time limit and towards everyone. It does not end with the mandate, and it does not end with the entry in the register.
From this follows the construction every firm knows that has ever brought in an IT company: IT service providers count as auxiliary persons and are therefore themselves subject to Article 321 of the Swiss Criminal Code. For that to be permissible, several conditions apply. The provider has to be made aware of the duty of secrecy and confirm that it will be observed. It must be contractually bound by instructions. And it may not use the data for any purpose of its own. For an AI tool that means, concretely: your own instance rather than a shared account, that is a system belonging to your firm alone; a data processing agreement; an explicit commitment that customer data is not used for training; and a disclosed chain of subcontractors.
EU Cowork AI is built for this. Operation runs in ISO 27001 certified data centres of Green in Lupfig or on your own server. The data processing agreement states explicitly, in its section on training, that no models are trained on customer data, and the subprocessor list is published openly on the website. Telemetry, the automatic reporting of usage data to the provider, is off by default. Every access is recorded in the audit log, and you can export it. Permissions apply down to individual tools.
Fiduciaries are not in the catalogue of Article 321 of the Criminal Code, yet in practice the situation is hardly more relaxed. Confidentiality follows from the mandate contract. On top of it come bank client data as well as payroll and personnel data; under the revised Swiss Data Protection Act these can count as sensitive personal data. In audit mandates the audit secrecy obligation comes on top. Anyone who pastes payroll data into a chat window whose operator they do not know has a problem that no terms of use can define away.
That is why operation in Switzerland or on your own server is not a preference for a law firm but the precondition under which the use is permissible at all. What you need in a conversation with the supervisory authority, the audit client or the client themselves is not a leap of faith but a contract, a list and a log. All three exist. This article is not legal advice.
Frequently asked questions from law firms and fiduciary offices
Are we even allowed to put client data into an AI?
That depends on the setup. IT service providers count as auxiliary persons. Bringing one in is permissible if the provider is made aware of the duty of secrecy, confirms that it will be observed and is contractually bound by instructions. The building blocks for this: your own instance in Switzerland or on your server, a data processing agreement and the commitment that no models are trained on your data. Assess the individual case with your mandate in mind. This answer is not legal advice.
Does the AI invent court decisions?
Language models can produce citations that do not exist, and in this profession that is the most expensive mistake of all. That is why the AI colleague works against your own files and your knowledge base and points to the place each statement comes from. Quotations, citations and decisions still have to be verified before they go into a legal submission. This answer is not legal advice.
What about the duty of confidentiality towards the operator?
With self-hosting nobody but you sees the data, because the instance runs on your infrastructure. In managed operation the data processing agreement sets the frame: maintenance access is bound by instructions, the subprocessors are disclosed, and every access is recorded in an audit log you can export. This answer is not legal advice.
Will trainees and the back office then see everything?
No. Permissions apply down to individual tools. The order is user, role, group, server default. Whoever may not see a knowledge base or a connected system does not reach it through the AI colleague either. Mandates that have to stay walled off from each other can be separated through distinct groups.
Does the AI calculate deadlines or file anything?
No, and that is deliberate. Deadline calculation, deadline control and filing stay in the practice management system and with a person. The AI colleague indexes files, drafts texts and answers questions from your own documents; it sends nothing on its own.
Does EU Cowork AI work with Vertec, or does it replace our practice management and fiduciary software?
It does not replace them: the AI colleague works on top of it, not beside it. Current versions of Vertec ship their own MCP server, in which permissions follow the Vertec user model. That makes master data, projects and services available for queries without the case file itself leaving the specialist application.
What does it cost for a firm of ten people?
Managed operation costs €15 per person per month, in Switzerland CHF 14, of which €8 or CHF 7.50 is model credit in your organisation’s shared pool. If you self-host, the software costs nothing: it is MIT licensed. All details are on the pricing page.
How do we start without rebuilding half the firm?
With one type of mandate and your own template library. Take the matter that comes up most often, load the corresponding templates and fact sheets into a knowledge base, and let two people work with it for two weeks. After that you know what the workflow delivers, and the permissions for it are set in an hour.
Walk through it on a matter of your own

# AI and software in property management

URL: https://eucowork.ai/en/blog/ki-immobilienverwaltung

AI and software in property management | EU Cowork AI
-

AI in everyday work
AI in property management: three workflows that ease the shared inbox
A repair report, a service charge question, a noise complaint: in the shared inbox of a management office, everything lands at once. This article walks through three workflows. You see how an AI colleague works with the documents of your properties. You also see what can be connected to your property management software, from GARAIO REM to Abacus, and where the limits are.
Real estate
9 June 2026
Reading time: 10 minutes
- Starting point
- Sorting and answering tenant enquiries
- Explaining the service charge statement
- Handover reports and contractor orders
- Connectors to property management software
- Data protection
- Frequently asked questions
In brief
- In the Digital Real Estate Index 2026, property management reaches 4.4 out of 10 points. That is the highest value since the survey began. AI and machine learning are the only one of the twelve technologies surveyed with clear progress. 1
- EU Cowork AI works with the documents of your properties: tenancy agreements, house rules, regulations and past correspondence become the knowledge base the drafts are built from.
- Every reply to a tenant is a draft that someone approves. Legally binding notices such as terminations and rent adjustments stay with the property manager.
- Tenant data stays in Switzerland or on your own server and does not train any models. Software with a documented interface for exchanging data can be connected, for example Microsoft 365 or GARAIO REM. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is what carries that connection.
On this page
- Starting point
- Sorting and answering tenant enquiries
- Explaining the service charge statement
- Handover reports and contractor orders
- Connectors to property management software
- Data protection
- Frequently asked questions
Starting point: more correspondence than people to write it
Digitalisation in the Swiss construction and real estate sector is moving in small steps. For the Digital Real Estate Index 2026 by pom+ Consulting, around 200 specialists and executives were surveyed. Property management reaches 4.4 out of 10 points, the highest value since the survey began. The overall index stands at 4.3. AI and machine learning are the only one of the twelve technologies surveyed with clear progress. Two thirds of respondents see high value in them. What slows the development down are questions of investment and cost. 1
On top of that comes the shortage of qualified staff. The sector does not find enough trained property managers, which gets in the way of efficient operation. 2 Whoever cannot fill an open position spreads the work across the existing team. The first thing to suffer is the response time towards tenants, and an unanswered repair report turns into a complaint to the owner two weeks later.
A large part of that work is correspondence that follows a fixed pattern: the service charge statement and the questions that follow it, the rent adjustment tied to the reference interest rate, the formal requirements for terminations, the handover report with the orders to the contractors. Then there is the language mix. The same matter goes out in German, French, Italian or English depending on the tenant. So the question is no longer whether a management office uses AI. The question is whether the AI works with the documents of its own properties, and where the tenant data sits while it does.
1
2
3
4
- An enquiry in the shared inbox, exactly as it arrives
- Assigned by type of request and by property
- A reply drafted from the property’s own documents
- Review and approval by the property manager
How a tenant enquiry moves through the office: from the inbox to the approved reply. The last step stays with a person.
Use case 1: sorting and answering tenant enquiries
On Monday morning the shared inbox holds the messages from the weekend: a dripping boiler, questions about the service charge statement, a noise complaint from the third floor, a termination for the end of the quarter, several requests for a spare key. The AI colleague reads the inbox through the connected mailbox. It assigns each message to a type of request and to a property, and places a draft reply next to it.
The draft comes from the documents of the property concerned: the tenancy agreement, the house rules, the regulations and the previous correspondence with this tenant. For the repair report, the draft states who fixes the fault and what information is still missing. For the spare key request, it states the rule from the regulations, with the source reference, so the statement can be checked in seconds. The message goes to the responsible property manager, who reads it, corrects it and approves it.
1
2
3
- An enquiry from the shared inbox, in the tenant’s language
- The property’s documents, with permissions per tool and a full log
- A draft reply with its source, ready for approval
The draft is built from the property’s documents, not from what the language model has learned in general. Approval happens in the office.
What matters in practice: no new tenant portal and no second system appear. The AI colleague works in the mailbox you already have, and tenants keep writing to the same address. The red lines stay in place too: terminations, rent adjustments and formal warnings are legally binding notices and never go out automatically. The formal requirements of Swiss tenancy law remain the responsibility of the management office.
Use case 2: explaining the service charge statement in plain words
After the statements go out, the same wave arrives every year: why is my statement higher than last year. The questions all land within the same two weeks, and they land on a team that is processing the additional payments and the refunds at the same time.
The AI colleague pulls up the statement for that apartment, the allocation key and the figures from the previous year, and drafts an explanation in plain language: which item has gone up, how the share is calculated, what the comparison with last year shows. The draft is written in the language the enquiry came in, in German, French, Italian or English. The property manager checks the figures and approves. That makes the seasonal peak manageable. It no longer has to be absorbed through temporary staff alone.
1
2
3
- The tenant’s question about the statement
- The statement, the allocation key and last year’s figures
- An explanation in the tenant’s language, ready for approval
The explanation is built from the statement for that apartment. Checking and approval happen in the office.
What the workflow does not do: it does not correct a statement and it does not charge anything. It explains what the statement says. If an item really is wrong, the case goes to accounting, as before. And because every explanation rests on the stored statement, the property manager sees immediately what the draft is based on.
Use case 3: from the handover to the contractor orders
The handover takes an hour, the paperwork afterwards often takes longer. On the way back the property manager dictates the notes into the phone, the device’s dictation function is enough, or types them in: kitchen front scratched, silicone in the bathroom to be renewed, living room walls to be painted, photo list attached.
Out of that come the draft handover report in the company format and the worded orders to the painter, the plumber and the cleaning company, with address, apartment number, access arrangements and deadline. On the same day, instead of at the weekend. Who gets the job, who bears the cost and where normal wear ends and damage begins is decided by the management office. The AI colleague supplies the text.
1
2
3
- Notes and photo list from the handover
- One input, three documents in the company format
- Report and contractor orders, ready for approval
The notes from the handover become a report and contractor orders. Allocation and cost decisions stay with the management office.
Here too: no order goes out without approval, and nothing is charged automatically. What is billed to the tenant is decided by the office, and every change to a draft stays traceable.
Connectors: what can be linked to GARAIO REM, Abacus and the rest of your software
An AI colleague is only as useful as what it is allowed to reach. MCP is an open standard for connecting external systems. Through it, programs with a documented interface can be addressed. An interface, often called an API, is a described route along which two programs exchange data. Permissions apply per individual tool, and every call is written to the log. This is the state of play for common property management software, checked in August 2026:
Software
Interface
Connection to EU Cowork AI
Microsoft 365 (shared Outlook mailbox, SharePoint)

Is your software missing from the list? Much of the daily work runs on the mailbox and on documents and needs no system connection at all: sorting the enquiries, the service charge explanation, the handover report. How a connection via MCP works in principle, and which systems are prepared, is described on the integrations page.
Data protection: tenant files are sensitive
A tenant file holds more than a name and an address: debt collection register extracts, credit reports, proof of income, sometimes details that count as sensitive personal data. Under the revised Swiss Data Protection Act, the management office remains responsible for that data even when an AI tool processes it. If a provider processes the data, a data processing agreement is required. This article is not legal advice.
On top of that come the expectations of the owners. Institutional owners such as pension funds and insurers regularly require in their management contracts that the data of their properties is processed in Switzerland. EU Cowork AI runs in ISO 27001 certified data centres operated by Green in Lupfig, or on your own server.
Customer data does not train any models, and permissions apply down to individual tools. Every access is recorded in the audit log, a record you can export at any time. The data processing agreement and the subprocessor list are published openly on the website. When an owner asks where the data of their properties is held, you answer in one sentence.
Frequently asked questions from property management
Does the AI reply to tenants directly?
No. Every reply to a tenant is a draft that the responsible property manager reads, corrects and approves. A language model, the program behind the AI, can produce errors. That is why every text is a draft for review, not a verified statement.
What about terminations and rent adjustments?
They stay with the management office. Legally binding notices such as terminations, rent adjustments tied to the reference interest rate and formal warnings are subject to formal requirements and never go out automatically. Terminations and rent increases also require the official cantonal form and are tied to deadlines. At most, the AI colleague prepares text. The form, the deadlines and the dispatch remain the responsibility of the office. This answer is not legal advice.
How does the AI know what the tenancy agreement says?
From the knowledge base. For each property you upload the tenancy agreements, the house rules, the regulations and the previous correspondence. The draft is built from them and names the source, so the statement can be checked in seconds.
May tenant data go into an AI tool at all?
Under the revised Swiss Data Protection Act the management office remains responsible and signs a data processing agreement with the provider. EU Cowork AI runs in Switzerland or on your own server, customer data does not train any models, and every access is recorded in the audit log. The data processing agreement and the subprocessor list are published openly on the website. This answer is not legal advice.
Do we need a tenant portal for this?
No. The AI colleague works in the shared inbox you already have. Tenants write to the same address as before and notice nothing of the workflow behind it.
Does EU Cowork AI work with GARAIO REM, Abacus or ImmoTop2?
That depends on the interface. The table above shows the state of play for GARAIO REM, Abacus, ImmoTop2, Rimo R5 and other programs. Where a connection is missing, the route runs via exports and documents. The workflows built on the mailbox and the knowledge base work without any system connection anyway.
What does it cost for an office with fifteen people?
Managed operation costs €15 per person per month, in Switzerland CHF 14. Of that, €8 or CHF 7.50 is model credit in your organisation’s shared pool. If you self-host, the software costs nothing: it is MIT licensed. All details are on the pricing page.
How do we start?
With one property. The house rules, the regulations and the tenancy agreements of that property go into the knowledge base, the shared inbox is connected, and the property manager works with drafts for two weeks. Whatever comes up flows back into the templates, and the next properties follow.
See it on a property of your own
Bring a set of house rules and a few real tenant enquiries, and we will walk through the workflow together. Or sign up and be among the first to start.

AI in everyday work
AI in practice and pharmacy: three workflows that give writing time back
Cost approval requests, disability insurance enquiries, discharge letters: the writing for insurers and authorities eats the evening, not the consultation hour. This article walks through three workflows to show how an AI colleague works with your own released documents, where the line to a medical device runs, and what applies to health data.
Practice and pharmacy
17 August 2026
Reading time: 12 minutes
- Starting point
- Reports and insurance enquiries
- A knowledge base for the team
- Multilingual information
- Connectors to industry software
- Data protection and professional secrecy
- Frequently asked questions
In brief
- Doctors in ambulatory practice spend an average of 54 minutes per working day on requirements from authorities and insurers alone; 87% of those in ambulatory care name insurers as the heaviest burden. 1
- EU Cowork AI works on the administration around the care: report drafts for insurers and authorities, a knowledge base the team can query, fact sheets in several languages.
- No diagnosis, no triage, no dosing, no medication check: such functions would make it a medical device, and they are deliberately not part of the system.
- Health data is sensitive personal data. The instance, meaning your own copy of the system, runs in Switzerland or on your own server. Permissions apply down to individual tools. Programs with a documented interface, meaning an official route for exchanging data, can be connected via the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Every access appears in the audit log, the record of all accesses. Customer data does not train any models.
On this page
- Starting point
- Reports and insurance enquiries
- A knowledge base for the team
- Multilingual information
- Connectors to industry software
- Data protection and professional secrecy
- Frequently asked questions
Starting point: the paperwork grows faster than the consultation hour
Doctors in ambulatory practice spend an average of 54 minutes per working day on requirements from authorities and insurers alone, and 87% of those in ambulatory care name insurers as the heaviest burden. 1 That is close to an hour arising every day in a place where nobody is treated: at the desk, usually after the last consultation.
At the same time, the hours are getting shorter. General practitioners today have 6 hours per week less available for treatment than 20 years ago, and by 2035, 40% of them have to be replaced. 2 Those who stay take on more patients, not fewer forms.
The federal government is now measuring the effort itself: since May 2026 the Federal Office of Public Health has been collecting data from general practitioners, with first interim results announced for August 2026 and the final report for January 2027. 3 So the debate about relief is under way. Today’s post is waiting all the same.
In the pharmacy the arithmetic differs, the result is similar: since 1 January 2020, Article 30 of the Therapeutic Products Act has required a quality assurance system. 4 Around 1,800 pharmacies with an average of 12.7 people and 9 full-time equivalents therefore each run their own quality management system (QMS). That includes work instructions, training records and an annual review. 5 In home care, around 400 non-profit Spitex organisations with more than 40,000 employees serve about three quarters of all clients. 6 Every one of them writes progress reports to insurers and authorities.
That sets the frame for this article, and it is a narrow one. An AI colleague makes no diagnosis, performs no triage, recommends no therapy and no dose, checks no interactions and replaces no medication check. Such functions would make it a medical device, with everything that conformity assessment brings with it. This is about administration, documentation, the knowledge base and translation. The medication check stays in the pharmacy’s specialist system; the AI colleague writes the text around it.
1
2
3
4
- An enquiry from an insurer or authority, with a deadline
- Released extracts from your own documentation
- A report draft in your own report format, with source references
- Review and signature by the professional
How an insurance enquiry moves through the practice: from the incoming post to the signed report. The signature stays with the professional.
Use case 1: reports and insurance enquiries as a draft
An enquiry is in the inbox in the morning: cost approval for a therapy, with a deadline. The practice releases the enquiry and the matching extracts from the documentation to the AI colleague. Back comes a structured report draft in your own report format, with the details in the places where the insurer expects them, and with a source reference for every detail taken over. The doctor reads, deletes, adds the assessment and signs.
The same pattern carries the other reports: referral, discharge, disability insurance enquiry, and in home care the progress report to the insurer and the report to the child and adult protection authority. The accompanying text for the medical order or the needs notification under Article 7 of the health insurance benefits ordinance (KLV) is drafted as well. The needs assessment and the care level classification stay in the specialist system and with the professional. The draft organises what is already documented. It invents nothing on top. Where a detail is missing, a marked gap remains instead of a phrase that merely sounds plausible.
1
2
3
- The enquiry, exactly as it arrives
- Released extracts and the report format of the business
- A report draft with source references, ready to sign
The draft organises existing details and shows the source of each one. The professional writes the clinical assessment.
This is exactly where the 54 minutes from the starting point sit. 1 What the draft deliberately does not contain is the clinical assessment: fitness for work, prognosis and indication are written by the professional. Nothing goes out automatically, every report waits for a signature.
Use case 2: the team’s knowledge becomes queryable
The practice assistant has a tariff question, is looking for the internal rule on a late cancellation or the right chapter in the practice manual. Today she interrupts the consultation for that. With a knowledge base built from the practice manual, the internal procedures and the billing documents of the business, she gets the answer with its source, checkable in seconds.
In the pharmacy the quality manual becomes queryable: “Where is our cold chain rule written down?” And the writing work for the quality management system is drafted from the existing documents, from the work instruction through the training record to the annual review. The medication check stays in the specialist system, where it belongs.
1
2
3
- A question in everyday language, at reception or in the lab
- Practice manual, quality manual and concepts, opened by permission
- An answer with its source, checkable in seconds
The knowledge base answers from your own documents and shows where each answer comes from. This workflow needs no patient data at all.
In home care it is the hygiene and emergency concepts and the onboarding of new employees, who ask in their own language and get answers from the same documents. Permissions apply down to individual tools: whoever may not see a folder does not see it through the AI colleague either, and every access appears in the audit log.
Use case 3: patient and customer information in several languages
A fact sheet on preparing for an examination exists in German, cleared by a professional. From it come the French, Italian and English versions, plus the languages actually spoken in the catchment area, and a plain-language version for everyone who is shut out by officialese.
The same applies to intake instructions at the counter and to aftercare instructions following a procedure. Before being handed over, every version goes through professional clearance, just as the German original did. What becomes noticeable afterwards: fewer calls back and fewer misunderstandings at the counter.
1
2
3
- A cleared fact sheet from your own collection
- Translation and plain-language simplification
- Several versions, each for professional clearance
One original, several language versions. None of them is handed over before a professional has cleared it.
The line is clear here too. The AI colleague transfers and simplifies a cleared text; it adds no advice that is not in the original, and it leaves out no warnings. Quantities, timings and dosage figures are checked against the original before clearance. It does not replace the consultation.
Connectors: what can be linked to your industry software
An AI colleague is only as useful as what it is allowed to reach. A connector is nothing more than the link to another program. MCP is an open standard for such links. Through it, programs with a documented interface can be addressed. Each individual tool has its own permission, and every call is logged. In healthcare the starting position is particular: much of the field is closed. This is what an AI connection looks like for common software in practices, pharmacies and home care, checked in August 2026:
Software
Interface
Connection to EU Cowork AI
Microsoft 365 (Outlook, Teams, SharePoint)
Graph API, openly documented
MCP server available from Microsoft; email, calendar and files directly addressable

Vitodata vitomed
Interfaces through the vendor
Connection via MCP possible; the route runs through the vendor

Connection via MCP possible

Usable as a document format
Lobos, Perigon, careCoach (care homes and home care)
Interfaces on a project basis
Connection possible; the route runs through the vendor
Achilles and Axenita (Axon Lab), curaMED, Ärztekasse systems
No publicly documented API
The route runs via exports and documents
The honest summary: this field is largely closed. That is precisely why system connections are not at the centre of this article. Report drafts, the knowledge base and fact sheets work with documents and run without any link to the practice software. Where the specialist system speaks the FHIR data standard, one route runs through generic MCP servers. Generic means: they are tied to no single vendor, and they exist as open source. 8 For service billing, the Forum Datenaustausch standard invoice 5.0 has been mandatory since 1 January 2026. It is an open file format built on XML that can be read and written as a document. 7 How a connection works in principle is described on the integrations page.
Data protection and professional secrecy: the strictest section
Article 321 of the Swiss Criminal Code names doctors and pharmacists explicitly. It covers their auxiliary staff as well. Under the revised Swiss Data Protection Act, health data counts as sensitive personal data. Together this means: a tool that processes such data is not introduced on the side. This article is not legal advice.
The first step is therefore the easiest: two of the three use cases in this article need no patient data at all. The knowledge base lives on the practice manual, the quality manual and internal procedures; the fact sheets are your own texts. You can start there without a single file leaving the business.
Where patient data does belong, namely in the report draft, the usual measures apply in strict form. The instance runs in ISO 27001 certified data centres in Switzerland or on your own server. There is a data processing agreement and a public subprocessor list . Customer data does not train any models. Permissions reach down to individual tools, and the audit log can be exported.
What we do not claim: that patient data is anonymised in the process. A progress report remains personal data even without a name, and anyone promising otherwise is promising too much. The answer lies in where the processing happens and in access control, not in a text filter.
For Spitex organisations and institutions there is more: data of people lacking capacity is processed. Contact with the child and adult protection authority is part of the work as well. Deletion policies and access logging have to be set more strictly there than in a single practice. Care level assessments under BESA or RAI are untouched by all this: they arise in the specialist system and are answered for there. The evidence on operations is available in the Trust Center .
Frequently asked questions from practices, pharmacies and home care
Is it even permissible to put patient data into an AI system?
You decide that, not the provider. Doctors and pharmacists are bound by Article 321 of the Swiss Criminal Code. Health data is sensitive under the revised Data Protection Act, and processing by a provider requires a data processing agreement. For that reason EU Cowork AI runs in Switzerland or on your own server, customer data does not train any models, and every access appears in the audit log. A large share of the use cases also works entirely without patient data. This answer is not legal advice.
Does the AI make diagnoses or check medication?
No, and deliberately so. Diagnosis, triage, therapy and dosing recommendations, interaction checking and medication checking are not part of the system; such functions would make it a medical device. EU Cowork AI works on administration, documentation, the knowledge base and translation. The medication check stays in the pharmacy’s specialist system.
What does the practice assistant see, and what does the doctor see?
Whatever you define. Permissions apply down to individual tools. They take effect in the order user, role, group and server default, and they are managed in the admin panel. Whoever may not see a folder does not see it through the AI colleague either, and every access lands in the exportable audit log.
Does EU Cowork AI work with our practice software, such as vitomed or Elexis?
Honest answer: usually not directly, because this field is largely closed. That is precisely why the use cases in this article build on documents rather than on system access. Report drafts, the knowledge base and fact sheets run without any connection. Where your specialist system speaks the FHIR data standard or the vendor offers a partner route, a connection via MCP is possible.
What does it cost for a practice with eight staff?
Managed operation costs €15 per person per month, in Switzerland CHF 14, of which €8 or CHF 7.50 is model credit in your organisation’s shared pool. If you self-host, the software costs nothing: it is MIT licensed. All details are on the pricing page.
Who is liable if a report draft is wrong?
The professional who signs it. That is why every result is a draft with source references and not a finished report: a language model can produce errors, and the review before the signature is part of the workflow, not an optional extra. This answer is not legal advice.
What applies to clients who lack capacity?
The same rules apply to them, in a stricter form. Deletion policies and access logging have to hold up in a context where the child and adult protection authority reads along, and reports to authorities remain drafts until management clears them. Care level assessments under BESA or RAI still arise in the specialist system. This answer is not legal advice.
How do we start?
With the documents that are yours anyway: fact sheets, the practice manual, the quality manual, hygiene and emergency concepts. This knowledge base needs no patient data, it shows within a few days whether the team actually works with it, and only after that is the question of report drafts worth asking.
Walk through a case of your own with us
Bring an insurance enquiry, a fact sheet or a chapter from your quality manual, and we will walk through the workflow together, without patient data. Or sign up and be among the first to start.

# Data Processing Agreement (DPA)

URL: https://eucowork.ai/en/avv

EU Cowork AI
Pricing Docs Blog
EN
Self-host for free Get started
← Back to Trust Center
As of: August 2026
Data Processing Agreement (DPA)
This agreement governs how Herr Informatik GmbH processes personal data on behalf of the Customer when it operates the EU Cowork AI service as a managed service. It follows Art. 28 GDPR and Art. 9 of the revised Swiss Federal Act on Data Protection (revised FADP, German abbreviation DSG) and consists of seventeen sections and two annexes.
1 Parties, subject matter, order of precedence and definitions
The parties to this agreement are Herr Informatik GmbH, Klosterzelgstrasse 1a, 5210 Windisch, company identification number CHE-112.168.836 (hereinafter “the Provider”), and the Customer. “EU Cowork AI” is the name of the service and not a party to this agreement. The subject matter is the processing of personal data on behalf of the Customer in the managed operation of the service. The Customer is the controller (Art. 4(7) GDPR, Art. 5(j) revised FADP) and decides on the purposes and means; the Provider is the processor. The Provider is a controller in its own right solely for its billing data, for the security and operating logs of its own infrastructure, for the contact details of the contractual points of contact and for statutory record-keeping duties; its privacy policy applies to those. This agreement takes precedence over the General Terms and Conditions; the deemed-approval provision under clause 12 of the General Terms and Conditions does not apply to it. Annexes 1 and 2 in their dated version and the list of subprocessors form part of this agreement. This agreement uses the terminology of the GDPR and of the revised FADP with the same meaning; the terms processor and subprocessor cover the corresponding roles under both bodies of law.
2 Scope and status of the service
This agreement applies to the managed operation on the Provider’s infrastructure. Where the Customer self-hosts the open source software on its own infrastructure, no data flows to the Provider; no processing on behalf of the Customer arises, and this agreement remains without object for as long as no operating or support services involving access to data are agreed separately. The managed service is released. Measures that are not implemented today are not warranted.
3 Special categories and professional secrecy
The service is not designed for special categories of personal data (Art. 9 and Art. 10 GDPR) or for sensitive personal data (Art. 5(c) revised FADP). Without a separate written agreement on additional safeguards, the Customer may not introduce such data and shall instruct its users accordingly. The service does not technically prevent such input. If such data nevertheless enters the service, the same technical and organisational measures apply as for all other content; the Customer is answerable for its admissibility. Customers subject to professional or official secrecy (including Art. 321 of the Swiss Criminal Code and Art. 47 of the Swiss Banking Act) may use the service only on the basis of a separate written agreement.
4 Instructions
The Customer issues instructions in text form to info@herr-informatik.ch. The configuration in the admin panel also counts as a documented instruction, in particular retention periods, model selection, connections and permissions, web search and the memory function, and the export and deletion of individual persons. The Provider documents the instructions it receives. Instructions within the agreed scope of services and within the settings provided for in the admin panel are covered by the fee. The Provider implements instructions going beyond that only in so far as this is technically and legally possible and reasonable for it, and against remuneration on a time and materials basis. Where implementation is not possible or not reasonable, the Provider shall say so; there is no obligation to implement. If, in the Provider’s view, an instruction infringes the GDPR, the revised FADP or other data protection provisions, it shall inform the Customer without delay (Art. 28(3), second subparagraph, GDPR). It may suspend execution of the instruction concerned until the matter is clarified, without thereby being in breach of contract. If the Customer insists on a manifestly unlawful instruction, the Provider may refuse to execute it and terminate the affected part of the services.
5 The Customer’s obligations and warranties
The Customer is responsible for the lawfulness of the collection and of its instructions, has its own legal basis and informs the data subjects. It administers accounts, roles and permissions and blocks users who have left. It is responsible for the connections it configures, for the service accounts stored there and the scope of their permissions, and for model endpoints it integrates. It warrants that no statutory or contractual duty of confidentiality stands in the way of the processing (Art. 9 revised FADP) and shall notify any such duty arising later without delay. Before the processing begins, the Customer has satisfied itself that the Provider is able to guarantee data security; Annex 2 and the information in the Trust Center serve this purpose. The Provider processes the data only as the Customer itself would be permitted to process it (Art. 9 revised FADP).
6 Confidentiality of the persons used
The Provider uses only persons who are bound to confidentiality or subject to an appropriate statutory duty of secrecy (Art. 28(3)(b) GDPR). The undertaking is given in text form before the activity begins, continues in force without time limit after the employment or engagement ends, and is evidenced on request. The persons used are trained in data protection.
7 Technical and organisational measures and the extent of the warranties
The Provider takes the measures required under Art. 32 GDPR and Art. 8 revised FADP; the details are set out in Annex 2. It may adapt them to the state of the art without falling below the agreed level of protection. The following is warranted: transmissions over public networks between the user device and the service, and between the components of the service, are encrypted according to the state of the art. At rest, encryption of the storage media is part of the server provisioning; encryption of individual records at application level beyond that is not warranted. Each customer receives its own stack (database, search index, file storage, configuration, network, inference key). The dividing line is this stack and not the physical machine; several customers may share a machine, with container images and an upstream reverse proxy being used in common. Subsequent interference with the log of administrator actions becomes apparent; technical immutability is not warranted. Where the identity of the person is passed through into a connected target system, the Provider’s logging ends at the system boundary, and the logging of the target system applies. Operation takes place in data centres certified to ISO 27001; that certification is held by Green, not by the Provider, and is not a technical measure of its own. The Provider holds no certification of its own today; no SOC 2 report is available. An egress proxy with an allow list, the highest isolation level of the code sandbox and automatic account provisioning via SCIM are not subject matter of this agreement and are not warranted.
8 Subprocessors
The Provider engages subprocessors only with the Customer’s prior authorisation; for the bodies set out in the list of subprocessors the Customer grants that authorisation upon conclusion of this agreement. The Provider announces a change 30 days in advance in text form, stating the name, legal entity, registered office, purpose and transfer basis; the Customer may object within 14 days of receipt on a data protection ground. If the Customer objects in time and with reasons, the parties shall seek a solution for 30 days. If none is reached, either party may terminate the affected part of the services with effect from the end of the current billing period; fees paid in advance are refunded pro rata for the period not used. The Customer has no further claims. The Provider imposes on each subprocessor in writing essentially the same obligations as this agreement imposes on it (Art. 28(4) GDPR). Where a subprocessor fails to fulfil its data protection obligations, the Provider remains liable to the Customer for that subprocessor’s conduct as for its own. Components that the Provider operates on its own infrastructure are not subprocessors; this applies to the self-hosted search service.
9 Place of processing, third countries and requests from authorities
Storage and operation take place in Switzerland, model inference in the EU or the EEA; the bodies used are set out in the list of subprocessors. Two exceptions are identified. Web search queries are forwarded to external search engines without user identity and may in doing so leave the EU, EEA and Swiss area; the statement that everything remains in Europe applies to storage and inference, not to the search query itself. An additional model provider outside Europe can be integrated. Where that is the case in the Customer’s instance, the EU warranty does not apply to that provider, and the transfer basis lies with the Customer as controller. For Switzerland there is an adequacy decision of the European Commission, and for the EEA States a basis under Art. 16 revised FADP; where the registered office is outside that area, the transfer is based on the European Commission’s standard contractual clauses together with an assessment of the legal situation in the destination country, and in addition on a separate Swiss basis. Without an instruction from the Customer, the Provider transfers data only where it is legally obliged to do so; in the event of an order to hand over data it reviews the lawfulness of that order, exhausts the legal remedies that can reasonably be expected, limits disclosure to what is legally required and notifies the Customer as early as this is permitted.
10 No training with Customer data
The Provider does not use Customer data for the training or improvement of models and does not pass it on for that purpose. It sets the access channels it operates so that content is not retained at the gateway and not used for training, in so far as the gateway offers this setting. According to the gateway, usage metadata such as timestamps and token counts are retained there for up to twelve months. Where the Customer integrates a model endpoint of its own, that endpoint’s terms apply; the Provider’s undertaking does not extend to that endpoint.
11 Assistance to the Customer and its remuneration
The Provider assists the Customer, in so far as possible and taking into account the nature of the processing, in complying with requests from data subjects (Art. 28(3)(e) GDPR). For that purpose the service provides data export and per-person deletion in the admin panel, including full deletion; the Customer carries out these operations itself. Where a data subject approaches the Provider directly, the Provider forwards the request to the Customer and informs the data subject of this. Where the functions of the service are not sufficient in an individual case, the Provider assists in so far as possible against remuneration on a time and materials basis. In relation to a data protection impact assessment and any prior consultation (Art. 35 and 36 GDPR, Art. 22 and 23 revised FADP), it assists taking into account the information available to it and makes available the information in its possession, as a rule: processing operations and data flows, subprocessors and third country connections, technical and organisational measures, retention and deletion. Assistance of the usual extent is covered by the fee; where the effort clearly exceeds that measure, the Provider charges for it at the agreed rates, after prior notification of the expected effort. If the Customer maintains its request, the remuneration is deemed agreed.
12 Notification of breaches
The Provider notifies the Customer of a personal data breach in text form to the body designated by the Customer, without delay and at the latest within 48 hours after the Provider has obtained confirmed knowledge of a breach within the meaning of Art. 4(12) GDPR. The notification contains the information referred to in Art. 33(3) GDPR in so far as it is available to the Provider; it is supplemented on an ongoing basis. The notification is not an acknowledgement of a breach of duty. Notification to the competent supervisory authority in the EU (Art. 33 GDPR), notification to the EDÖB (Art. 24 revised FADP, which applies a higher risk threshold and sets no fixed deadline) and communication to the data subjects are incumbent on the Customer.
13 Demonstration, review, authorities and record
The Provider makes available to the Customer the information necessary to demonstrate compliance with Art. 28 GDPR and allows for reviews (Art. 28(3)(h) GDPR); it provides information in text form within 30 days. The Customer may carry out one audit per calendar year itself or have it carried out by an auditor, with 30 days’ prior notice and during ordinary business hours. Following a notifiable incident affecting this Customer’s data, or upon order of a supervisory authority, an unscheduled audit is permissible. The auditor is bound to secrecy and may not be a competitor of the Provider. Certificates, audit reports and attestations replace an on-site inspection in so far as they cover the purpose of the review; they do not exclude an inspection where open points remain. In relation to subprocessors, the Provider secures these rights for the Customer by contract or may, at its option, carry out the review on the Customer’s behalf. The Customer bears the costs of the review. The Customer remunerates the Provider’s effort for preparation, attendance and follow-up at the agreed rates. Where the occasion for the review is a breach of duty for which the Provider is responsible, it bears its own effort. On request, the Provider cooperates with the EDÖB and with the competent supervisory authority; the point of contact is info@herr-informatik.ch. It maintains a record of the categories of processing activities (Art. 30(2) GDPR, Art. 12 revised FADP) and makes available, on request, the entries relating to the Customer. In so far as it is subject to the obligation under Art. 27 GDPR, it designates a representative in the Union and identifies that representative in its legal notice.
14 Retention, return and deletion
This agreement begins and ends with the main contract; its obligations continue in force until return and deletion are completed, and the confidentiality obligations without time limit. The Customer sets the retention period in the admin panel; setting and changing that period counts as an instruction. No period is set by default: without a period set, conversations remain stored until users or the administration delete them; where a period is set, expired conversations are removed together with their messages, shared links and search index entries. Billing data is not covered by that period. After the agreement ends, the Customer chooses between return and deletion (Art. 28(3)(g) GDPR). If the Customer gives no notice by the end of the term, the Provider deletes. An export can be requested up to 30 days after the agreement ends, in a common, machine-readable format chosen by the Provider; in the standard scope it is free of charge, further preparation on a time and materials basis. Data in backup copies is not deleted individually; it expires with the respective backup cycle, at the latest within six months of the end of the agreement. Until then it remains blocked and is processed exclusively for recovery in an emergency. Excepted from deletion are the audit and access logs, the billing data and data subject to a statutory retention obligation; these are blocked and deleted once the obligation expires. On request, the Provider confirms the deletion in text form.
15 Liability
For damage arising from the processing of personal data, the mandatory statutory provisions take precedence, in particular Art. 82 GDPR. In all other respects, clause 10 of the General Terms and Conditions applies. The Provider’s liability under and in connection with this agreement is limited, per damaging event and in aggregate per contract year, to the fee that the Customer paid in the twelve months before the event giving rise to the damage. The limitation does not apply to intent and gross negligence, nor where a limitation is not legally permissible. The Provider bears fines and sanctions imposed on the Customer only to the extent of its share of responsibility under Art. 82(5) GDPR. The Provider is not liable for damage arising from the Customer’s instructions, from its configuration, from model endpoints integrated by it or from content that it has introduced contrary to section 3; the Customer shall indemnify the Provider accordingly.
16 Applicable law, place of jurisdiction and language versions
Swiss law applies, to the exclusion of its conflict of laws rules. The exclusive place of jurisdiction is Windisch, Canton of Aargau, in so far as legally permissible. The mandatory places of jurisdiction of data subjects, in particular under the Lugano Convention, the competence of the supervisory authorities and the direct applicability of the GDPR are reserved. This agreement exists in five languages; the German version prevails.
17 Final provisions
Amendments and supplements require text form and the consent of both parties. Excepted from this are the updating of the list of subprocessors in accordance with the procedure agreed for that purpose and the further development of the technical and organisational measures within the limits of the prohibition on deterioration. As of: August 2026, version 1.0.
A1 Annex 1: description of the processing
Purposes: operation of the chat and assistance function, forwarding of inputs to the inference provider in order to generate responses, web search with source references, calls to connected systems via the MCP gateway and via direct connections, generation of files, searchability via a search index, automated storage of memory entries, logging of use and administration, data backup, fault resolution and support, billing. Operations: collection, recording, organisation, storage, adaptation, retrieval, consultation, use, disclosure by transmission to subprocessors, combination, restriction, erasure and destruction. Categories of data: user inputs including attachments and the responses generated, account and profile data, usage metadata (timestamps, model selection, token counts), billing data, audit and access logs including the logs of administrator actions, content read from connected systems at the users’ request (for instance ERP, SharePoint, file storage), web search queries, and memory entries that the service derives from conversations and stores without a separate action by the users. Data subjects: the Customer’s employees and its auxiliary personnel, business contacts, the Customer’s customers, suppliers and their employees, applicants, and all other persons mentioned in texts, in attachments or in content of connected systems. Within the scope of this agreement the Provider takes no automated decisions within the meaning of Art. 22 GDPR; whether outputs of the service are used for such decisions is determined by the Customer alone.
A2 Annex 2: technical and organisational measures
Access: access to the Customer’s systems is granted only to individually named persons of the Provider, in so far as this is necessary for operation, maintenance, fault resolution or support; on request the Provider names this group. Every administrative access is logged. Access to user content takes place only at the Customer’s request or in order to resolve a specific fault, as a rule under the four eyes principle; where an emergency requires immediate intervention, this may be departed from, which is documented afterwards. Logs: the log of administrator actions is chained, each entry carries a checksum over the preceding one, and a built-in check reports a broken chain; the Customer can inspect these logs and export them as CSV. Level of protection: pseudonymisation in so far as compatible with the purpose; encryption of the transmission and of the storage media; confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience of the systems; rapid restoration after an incident; regular review of effectiveness; separation of customers in accordance with section 7; regular backup copies. This annex applies in its respective dated version.
Note: this text does not constitute legal advice. It becomes binding upon signature by both parties or upon acceptance within the framework of the main contract.

# Privacy Policy

URL: https://eucowork.ai/en/datenschutz

EU Cowork AI
Pricing Docs Blog
EN
Self-host for free Get started
Privacy
How we handle personal data under revDSG (Switzerland) and GDPR. Short, because we collect little.
Telemetry off by default
1 Controller
Herr Informatik GmbH, Klosterzelgstrasse 1a, 5210 Windisch, Switzerland (provider of EU Cowork AI). Contact: info@herr-informatik.ch.
2 What data we process
Account and billing data plus the content you actively enter into the service. No advertising trackers, no sharing with ad networks.
3 No training on your data
Your content is never used to train models. No-training is contractually assured.
4 Telemetry
Disabled by default. Optional, aggregated usage metrics only after explicit opt-in.
5 Place of processing
Operated in Switzerland (Green, Lupfig); model inference EU-processed via EuRouter. When self-hosting, data stays entirely with you.
6 Retention
Data is stored only as long as needed for the service or required by law. Deletion on request.
7 Appointment booking
For appointment booking we use Microsoft Bookings, a service of Microsoft Corporation. When you book an appointment, Microsoft processes the data you provide (name, email address, chosen slot, optional details) under the terms of Microsoft. Booking is voluntary; all content on this website is accessible without it.
8 Your rights
Access, rectification, erasure, restriction and data portability. Requests to privacy@eu-cowork.example.
Note: this privacy statement is a preview. The binding version with full company details will be published shortly and replaces placeholders.

# Terms and Conditions

As of: July 2026
General Terms & Conditions
These General Terms and Conditions (the “GTC”) govern the contractual relationship between Herr Informatik GmbH (“HERR INFORMATIK”, Windisch) and the customer regarding use of the EU Cowork AI service. Based on the terms of Herr Informatik GmbH.
1 Scope
These GTC apply to all contracts for the use of EU Cowork AI between HERR INFORMATIK and the customer. Deviating terms of the customer apply only where HERR INFORMATIK expressly agrees to them in writing.
2 Subject & services
HERR INFORMATIK provides EU Cowork AI as a Swiss-hosted service or enables self-hosting under the MIT license. Model access is EU-processed via EuRouter. Scope and features follow the chosen edition (Starter/Pro/Max) and the product description.
3 Conclusion & registration
The contract is concluded upon registration or order and its confirmation by HERR INFORMATIK. The customer ensures that the data provided is complete and correct.
4 Prices, model credit & payment
Prices are per person and month, excluding VAT. Each edition includes a model credit that is available to the organisation as a shared pool. When the credit is used up, a soft block takes effect: further requests are refused until the customer tops up the credit or expressly enables a cheaper fallback model in the administration. Without one of these releases, no additional charge arises. Invoicing is periodic and in advance.
5 Customer obligations
The customer uses the service lawfully, keeps access credentials confidential and refrains from unlawful, infringing or abusive content and actions. The customer is responsible for the content it enters and for compliance with applicable regulations.
6 Availability & support
HERR INFORMATIK provides the service with reasonable care and strives for high availability. Maintenance, security and update windows may cause temporary interruptions. A specific availability (SLA) applies only under a separate agreement.
7 Data protection & security
Processing of personal data follows revDSG and GDPR; details are set out in the privacy statement and the Data Processing Agreement (DPA). Customer data is not used to train models; telemetry is off by default. Operated in ISO 27001-certified data centres by Green (Lupfig).
8 Open source & intellectual property
The self-hostable software is provided under the MIT license, whose terms apply to that use. Trademarks, names, design and other marks of EU Cowork AI and HERR INFORMATIK remain protected and are not transferred by the MIT license.
9 Backups & cooperation
Within the statutory framework, the customer is responsible for backing up its data and adequately tests business-critical processes before productive use. HERR INFORMATIK assists to the agreed extent.
10 Liability
HERR INFORMATIK is liable under the Swiss Code of Obligations (OR). Liability for slight negligence as well as for indirect damages, consequential damages, data loss and lost profit is excluded to the maximum extent permitted by law. Mandatory statutory liability is reserved.
11 Term & termination
The contract runs according to the chosen billing period (monthly or annual) and may be terminated at its end. After the contract ends, customer data is exported on request and then deleted, unless a statutory retention obligation applies.
12 Changes to the GTC
HERR INFORMATIK may amend these GTC. Changes are communicated to the customer in advance in a suitable form and are deemed accepted unless the customer objects within the notified period.
13 Governing law & jurisdiction
Swiss law applies exclusively, excluding conflict-of-law rules and the UN Convention on Contracts for the International Sale of Goods. The exclusive place of jurisdiction is the registered seat of HERR INFORMATIK in Windisch (Canton of Aargau), to the extent permitted by law.
Note: these GTC are based on Herr Informatik GmbH and do not constitute legal advice.
